cards.a: dV/dr is the rate of change of volume with respect to the radius, in cm³ per cm; it depends only on the geometry: dV/dr = 4πr². dV/dt is the rate of change of volume with respect to time, in cm³ per second; it depends on how fast air is pumped in. The chain rule links them: dV/dt = (dV/dr)(dr/dt).
cards.h: → two rates, two input variables, one chain-rule link
cards.n: Calling 4πr² 'how fast the balloon inflates' is the trap: it is per centimeter of radius, not per second.

cards.q: Calculate the average rate of change of P(t) = 200 + 30t − t² on 0 ≤ t ≤ 10 and the value of P'(10), where P(t) is the number of fish in a pond t weeks after stocking. Interpret each with units.
cards.a: Average rate = (P(10) − P(0))/(10 − 0) = (400 − 200)/10 = 20 fish per week: over the first 10 weeks the population grew by 20 fish per week on average. P'(t) = 30 − 2t, so P'(10) = 10: at the instant t = 10 weeks the population is increasing at 10 fish per week. The average describes the interval; the derivative describes one instant.
cards.h: → difference quotient, derivative, two sentences
cards.n: Calling 20 fish per week 'the rate at t = 10' mixes the two ideas: an average rate needs its interval, an instantaneous rate its instant.

cards.q: Interpret H'(12) = 0 in context, where H(t) is the height, in feet, of a hot-air balloon t minutes after launch.
cards.a: At t = 12 minutes the balloon's height is changing at 0 feet per minute: at that instant it is neither rising nor falling. By itself this does not say the balloon is at its highest point or that it stays at that height; that depends on whether H' changes sign at t = 12.
cards.h: → one sentence, then what it does not say
cards.n: 'The balloon is at its maximum height' claims more than H'(12) = 0 shows; an extremum needs a sign change of H′ (Unit 5).

cards.q: Explain why the units of f'(x) are the units of f divided by the units of x.
cards.a: f'(x) is the limit of difference quotients [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. The numerator is a change in f, measured in f's units; the denominator h is a change in x, measured in x's units. Taking a limit does not change units, so f'(x) is in units of f per unit of x.
cards.h: → f′ is a limit of Δf/Δx → Δf in f's units, Δx in x's units → the limit keeps the ratio
cards.n: 'Because that is the rule' earns nothing; the reason is the difference quotient Δf/Δx that defines the derivative.
o: Near x, f(x + h) − f(x) ≈ f'(x)·h, so f'(x) must convert units of x into units of f: units of f per unit of x.
Every secant slope is rise over run, with the rise in f's units and the run in x's units; the tangent slope is their limit and keeps those units.

w.a: The units of f'(x) are the same as the units of f because the derivative is just another function.
w.why: a derivative is a rate, so its units are a ratio

w.a: f'(x) is in units of x per unit of f because you divide by f.
w.why: the ratio is upside down: the change in f is on top

w.a: The units of a derivative are always units per second.
w.why: the input need not be time

cards.q: Explain why h'(3) = 5, where h(t) is a rocket's height in meters at t seconds, does not guarantee that the rocket rises exactly 5 meters between t = 3 and t = 4.
cards.a: h'(3) = 5 m/s is the rate at the instant t = 3 only. Between t = 3 and t = 4 the velocity h'(t) can change, so the rise h(4) − h(3) is exactly 5 meters only if h' stays 5 the whole second; otherwise 5 meters is just the tangent-line estimate of the rise.
cards.h: → h′(3) is a rate at one instant → the rate changes during the second → 5 m is only an approximation
cards.n: 'It rises 5 meters in the next second' treats an instantaneous rate as the average rate over [3, 4].
o: The rise over [3, 4] equals the average velocity on [3, 4] times 1 second, and that average need not equal h'(3).
If the rocket is speeding up (h'' > 0) it rises more than 5 meters, and if slowing down, less; 5 meters is exact only for constant velocity.

w.a: It rises exactly 5 meters because the velocity at t = 3 is 5 meters per second.
w.why: treats an instant's rate as constant over the interval

w.a: h'(3) = 5 means the rocket is 5 meters high at t = 3.
w.why: confuses the rate with the height

w.a: It rises 5 meters every second because the derivative is 5.
w.why: the derivative is 5 only at t = 3

cards.q: Explain why P'(t) > 0 together with P''(t) < 0 does not mean the population P is decreasing.
cards.a: The sign of P' decides whether P increases, and P'(t) > 0, so the population is increasing. P''(t) < 0 says only that P' is decreasing: the population grows more and more slowly. P would be decreasing only if P'(t) < 0.
cards.h: → P′ > 0 → P increasing → P″ < 0 only shrinks P′ → growth slows, P still rises
cards.n: 'The second derivative is negative, so the population decreases' reads P″ as if it were P′.
o: P'' is the rate of change of the growth rate, so a negative P'' means the growth rate is shrinking while still positive.
Graphically, P is rising and concave down: the curve goes up while its slope flattens.

w.a: The population is decreasing because the second derivative is negative.
w.why: P″ describes the rate, not the population

w.a: The population is decreasing at a decreasing rate.
w.why: P is increasing, since P′ > 0

w.a: P' > 0 and P'' < 0 cancel out, so the population stays the same.
w.why: signs of different derivatives do not cancel

cards.q: Explain why 'the velocity of the savings is 300' does not earn the interpretation point for S'(5) = 300, where S(t) is the amount in a savings account, in dollars, t years after it is opened.
cards.a: It uses a motion word for money and gives no units and no instant. A correct interpretation reads: at t = 5 years, the amount in the account is increasing at a rate of 300 dollars per year. It must name the quantity, the instant, the direction, and dollars per year.
cards.h: → wrong context word + no units + no instant → 'increasing at 300 dollars per year at t = 5'
cards.n: The CED warns against saying 'velocity' for a rate such as income: the structure is the same as motion, but the words and units must fit the context.
o: Velocity is the rate of change of position; S is money, so the correct phrase is 'the rate of change of the amount in the account'.
Without 'dollars per year' and 't = 5', the sentence cannot be told apart from a statement about S(5) or about S' at some other time.

w.a: The savings account has 300 dollars after 5 years.
w.why: that is S(5), an amount, not a rate

w.a: The savings are going up by 300.
w.why: no units per year and no instant named

w.a: The account moves at 300 dollars per year.
w.why: a motion verb replaces the quantity and the instant is missing

cards.q: Explain why R'(t) can be negative even though R(t), the number of gallons of water in a tank, is never negative.
cards.a: R'(t) measures how R is changing, not how much water is present. When water drains, R is decreasing, so its rate of change is negative, while the amount R(t) still remaining is a positive number of gallons. The sign of R' reports the direction of change; R itself reports the amount.
cards.h: → R′ measures change, not amount → draining means R decreasing → R′ < 0 while R > 0
cards.n: 'R′ < 0 means the tank holds a negative amount' is the trap; the sign of a derivative is about the direction of change.
o: A graph of R can lie above the t-axis (R > 0) while sloping downward (R' < 0).
R'(t) is a limit of [R(t + h) − R(t)]/h, and that difference is negative whenever the later amount is smaller, however large both amounts are.

w.a: A negative R'(t) would mean a negative amount of water, which is impossible, so R' must be positive.
w.why: confuses the rate with the amount

w.a: R'(t) is negative only when the tank is empty.
w.why: an empty tank has R = 0; draining gives R′ < 0

w.a: Derivatives of real quantities are always positive.
w.why: a decreasing quantity has a negative derivative

cards.q: Explain why C'(50) = 3.2, where C(x) is the cost in dollars of producing x widgets, is a reasonable estimate of the cost of producing the 51st widget.
cards.a: The 51st widget costs C(51) − C(50). Since C is differentiable, over the one-widget step from 50 to 51 its rate stays close to C'(50), so C(51) − C(50) ≈ C'(50)·1 = 3.2 dollars. It is an estimate, not the exact cost, because C' can change between 50 and 51.
cards.h: → 51st costs C(51) − C(50) → rate ≈ C′(50) over a 1-unit step → ≈ 3.2 × 1 dollars
cards.n: Calling 3.20 dollars the exact cost of the 51st widget drops the approximation; the derivative gives an estimate unless C′ is constant.
o: The tangent line at x = 50 gives C(51) ≈ C(50) + C'(50)(51 − 50), so the added cost is about C'(50) = 3.2 dollars.
C'(50) is the limit of [C(50 + h) − C(50)]/h as h → 0; the quotient with h = 1 is close to that limit when C is nearly linear near 50.

w.a: The 51st widget costs exactly 3.20 dollars because C'(50) = 3.2.
w.why: the derivative gives an approximation, not an exact difference

w.a: C'(50) = 3.2 means the first 50 widgets cost 3.20 dollars in total.
w.why: that would be C(50), an amount

w.a: Every widget costs 3.20 dollars to make.
w.why: the rate applies near x = 50 only

cards.q: Define the relationship among position, velocity, and acceleration for straight-line motion.
cards.a: If s(t) is the position of a particle on a line at time t, its velocity is v(t) = s'(t) and its acceleration is a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t); its speed is |v(t)|. The units follow: position in meters gives velocity in m/s and acceleration in m/s².
cards.h: → s, then v = s′, then a = v′ = s″
cards.n: Writing a(t) = s'(t) or v(t) = a'(t) scrambles the chain; each derivative moves one step: position → velocity → acceleration.

cards.q: Contrast velocity and speed.
cards.a: Velocity v(t) is signed: its sign gives the direction of motion (positive: right or up; negative: left or down) and its size gives the rate. Speed is |v(t)|, the size alone, never negative. So v(2) = −3 m/s and v(5) = 3 m/s are opposite directions but the same speed, 3 m/s.
cards.h: → signed vs absolute value, one example
cards.n: 'Speed is the derivative of velocity' is wrong: that is acceleration. Speed is |v|, not another derivative.

cards.q: State the rule for when the speed of a particle is increasing.
cards.a: The speed is increasing at time t when v(t) and a(t) have the same sign (both positive or both negative), and decreasing when they have opposite signs. The justification states both signs, for example: v(2) < 0 and a(2) < 0, so the speed is increasing at t = 2.
cards.h: → sign of v against sign of a
cards.n: 'a > 0, so the particle speeds up' earns nothing: a positive acceleration slows a particle that is moving left (v < 0).

cards.q: Identify the condition under which a particle changes direction.
cards.a: A particle changes direction at t = c when v(t) changes sign at c (from positive to negative or from negative to positive). That can happen only where v(c) = 0 or v is undefined, but a zero of v with no sign change is not a change of direction.
cards.h: → v changes sign, not merely v = 0
cards.n: v(t) = (t − 2)² has v(2) = 0 but never goes negative, so the particle only pauses at t = 2; 'v = 0' alone is not the justification.

cards.q: Identify what it means for a particle to be at rest, and what it does not imply.
cards.a: At rest at time t means v(t) = 0: speed 0 at that instant. It does not imply a(t) = 0, and it does not mean the particle stays put or turns around. A ball thrown upward has v = 0 at the top while a = −9.8 m/s², and it reverses there only because v changes sign.
cards.h: → v = 0 at an instant, plus two non-consequences
cards.n: 'At rest means the acceleration is zero' is the trap; rest is about v only, and only at an instant unless v = 0 on a whole interval.

cards.q: Explain how to find the times when a particle is moving left or downward.
cards.a: Solve v(t) < 0 on the given time domain: find where v(t) = 0 or is undefined, test the sign of v on each resulting interval, and report the intervals of time on which v is negative. The answer is a set of times (such as 1 < t < 3), not a set of positions.
cards.h: → zeros of v, sign test, report time intervals
cards.n: Solving s(t) < 0 answers a different question: a particle to the left of the origin can be moving right.

cards.q: Explain how to describe a particle's motion from the graph of v(t).
cards.a: Above the t-axis the particle moves right (or up); below it, left (or down); a crossing of the axis is a change of direction. The slope of the v graph is the acceleration. Speed is the distance of the graph from the axis, so the particle speeds up where the graph moves away from the axis and slows down where it moves toward it.
cards.h: → sign, crossings, slope, distance from the axis
cards.n: Reading the height of the v graph as position is the trap; position comes from the accumulated area under v (Unit 6), not from the height.

cards.q: A particle has position $s(t)=t^{3}-6t^{2}+9t$. Find all times on $t \ge 0$ when the particle is at rest.
cards.a: t = 1 and t = 3. v(t) = s'(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3), and v(t) = 0 exactly when t = 1 or t = 3, both in t ≥ 0.
cards.h: → differentiate, factor, set v = 0
cards.n: Setting s(t) = 0 (giving t = 0 and t = 3) finds when the particle is at the origin, not when it is at rest.

cards.q: A particle has velocity $v(t) = t^{2}-5t+4$ and acceleration a(t) = 2t−5. Decide whether the particle is speeding up or slowing down at t = 0, and justify.
cards.a: Slowing down. v(0) = 4 > 0 and a(0) = −5 < 0: velocity and acceleration have opposite signs at t = 0, so the speed is decreasing.
cards.h: → evaluate v and a, compare signs
cards.n: 'a(0) < 0, so it slows down' is incomplete: the conclusion needs the sign of v(0) as well, stated.

cards.q: v(t) is a line decreasing from v(0)=6 to v(3)=-3, then constant at -3 until t=5. Identify the time interval on which the particle is speeding up.
cards.a: 2 < t < 3. The line has slope −3, so a(t) = −3 on (0, 3), and v crosses zero at t = 2. On (2, 3), v < 0 and a < 0 share a sign, so the particle speeds up. On (0, 2), v > 0 and a < 0: slowing down. On (3, 5), a = 0 and the speed stays 3.
cards.h: → zero of v, sign of the slope, compare on each piece
cards.n: Answering (0, 3) because the slope is negative there ignores the sign of v: on (0, 2) the particle moves right while slowing down.

cards.q: A particle has position $s(t) = -t^{3}+6t^{2}-9t+2$. Determine the time interval(s) on $t \ge 0$ during which the particle is moving to the left.
cards.a: 0 ≤ t < 1 and t > 3. v(t) = s'(t) = −3t² + 12t − 9 = −3(t − 1)(t − 3). Test values: v(0) = −9 < 0, v(2) = 3 > 0, v(4) = −9 < 0. So v < 0, and the particle moves left, on [0, 1) and on (3, ∞).
cards.h: → factor v, test a value in each interval
cards.n: Solving s(t) < 0 finds where the particle is left of the origin, not where it moves left; the sign of v decides the direction.

cards.q: Contrast what a positive value of v(t) tells you about a particle's motion with what a positive value of a(t) tells you.
cards.a: v(t) > 0 means the particle is moving in the positive direction (right or up) at time t. a(t) > 0 means the velocity is increasing at time t; that speeds the particle up only if v(t) > 0 too, and slows it down if v(t) < 0.
cards.h: → direction vs change in velocity
cards.n: Equating a > 0 with 'speeding up' ignores direction: a particle moving left with a > 0 is slowing down.

cards.q: A particle has velocity $v(t) = t^{2}-6t+8$. Identify the time(s) at which the particle changes direction.
cards.a: t = 2 and t = 4. v(t) = (t − 2)(t − 4) is positive for t < 2, negative for 2 < t < 4, and positive for t > 4, so v changes sign at t = 2 and at t = 4.
cards.h: → factor v, confirm each sign change
cards.n: Listing the zeros of v without the sign change loses the justification; a double root such as (t − 3)² gives v = 0 with no turn.

cards.q:
Calculate each of the following for a particle moving along the x-axis with position x(t) = t³ − 9t² + 24t meters at t seconds.
1. v(1)
2. a(1)
3. the speed at t = 1
4. the direction of motion at t = 1
5. whether the speed is increasing or decreasing at t = 1
6. v(3.5) and a(3.5)
7. the direction of motion at t = 3.5, and whether the speed is increasing or decreasing then
8. the average velocity over 0 ≤ t ≤ 4
cards.a:
v(t) = 3t² − 18t + 24 and a(t) = 6t − 18.
1 → v(1) = 9 m/s
2 → a(1) = −12 m/s²
3 → |v(1)| = 9 m/s
4 → right, since v(1) > 0
5 → decreasing, since v(1) > 0 and a(1) < 0 have opposite signs
6 → v(3.5) = −2.25 m/s and a(3.5) = 3 m/s²
7 → left, since v(3.5) < 0; speed decreasing, since v < 0 and a > 0 have opposite signs
8 → [x(4) − x(0)]/(4 − 0) = (16 − 0)/4 = 4 m/s
cards.h: → v and a formulas first, then one answer per line
cards.n: At t = 3.5 a positive acceleration slows the particle because it is moving left; item 8 is an average rate, x(4) − x(0) over 4, not v(4).

cards.q: Calculate the displacement and the total distance traveled on 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 by a particle whose position is s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t feet at t seconds.
cards.a: Displacement 4 ft; total distance 12 ft. v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) changes sign at t = 1 and t = 3, so split there: s(0) = 0, s(1) = 4, s(3) = 0, s(4) = 4. Displacement = s(4) − s(0) = 4 ft. Distance = |4 − 0| + |0 − 4| + |4 − 0| = 12 ft.
cards.h: → turning times, positions there, add the legs
cards.n: |s(4) − s(0)| = 4 ft is only the displacement; the particle reverses twice, so the distance adds each leg between turning points.

cards.q: Find the maximum height and the velocity at impact of a ball whose height is h(t) = −16t² + 64t + 80 feet at t seconds.
cards.a: Maximum height 144 ft; impact velocity −96 ft/s. v(t) = −32t + 64 is positive for t < 2 and negative for t > 2, so the height peaks at t = 2: h(2) = 144 ft. The ball lands when h(t) = −16(t − 5)(t + 1) = 0, so t = 5, and v(5) = −96 ft/s: moving down at 96 ft/s.
cards.h: → v = 0 for the peak; h = 0 for impact, then v there
cards.n: Reporting t = 2 (a time) instead of h(2), or +96 for the velocity, loses the point: a downward velocity is negative.

cards.q: Explain why a particle with velocity v(t) = (t − 2)² does not change direction at t = 2.
cards.a: v(2) = 0, but (t − 2)² > 0 for every t ≠ 2, so v is positive just before and just after t = 2. The velocity does not change sign, so the particle keeps moving in the positive direction; it only pauses for an instant at t = 2.
cards.h: → v(2) = 0 → v > 0 on both sides → no sign change → no change of direction
cards.n: 'v(2) = 0, so it turns around' is the trap: a change of direction needs v to change sign.
o: Direction is the sign of v, and that sign is + on both sides of t = 2.
A position function is s(t) = (t − 2)³/3 + C, which is increasing on both sides of t = 2, so the particle never moves back.

w.a: The particle changes direction at t = 2 because its velocity is zero there.
w.why: zero velocity without a sign change is only a pause

w.a: It changes direction at t = 2 because a(2) = 0.
w.why: acceleration does not decide direction

w.a: It stops for good at t = 2.
w.why: v is positive right after t = 2, so it keeps moving

cards.q: Explain why a particle with v(3) = −4 m/s and a(3) = −2 m/s² is speeding up at t = 3.
cards.a: Speed is |v|. At t = 3 the velocity is negative and the acceleration is also negative, so the velocity is becoming more negative and its absolute value, the speed, is increasing. Velocity and acceleration with the same sign means speeding up.
cards.h: → v < 0 and a < 0 → v grows more negative → |v| grows → speeding up
cards.n: 'a(3) < 0, so it slows down' ignores direction: with v and a both negative, the particle moves left faster and faster.
o: The acceleration points the same way as the motion (both left), so it pushes the particle faster in that direction.
The rate of change of speed is a·v/|v| = (−2)(−4)/4 = 2 m/s², which is positive.

w.a: The particle is slowing down because its acceleration is negative.
w.why: a < 0 speeds up a particle that is moving left

w.a: It is slowing down because its velocity is negative.
w.why: the sign of v alone gives direction, not the change in speed

w.a: It is speeding up because its velocity is decreasing.
w.why: a decreasing velocity also fits slowing down when v > 0

cards.q: Explain why a particle with position x(2) = −3 and velocity v(2) = 4 is moving toward the origin at t = 2.
cards.a: At t = 2 the particle is at x = −3, left of the origin, and v(2) = 4 > 0 means it is moving right, toward 0. So its distance from the origin is decreasing at t = 2: position and velocity with opposite signs means moving toward the origin.
cards.h: → x < 0 (left of the origin) → v > 0 (moving right) → heading toward 0
cards.n: 'v > 0, so it moves away from the origin' ignores where the particle is; motion relative to the origin needs the signs of both x and v.
o: The distance from the origin is |x(t)|; with x(2) < 0 its derivative is −v(2) = −4 < 0, so the distance is shrinking.
The product x(2)·v(2) = −12 is negative, which means the particle is moving toward the origin.

w.a: The particle is moving away from the origin because its velocity is positive.
w.why: moving right from x = −3 is moving toward 0

w.a: It is moving toward the origin because its position is negative.
w.why: position alone gives location, not direction

w.a: It is at rest because x and v have opposite signs.
w.why: at rest means v = 0

cards.q: Explain why the total distance traveled by the particle with position s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t on 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 is not |s(4) − s(0)|.
cards.a: |s(4) − s(0)| = 4 ft counts only the net change in position. v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) changes sign at t = 1 and t = 3, so the particle goes right, then left, then right; the backward leg cancels in the net change but still adds to the distance. The legs give 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 ft.
cards.h: → v changes sign → particle reverses → legs cancel in s(4) − s(0) → distance adds them
cards.n: Using |s(4) − s(0)| when the particle reverses reports displacement, not distance; locate the sign changes of v first.
o: Distance equals |displacement| only when v keeps one sign on the interval, and here v changes sign twice.
Distance is |s(1) − s(0)| + |s(3) − s(1)| + |s(4) − s(3)|, one term for each stretch of constant direction.

w.a: The total distance is |s(4) − s(0)| = 4 feet because that is how far the particle ends up from where it started.
w.why: that is displacement; reversals are ignored

w.a: The distance is s(4) + s(0) = 4 feet.
w.why: adding endpoint positions does not measure the path

w.a: The total distance is 0 because s(3) = s(0).
w.why: returning to the start cancels displacement, not distance

cards.q: Explain why a particle's speed is decreasing on an interval where its velocity graph is below the t-axis and rising toward it.
cards.a: Below the axis v < 0, and a rising graph means v is increasing, so a > 0. With v and a of opposite signs the speed |v| decreases. Graphically, the graph is getting closer to the axis, so its distance from the axis, the speed, shrinks.
cards.h: → below axis: v < 0 → rising: a > 0 → opposite signs → speed decreasing
cards.n: 'The velocity is increasing, so the particle speeds up' is the trap: rising toward zero from below is slowing down.
o: Speed is the distance of the v graph from the t-axis, and a graph moving toward the axis has a shrinking speed.
For example, v going from −5 to −2 is an increase in velocity of 3 but a drop in speed from 5 to 2.

w.a: The particle speeds up because the velocity graph is increasing.
w.why: increasing velocity with v < 0 means slowing down

w.a: The speed decreases because the velocity is negative.
w.why: v < 0 alone gives direction only

w.a: The particle is moving right because the graph is rising.
w.why: direction is the sign of v, which is negative

cards.q: Explain why a ball with height h(t) = −16t² + 64t + 80 feet at t seconds reaches its maximum height at t = 2.
cards.a: v(t) = h'(t) = −32t + 64 is positive for t < 2 and negative for t > 2. The ball rises until t = 2 and falls afterward, so its height is greatest at t = 2, where v changes from positive to negative.
cards.h: → v = −32t + 64 → v > 0 before 2, v < 0 after → rises then falls → maximum at t = 2
cards.n: 'v(2) = 0, so it is a maximum' is incomplete; the reason is v changing from + to −, the First Derivative Test borrowed from Unit 5.
o: h is a downward-opening parabola (leading coefficient −16), so its vertex at t = −64/(2·(−16)) = 2 is its maximum.
h'(2) = 0 and h''(t) = −32 < 0, so the Second Derivative Test gives a relative maximum at t = 2, the only critical point.

w.a: The maximum height is at t = 2 because the velocity is zero there.
w.why: v = 0 alone does not show a maximum

w.a: The maximum is at t = 2 because the acceleration is zero there.
w.why: a = −32 is never zero

w.a: The height is greatest at t = 5 because that is when the ball lands.
w.why: at t = 5 the height is 0

cards.q: Describe how to answer 'how fast is the quantity changing' in a non-motion applied context.
cards.a: Differentiate the model with respect to its input, evaluate at the requested input, and answer in a sentence: the quantity, increasing or decreasing, the size of the rate, units of the quantity per unit of the input, and the instant. For P(t) people at t years, P'(4) = −120 reads: at t = 4 years the population is decreasing at 120 people per year.
cards.h: → differentiate, evaluate, sentence with units
cards.n: Reporting P(4), the amount, when the question asks 'how fast' is the trap; a rate question always wants the derivative, in units per unit of input.

cards.q: Describe how to estimate the rate at which a tabulated quantity is changing.
cards.a: Use a difference quotient built from the table values closest to the input on either side: f'(c) ≈ [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a) with a < c < b. Divide by the actual gap in the input, write the quotient itself as the work, give units of f per unit of input, and call the result an estimate.
cards.h: → bracketing values, quotient, units, 'approximately'
cards.n: Dividing by the number of rows instead of the input gap, or using values that do not bracket c, loses the point; a bare decimal with no quotient shows no work.

cards.q: A spherical snowball melts so that its volume is $V(t)=\frac{4}{3}\pi\left(10-t\right)^{3}$ cubic centimetres, where t is in minutes. Find the rate at which the volume is changing at t = 2 minutes, with units.
cards.a: V'(2) = −256π ≈ −804.2 cm³/min: at t = 2 minutes the volume is decreasing at 256π cubic centimeters per minute. By the chain rule, V'(t) = (4/3)π·3(10 − t)²·(−1) = −4π(10 − t)², so V'(2) = −4π(8)² = −256π.
cards.h: → chain rule, evaluate, sentence with units
cards.n: Dropping the inner derivative −1 gives +256π, a growing volume for a melting snowball; check that the sign fits the story.

cards.q: A tank's volume at t=0,2,4,6 min is V=100,84,72,65 liters. Estimate the rate the volume is changing at t=4 using the table, with units.
cards.a: V'(4) ≈ −4.75 liters per minute. The values at t = 2 and t = 6 bracket t = 4: [V(6) − V(2)]/(6 − 2) = (65 − 84)/4 = −19/4 = −4.75. So at t = 4 the volume is decreasing at about 4.75 liters per minute.
cards.h: → bracketing quotient, units, direction
cards.n: Dividing by 2, one table step, when the values used are 4 minutes apart is the standard slip; the denominator must match the t-values in the numerator.

cards.q: A tank's depth h(t) in cm is h(0)=2, h(3)=5, h(6)=11, h(9)=20. Decide whether the filling rate appears to be increasing or decreasing, and justify.
cards.a: The filling rate appears to be increasing. Over the equal 3-unit steps the depth rises by 3, 6 and 9 cm, so the average rates of change are 1, 2 and 3 cm per unit of time, each larger than the last. The table gives only average rates between the listed times, so this is what the data suggest, not a proof.
cards.h: → successive average rates, compare, hedge
cards.n: 'The depth is increasing, so the rate is increasing' confuses h with h′; rising values alone say nothing about whether the rate grows.

cards.q: The temperature of a metal rod is $T(x) = 60 - 0.5x^{2}$ degrees at distance x cm from one end, for $0 \le x \le 8$. Compute the rate of change of temperature at x = 3, with units.
cards.a: T'(3) = −3 degrees per cm. T'(x) = −x, so T'(3) = −3: at 3 cm from the end, the temperature is decreasing at 3 degrees per centimeter as the distance from that end increases.
cards.h: → derivative, evaluate, units per cm
cards.n: 'The rod cools at 3 degrees per minute' puts a time unit on a rate with respect to distance; the input is x in centimeters.

cards.q: A colony's population P(t) in thousands is P(0)=2, P(2)=3.5, P(4)=6.5, P(6)=13. Decide whether the growth rate appears to be increasing or decreasing, and justify.
cards.a: The growth rate appears to be increasing. The population rises by 1.5, 3 and 6.5 thousand over successive equal steps of 2 units of time, so the average rates of change are 0.75, 1.5 and 3.25 thousand per unit of time, each larger than the last. This is what the data suggest; the table gives no values in between.
cards.h: → successive average rates, compare, hedge
cards.n: Comparing the P values rather than their differences only shows that P is growing; whether the growth rate grows needs the changes between rows.

cards.q:
Translate each question into the calculus quantity it asks for, with its units.
1. At what rate is the amount of a drug M(t), in milligrams, in a patient's blood changing at t = 3 hours?
2. How fast is the area A of a circle changing with respect to its radius r, in cm, when r = 4?
3. What is the rate of change of the air temperature T(h), in °C, with respect to altitude h, in meters, at h = 1000?
4. What is the average rate of change of a population P(t), in people, over 2 ≤ t ≤ 6 years?
5. Is the price p(t), in dollars at t weeks, increasing at an increasing rate at t = 5?
6. Is the rate at which the water level L(t), in feet at t hours, is changing increasing at t = 1?
cards.a:
1 → M'(3), in mg per hour
2 → A'(4), that is dA/dr at r = 4, in cm² per cm (it equals 8π)
3 → T'(1000), in °C per meter
4 → [P(6) − P(2)]/(6 − 2), in people per year: a difference quotient, not a derivative
5 → the signs of p'(5) and p''(5): yes exactly when both are positive; p' in dollars per week, p'' in dollars per week per week
6 → the sign of L''(1), in feet per hour per hour: the rate is increasing if L''(1) > 0
cards.h: → one expression and its units per line
cards.n: Item 4 is the trap: an average rate over an interval is a difference quotient; item 6 asks whether L′ is changing, so it needs L″, not L′.

cards.q: Calculate W'(6), and determine whether the volume is increasing or decreasing at t = 6, where W(t) is the volume of water in a tank that water enters at E(t) = 30 + 4t liters per minute and leaves at D(t) = 10 + t² liters per minute, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8.
cards.a: W'(6) = 8 liters per minute, so the volume is increasing at t = 6. The rate of change of the volume is the rate in minus the rate out: W'(t) = E(t) − D(t), so W'(6) = (30 + 24) − (10 + 36) = 54 − 46 = 8 L/min > 0.
cards.h: → net rate = in − out, evaluate, sign
cards.n: Comparing E′ and D′, or noting only that water drains, answers the wrong question; the sign of E(6) − D(6) decides whether W rises.

cards.q: Find P'(500), where P(x) = R(x) − C(x) is the profit in dollars from making and selling x units, with revenue R(x) = 50x − 0.02x² dollars and cost C(x) = 2000 + 12x dollars. Interpret the value in context.
cards.a: P'(500) = 18 dollars per unit. P'(x) = R'(x) − C'(x) = (50 − 0.04x) − 12 = 38 − 0.04x, so P'(500) = 38 − 20 = 18. When 500 units have been made and sold, profit is increasing at 18 dollars per unit, so the 501st unit adds about 18 dollars of profit.
cards.h: → R′ − C′, evaluate, sentence with units
cards.n: Giving P(500) = 12,000 dollars, the profit itself, answers a different question; P′(500) is a rate in dollars per unit.

cards.q: Calculate D'(2), where D(t) = 4 + 2 sin(πt/6) is the depth of water, in feet, at a dock t hours after midnight, and interpret it. Then state whether the depth is rising or falling at t = 8.
cards.a: D'(2) = π/6 ≈ 0.524 foot per hour: at 2 a.m. the depth is increasing at about 0.524 foot per hour. By the chain rule D'(t) = 2cos(πt/6)·(π/6) = (π/3)cos(πt/6), so D'(2) = (π/3)(1/2) = π/6. At t = 8, D'(8) = (π/3)cos(4π/3) = −π/6 < 0, so the depth is falling at 8 a.m.
cards.h: → chain rule, evaluate twice, read the signs
cards.n: Dropping the inner derivative π/6 gives D′(2) = 1 foot per hour, almost double; a calculator check must be in radian mode.

cards.q: Determine whether the temperature is increasing or decreasing at t = 4, and whether its rate of change is increasing or decreasing then, where G(t) = 10 + 6t − 0.5t² is the temperature, in °C, of a greenhouse t hours after 6 a.m., for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10.
cards.a: The temperature is increasing, and its rate of change is decreasing. G'(t) = 6 − t, so G'(4) = 2 °C per hour > 0: the temperature is rising at 2 °C per hour. G''(t) = −1, so G''(4) = −1 °C per hour per hour < 0: the rate of increase is falling, so the temperature rises more and more slowly.
cards.h: → sign of G′(4), then sign of G″(4)
cards.n: Reading G″(4) < 0 as 'the temperature is falling' confuses the rate of the rate with the rate; the direction of G comes from G′ alone.

cards.q: Interpret m'(10) in context, with units, where m(x) = 3x + 0.1x² is the mass, in grams, of the first x centimeters of a thin rod, for 0 ≤ x ≤ 20.
cards.a: m'(10) = 5 grams per centimeter: at the point 10 cm from the end, the mass of the rod is increasing at 5 grams per centimeter of length, the rod's linear density there. m'(x) = 3 + 0.2x, so m'(10) = 3 + 2 = 5.
cards.h: → evaluate, then 'grams per centimeter at x = 10'
cards.n: 'The first 10 cm weigh 5 grams' reads the rate as an amount (m(10) = 40 g); the derivative is grams per cm at one point of the rod.

cards.q:
Estimate T'(9) using the table, and interpret the estimate. T(t) is the temperature, in °F, of a cake t minutes after it is taken out of the oven.
t (min) · T(t) (°F)
0 · 350
5 · 300
12 · 245
20 · 200
30 · 160
cards.a: T'(9) ≈ −55/7 ≈ −7.86 °F per minute. The entries t = 5 and t = 12 are the closest on either side of 9: [T(12) − T(5)]/(12 − 5) = (245 − 300)/7 = −55/7. At t = 9 minutes the cake's temperature is decreasing at about 7.86 °F per minute.
cards.h: → bracketing quotient with unequal gaps, units
cards.n: Dividing by 5 instead of 12 − 5 = 7 is the slip; t = 0 and t = 30 also bracket 9, but the closest pair is the estimate scoring guidelines use.

cards.q: Explain why [V(6) − V(2)]/(6 − 2), computed from a table of a tank's volume, only estimates V'(4).
cards.a: The quotient is the average rate of change of V on [2, 6], the slope of a secant line. V'(4) is the instantaneous rate at t = 4, the slope of the tangent. They are equal only if V changes at a constant rate on [2, 6], and the table gives no values in between, so the quotient is an approximation.
cards.h: → quotient = average rate on [2, 6] → V′(4) is a rate at one instant → equal only if the rate is constant
cards.n: Calling the quotient 'the derivative at 4' without 'approximately' misstates it; a table can only give average rates.
o: V'(4) is the limit of such quotients as the interval shrinks to t = 4, and a table cannot shrink the interval below its spacing.
If the graph of V bends on [2, 6], the secant slope can differ from the tangent slope at t = 4 by an amount the table cannot reveal.

w.a: The quotient equals V'(4) exactly because t = 4 is the midpoint of 2 and 6.
w.why: a symmetric quotient still averages over the interval

w.a: V'(4) = 72 liters because the table says V(4) = 72.
w.why: that is the amount, not the rate

w.a: The quotient is exact because the table values are exact measurements.
w.why: exact data still give only an average rate

cards.q: Explain why the volume of water in a tank is increasing at t = 6 when water flows in at E(6) = 54 liters per minute and drains out at D(6) = 46 liters per minute.
cards.a: The volume changes at the net rate W'(t) = E(t) − D(t). At t = 6, W'(6) = 54 − 46 = 8 liters per minute, which is positive, so the volume is increasing at t = 6. The sign of the net rate decides, however fast the water drains.
cards.h: → W′ = rate in − rate out → W′(6) = 8 > 0 → volume increasing
cards.n: 'Water is draining, so the volume falls' ignores the inflow; only the sign of rate in minus rate out decides.
o: Near t = 6 more water enters than leaves each minute (54 against 46 liters), so the amount grows.
W'(6) = 8 > 0 is the rate of change of W, and a positive derivative means W is increasing.

w.a: The volume is decreasing because water is draining out of the tank.
w.why: ignores the larger inflow

w.a: The volume is increasing because E(t) is increasing.
w.why: whether E grows says nothing about E − D

w.a: The volume is 8 liters at t = 6.
w.why: 8 is a rate in liters per minute, not an amount

cards.q: Explain why T'(3) = −3, where T(x) is the temperature, in degrees, at x cm from one end of a rod, does not say the rod is cooling.
cards.a: T'(3) is a rate with respect to distance, in degrees per centimeter: moving along the rod past x = 3, the temperature drops 3 degrees per centimeter. T has no time input, so T' describes how temperature varies along the rod, not how the rod changes over time.
cards.h: → input is distance → T′ in degrees per cm → describes the rod at one moment, not change over time
cards.n: 'Cooling at 3 degrees per minute' borrows a time unit; the units of a rate always follow its input variable.
o: Cooling would need a function of time, such as H(t), with H'(t) < 0; T has no time input.
The units of T' are the units of T divided by the units of x, degrees per centimeter, and no time unit appears.

w.a: The rod is cooling at 3 degrees per centimeter.
w.why: cooling is change over time; x is distance

w.a: The temperature at x = 3 is −3 degrees.
w.why: that would be T(3), not T′(3)

w.a: The rod cools at 3 degrees per minute.
w.why: no time variable appears in T

cards.q: Explain why successive differences of 1.5, 3 and 6.5 thousand in a population table over equal 2-year steps suggest, but do not prove, that the growth rate P'(t) is increasing.
cards.a: Dividing by the 2-year steps gives average rates of 0.75, 1.5 and 3.25 thousand per year, each larger than the last, so the rate appears to rise. But a table gives only average rates over intervals; P′ between the listed times is unknown and could dip, so the claim is 'appears to'.
cards.h: → differences ÷ 2 = average rates → they grow → only averages are known → 'appears to'
cards.n: 'The population is increasing, so the growth rate is increasing' reads P as P′; the evidence is the growing differences.
o: Growing differences over equal steps mean the secant slopes increase, which is what an increasing P′ would produce.
A smooth curve through the four points bends upward, consistent with P'' > 0, but many different curves pass through the same points.

w.a: The growth rate is increasing because the population keeps going up.
w.why: rising values show P′ > 0, not P′ increasing

w.a: The table proves that P'' > 0 on the whole interval.
w.why: a table cannot fix P′ between rows

w.a: The growth rate is constant because the time steps are equal.
w.why: equal steps with unequal changes mean unequal rates

cards.q: Explain why a company already making x = 1000 units should not make more, if its profit is P(x) = −0.02x² + 38x − 2000 dollars, so that P'(x) = 38 − 0.04x.
cards.a: P'(1000) = 38 − 40 = −2 dollars per unit, which is negative, so at x = 1000 profit is decreasing as production increases: each additional unit lowers profit by about 2 dollars. Making more units would reduce profit, not raise it.
cards.h: → P′(1000) = −2 < 0 → profit decreasing in x → the next unit lowers profit by about 2 dollars
cards.n: Pointing to P(1000) = 16,000 dollars, a profit still being made, misses that the rate is negative; the sign of P′ decides whether more units help.
o: Marginal revenue at x = 1000 is 50 − 0.04(1000) = 10 dollars per unit, below the marginal cost of 12, so each extra unit costs more than it brings in.
P'(x) < 0 for every x > 950, so profit falls throughout that range of production.

w.a: They should make more units because the profit P(1000) = 16,000 dollars is positive.
w.why: a positive amount does not make the rate positive

w.a: Profit is increasing because revenue is still increasing.
w.why: revenue rising slower than cost still lowers profit

w.a: P'(1000) = −2 means the company loses 2 dollars in total.
w.why: it is a rate per unit, not a total

cards.q: Explain why estimating T'(9) from a cake-temperature table with entries at t = 0, 5, 12, 20 and 30 minutes uses the values at t = 5 and t = 12.
cards.a: A difference quotient is the average rate over its interval, and the cooling rate keeps changing, so the shortest interval containing t = 9 best reflects the rate at t = 9. The entries t = 5 and t = 12 are the closest on either side, giving (245 − 300)/7 ≈ −7.86 °F per minute.
cards.h: → quotient = average rate on its interval → rate varies → shortest interval around 9 is the most local
cards.n: Using t = 0 and t = 30 averages over half an hour of changing rates; it brackets 9 but describes a much longer stretch.
o: When the graph bends between table values, the secant through the two nearest points is closest to the tangent at t = 9.
A wider interval mixes in the fast cooling near t = 0 and the slow cooling near t = 30, which says less about t = 9.

w.a: Any two values in the table give the same estimate of T'(9).
w.why: different intervals give different average rates

w.a: Use t = 0 and t = 5 because they are the first two rows.
w.why: that interval does not contain t = 9

w.a: T'(9) cannot be estimated because 9 is not in the table.
w.why: a bracketing difference quotient estimates it

cards.q: Identify what dV/dt, dr/dt, and dθ/dt each represent.
cards.a: dV/dt, dr/dt and dθ/dt are the rates of change with respect to time t of the volume, the radius and the angle. Their units are volume per unit time (such as cm³/s), length per unit time (cm/s) and radians per unit time (rad/s). Every given or requested rate in a related rates problem is such a derivative.
cards.h: → three rates with respect to t, with units
cards.n: Writing dV/dr for 'how fast the volume changes' brings in the radius as the input; a rate in a story is with respect to time unless it says otherwise.

cards.q: Explain the standard method for solving a related rates problem.
cards.a: 1) Name the changing quantities and draw the figure. 2) Write an equation relating them that holds at every time t. 3) Differentiate both sides with respect to t: the chain rule on every variable, the product or quotient rule where variables multiply or divide. 4) Substitute the values at the instant. 5) Solve for the unknown rate and state it with units, in context.
cards.h: → five steps: name, relate, differentiate, substitute, solve
cards.n: Substituting the instant's values before step 3 turns a changing quantity into a constant whose rate then wrongly vanishes.

cards.q: A spherical balloon is inflated so its volume increases at 100 cm³/s. Find dr/dt when r = 5 cm.
cards.a: dr/dt = 1/π ≈ 0.318 cm/s. Differentiate V = (4/3)πr³ with respect to t: dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt). At r = 5, 100 = 4π(25)(dr/dt) = 100π(dr/dt), so dr/dt = 1/π centimeter per second.
cards.h: → differentiate, substitute, solve, units
cards.n: Differentiating to 4πr² without the factor dr/dt leaves nothing to solve for; the chain rule attaches dr/dt because r depends on t.

cards.q: The area of a circular oil slick grows at $\frac{dA}{dt} = 6$ m² per hour. Find $\frac{dr}{dt}$ when r = 3 m.
cards.a: dr/dt = 1/π ≈ 0.318 meter per hour. Differentiate A = πr²: dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt). At r = 3, 6 = 2π(3)(dr/dt) = 6π(dr/dt), so dr/dt = 1/π m/hr.
cards.h: → differentiate, substitute, solve, units
cards.n: dr/dt is in m/hr, not m²/hr; the square belongs to the given area rate dA/dt.

cards.q: Describe how to set up a related rates equation for two quantities described only in words, before any differentiation happens.
cards.a: Assign a letter to each quantity that changes (and note which stay fixed), translate each given and requested rate into d/dt notation with its sign, then write one equation that relates the quantities at every instant, from geometry (Pythagorean theorem, area, volume, similar triangles, trigonometry) or from the story.
cards.h: → variables, rates in d/dt form, one relating equation
cards.n: Writing the equation with the instant's numbers already in it (5 in place of x) makes it true only at that instant, so it cannot be differentiated.

cards.q:
Differentiate each equation with respect to t. Every letter other than the named constants is a function of t.
1. x² + y² = 25
2. V = (4/3)πr³
3. V = πr²h (r and h both change)
4. A = (1/2)xy
5. tan θ = y/10
6. z² = x² + y²
7. S = 6s²
8. PV = 500
9. y = x/(x + 1)
10. A = (1/2)ab sin θ, with a and b constant
cards.a:
1 → 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0
2 → dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt)
3 → dV/dt = π[2rh(dr/dt) + r²(dh/dt)]
4 → dA/dt = (1/2)[x(dy/dt) + y(dx/dt)]
5 → sec²θ(dθ/dt) = (1/10)(dy/dt)
6 → 2z(dz/dt) = 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt)
7 → dS/dt = 12s(ds/dt)
8 → P(dV/dt) + V(dP/dt) = 0
9 → dy/dt = [1/(x + 1)²](dx/dt)
10 → dA/dt = (1/2)ab cos θ(dθ/dt)
cards.h: → one differentiated equation per line
cards.n: Every variable term needs its own d/dt factor; 3, 4 and 8 need the product rule's two terms, and a constant such as 25 or 500 differentiates to 0.

cards.q: Calculate the rate of change of the volume of a cylinder at the instant its radius is 4 cm and its height is 10 cm, if the radius is increasing at 0.5 cm/s and the height is decreasing at 2 cm/s.
cards.a: dV/dt = 8π ≈ 25.1 cm³/s: the volume is increasing. V = πr²h, and by the product rule dV/dt = π[2rh(dr/dt) + r²(dh/dt)] = π[2(4)(10)(0.5) + 16(−2)] = π(40 − 32) = 8π cubic centimeters per second.
cards.h: → product rule, substitute with signs, units
cards.n: Entering the shrinking height as dh/dt = +2 gives 72π; a decreasing height enters as dh/dt = −2.

cards.q: Find dy/dt at the instant x = 3, if x and y are differentiable functions of t with xy = 12 and dx/dt = 2 at that instant.
cards.a: dy/dt = −8/3. At x = 3, y = 12/3 = 4. The product rule gives x(dy/dt) + y(dx/dt) = 0, so 3(dy/dt) + 4(2) = 0 and dy/dt = −8/3.
cards.h: → find y, product rule, solve
cards.n: Differentiating xy as (dx/dt)(dy/dt) = 0 is not the product rule; and y = 4 must come from xy = 12, since it is not given.

cards.q: Find dy/dt when x = 2, if y = x³ − 2x and x is increasing at 4 units per second at that instant.
cards.a: dy/dt = 40 units per second. By the chain rule dy/dt = (3x² − 2)(dx/dt) = (3·4 − 2)(4) = 10·4 = 40.
cards.h: → chain rule, substitute
cards.n: Stopping at dy/dx = 10 gives y per unit of x, not y per second; multiply by dx/dt = 4.

cards.q: Find the rate at which the surface area of a spherical balloon is changing when r = 5 cm, if air is pumped in so that the volume increases at 100 cm³/s.
cards.a: dS/dt = 40 cm²/s. From V = (4/3)πr³, 100 = 4π(5²)(dr/dt), so dr/dt = 1/π cm/s. Then S = 4πr² gives dS/dt = 8πr(dr/dt) = 8π(5)(1/π) = 40 square centimeters per second.
cards.h: → dr/dt from V, then dS/dt from S
cards.n: Relating S and V directly is the hard road; go through the shared rate dr/dt. The units are cm²/s for area, not cm³/s.

cards.q:
Translate each statement into a rate with its sign, naming the variable.
1. Air is pumped into a balloon at 50 cm³ per minute.
2. The radius of a puddle shrinks by 0.2 cm each second.
3. A plane flies horizontally away from a radar tower at 300 miles per hour.
4. Water leaks from a tank at 3 cubic feet per minute.
5. The angle of elevation to a rising rocket grows at 0.1 radian per second.
6. The top of a ladder slides down a wall at 2 feet per second.
cards.a:
1 → dV/dt = 50 cm³/min (V the volume)
2 → dr/dt = −0.2 cm/s (r the radius)
3 → dx/dt = 300 mi/hr (x the horizontal distance from the tower)
4 → dV/dt = −3 ft³/min (V the volume in the tank)
5 → dθ/dt = 0.1 rad/s (θ the angle of elevation)
6 → dy/dt = −2 ft/s (y the height of the top on the wall)
cards.h: → one signed rate with units per line
cards.n: Shrinks, leaks and slides down are decreases, so those rates are negative; writing +3 for a leak flips the sign of every answer built on it.

cards.q: Find the rate of change of the ratio L/W for a rectangle at the instant L = 10 cm and W = 4 cm, if the length L is increasing at 3 cm/s and the width W at 1 cm/s.
cards.a: d(L/W)/dt = 1/8 = 0.125 per second. By the quotient rule, d(L/W)/dt = [W(dL/dt) − L(dW/dt)]/W² = [4(3) − 10(1)]/16 = 2/16 = 1/8. The ratio has no units, so its rate is per second.
cards.h: → quotient rule, substitute, units
cards.n: Dividing the rates, (dL/dt)/(dW/dt) = 3, is the derivative-of-a-quotient error; the quotient rule is needed because both L and W change.

cards.q: Determine whether dA/dt is constant for a circle whose radius increases at a constant 2 cm/s, and find dA/dt when r = 5 cm and when r = 10 cm.
cards.a: dA/dt is not constant; it grows with r. dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt) = 4πr cm²/s, so dA/dt = 20π ≈ 62.8 cm²/s at r = 5 and 40π ≈ 125.7 cm²/s at r = 10.
cards.h: → dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt, then two values
cards.n: 'The radius grows steadily, so the area does too' is the trap; dA/dt carries the factor r, so each centimeter of radius adds more area.

cards.q: Explain why the derivative of r² with respect to t is 2r(dr/dt) and not 2r, when r is the radius of a growing circle.
cards.a: r is a function of t, so r² is a composite: the outer function squares and the inner function is r(t). The chain rule gives d/dt[r(t)²] = 2r(t)·r'(t) = 2r(dr/dt). Writing 2r differentiates with respect to r, not t.
cards.h: → r depends on t → r² is a composite → chain rule → 2r times dr/dt
cards.n: Dropping dr/dt leaves an equation with no rate in it; every variable term picks up its own d/dt factor.
o: 2r is the rate of change of r² with respect to r; the chain rule turns it into a rate per unit of time by multiplying by dr/dt.
If r = 3 + 2t, then r² = 9 + 12t + 4t², whose derivative 12 + 8t equals 2r·2 = 2r(dr/dt), not 2r.

w.a: The derivative of r² is 2r because of the power rule.
w.why: the power rule alone differentiates with respect to r

w.a: dr/dt only appears when the problem gives a rate for r.
w.why: r depends on t whether or not its rate is given

w.a: You differentiate r² to 2r and multiply by dt at the end.
w.why: the factor is dr/dt, not dt

cards.q: Explain why differentiating V = πr²h with respect to t requires the product rule when both the radius and the height of a cylinder change.
cards.a: V is π times the product of two functions of t, r(t)² and h(t). The product rule gives dV/dt = π[2r(dr/dt)h + r²(dh/dt)]: one term for the change in r, one for the change in h. Treating either as constant drops a term.
cards.h: → r and h both vary → V is a product of functions of t → product rule → two rate terms
cards.n: dV/dt = π(2r)(dr/dt)(dh/dt) multiplies the rates, which is not the product rule; the two terms add.
o: If h were fixed, dV/dt = 2πrh(dr/dt); if r were fixed, dV/dt = πr²(dh/dt); when both vary, both contributions add.
The volume changes because the base widens and because the cylinder grows taller, and the product rule counts each.

w.a: dV/dt = πr²(dh/dt) because the height is what changes.
w.why: the radius changes too

w.a: dV/dt = 2πr(dr/dt)(dh/dt) by the chain rule.
w.why: multiplies rates instead of adding product-rule terms

w.a: You substitute r and h first and then differentiate.
w.why: a number differentiates to 0

cards.q: Explain why the area of a circle grows faster and faster when its radius increases at a constant 2 cm/s.
cards.a: dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt) = 4πr cm²/s. The rate of the area depends on r, and r is increasing, so dA/dt increases. Each added bit of radius adds a thin ring whose area is about the circumference 2πr times its width, and that circumference keeps growing.
cards.h: → dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt → r grows → dA/dt grows
cards.n: 'Constant dr/dt means constant dA/dt' ignores the factor r that the chain rule brings in.
o: A = π(r₀ + 2t)² is a quadratic in t, so its rate is linear in t and increasing.
d²A/dt² = 2π(dr/dt)² = 8π > 0 when dr/dt is constant, so dA/dt increases.

w.a: The area grows at a constant rate because the radius grows at a constant rate.
w.why: misses the factor r in dA/dt

w.a: dA/dt = 2π·2 = 4π, a constant.
w.why: drops r from 2πr

w.a: The area grows more slowly as the circle gets bigger.
w.why: dA/dt = 4πr increases with r

cards.q: Explain why y must be decreasing when x is increasing, if x and y are positive functions of t with xy = 12.
cards.a: Differentiating gives x(dy/dt) + y(dx/dt) = 0, so dy/dt = −(y/x)(dx/dt). With x and y positive, y/x > 0, so when dx/dt > 0 the rate dy/dt is negative. The product must stay 12, so one factor shrinks as the other grows.
cards.h: → product rule → dy/dt = −(y/x)·dx/dt → y/x > 0 → opposite signs
cards.n: 'x and y are both positive, so both increase' ignores the constraint; the product rule forces the rates to have opposite signs.
o: y = 12/x, so dy/dt = −(12/x²)(dx/dt), which is negative whenever dx/dt > 0.
The curve xy = 12 in the first quadrant slopes downward (dy/dx = −y/x < 0), so moving right along it moves down.

w.a: y increases too, because the product rule adds the two rates.
w.why: the sum x(dy/dt) + y(dx/dt) equals 0

w.a: y stays constant because xy is constant.
w.why: the product is constant, not each factor

w.a: dy/dt = −dx/dt, so y falls exactly as fast as x rises.
w.why: the factor y/x is missing

cards.q: Explain why the radius of a spherical balloon grows more slowly as the balloon gets bigger, if air is pumped in at a constant 100 cm³/s.
cards.a: dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt), so dr/dt = 100/(4πr²). The same 100 cm³ each second spreads over a surface of area 4πr², which grows with r, so dr/dt decreases as r increases: 1/π cm/s at r = 5 but 1/(4π) cm/s at r = 10.
cards.h: → dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(4πr²) → surface area grows with r → dr/dt shrinks
cards.n: 'Constant inflow means the radius grows steadily' ignores the 4πr² factor, the area the new air spreads over.
o: Doubling the radius multiplies the volume by 8, so the same inflow takes longer to add each centimeter of radius.
dr/dt is proportional to 1/r², which decreases as r increases.

w.a: The radius grows at a constant rate because air is added at a constant rate.
w.why: ignores the 4πr² factor

w.a: The radius grows faster as the balloon gets bigger because there is more air inside.
w.why: dr/dt varies as 1/r²

w.a: dr/dt = 100 cm/s because dV/dt = 100.
w.why: cm³/s is not cm/s; the rates differ by 4πr²

cards.q: Explain why the quotient rule, or the product rule, is needed to differentiate tan θ = y/x with respect to t when both x and y change.
cards.a: y/x is a quotient of two functions of t, so its derivative is [x(dy/dt) − y(dx/dt)]/x², while the left side gives sec²θ(dθ/dt) by the chain rule. Treating x as a constant would drop the −y(dx/dt) term and give a wrong dθ/dt.
cards.h: → x and y both depend on t → y/x is a quotient of functions of t → quotient rule → two terms
cards.n: Writing d/dt(y/x) = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) is the ratio-of-rates error; the quotient rule is needed whenever both parts vary.
o: Writing y/x = y·x⁻¹ and using the product rule gives (1/x)(dy/dt) − (y/x²)(dx/dt), the same result.
Holding x fixed is right only when x really is constant, such as an observer's fixed distance from a launch point.

w.a: The derivative of y/x with respect to t is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
w.why: a derivative of a quotient is not a quotient of derivatives

w.a: Only dy/dt appears because x is in the denominator.
w.why: x varies, so its rate appears too

w.a: The derivative of tan θ is sec²θ, so the left side is just sec²θ.
w.why: the chain-rule factor dθ/dt is missing

cards.q: Recall the geometric relationships most often needed in related rates problems.
cards.a: The Pythagorean theorem a² + b² = c² (ladders, cars, kites); similar triangles (cones, shadows); area and volume formulas: circle A = πr², sphere V = (4/3)πr³ and S = 4πr², cone V = (1/3)πr²h, cylinder V = πr²h; and trigonometric ratios such as tan θ = opposite/adjacent for angles of elevation.
cards.h: → four families of formulas
cards.n: The cone formula has two changing variables; without the similar-triangle ratio r = (R/H)h the equation holds one unknown rate too many.

cards.q: Describe the extra step required in a cone problem where both the radius and the height vary.
cards.a: Use similar triangles from the full cone's fixed dimensions to write r in terms of h (r/h = R/H, so r = (R/H)h), substitute into V = (1/3)πr²h to get V in terms of h alone, and only then differentiate with respect to t. For a cone with R = 3 and H = 5, r = 3h/5 and V = (3π/25)h³.
cards.h: → similar triangles, substitute, then differentiate
cards.n: Differentiating V = (1/3)πr²h with both r and h left in produces an unknown dr/dt that the problem never gives.

cards.q: Describe the setup for a ladder sliding down a wall.
cards.a: With x the distance from the wall to the base and y the height of the top, x² + y² = L², where the length L is constant. Differentiating with respect to t: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0, so dy/dt = −(x/y)(dx/dt). At the instant, find the missing leg from x² + y² = L² before substituting.
cards.h: → Pythagorean equation, differentiate, solve for dy/dt
cards.n: The right side differentiates to 0 because L is fixed; writing 2L(dL/dt) with a nonzero dL/dt makes the ladder stretch.

cards.q: Identify the sign conventions for the given rates in a related rates problem.
cards.a: A decreasing quantity gets a negative rate and an increasing one a positive rate: a draining tank has dV/dt < 0, a falling ladder top dy/dt < 0, a base pulled away from the wall dx/dt > 0. Assign the signs when writing the givens, then check that the sign of the answer matches the physical story.
cards.h: → decreasing → negative, increasing → positive
cards.n: Entering a drain rate as +2 m³/min makes the water rise; a sign slip at the start flips the final answer.

cards.q: Water drains from a cone (vertex down, radius 3 m at height 5 m) so $\frac{dV}{dt}=-2$ m³/min. Find $\frac{dh}{dt}$ when h = 4 m.
cards.a: dh/dt = −25/(72π) ≈ −0.111 m/min: when the water is 4 m deep, the depth is decreasing at about 0.111 meter per minute. Similar triangles give r = 3h/5, so V = (1/3)π(3h/5)²h = (3π/25)h³ and dV/dt = (9π/25)h²(dh/dt). At h = 4: −2 = (144π/25)(dh/dt), so dh/dt = −50/(144π) = −25/(72π).
cards.h: → similar triangles, one variable, differentiate, solve
cards.n: Substituting h = 4 before differentiating, or keeping both r and h, leaves the problem unsolvable; the negative sign means the level is falling.

cards.q: A 13-ft ladder slides down a wall; the base moves away at 2 ft/s. Find the rate the top is falling when the base is 5 ft from the wall.
cards.a: The top is falling at 5/6 ft/s (dy/dt = −5/6). With x² + y² = 169, at x = 5 the height is y = 12. Differentiating, 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0, so 2(5)(2) + 2(12)(dy/dt) = 0 and dy/dt = −20/24 = −5/6 ft/s.
cards.h: → find y, differentiate, solve, sign in words
cards.n: Forgetting to compute y = 12 leaves an unknown; and 'falling at −5/6 ft/s' says the sign twice, which reverses it.

cards.q: A 6-ft person walks away from a 15-ft lamppost at 4 ft/s. Find the rate the TIP of their shadow moves.
cards.a: 20/3 ≈ 6.67 ft/s. With x the person's distance from the post and s the shadow length, similar triangles give 15/(x + s) = 6/s, so 15s = 6x + 6s and s = (2/3)x. The tip is at x + s = (5/3)x from the post, so it moves at (5/3)(dx/dt) = (5/3)(4) = 20/3 feet per second.
cards.h: → similar triangles, tip = x + s, differentiate
cards.n: ds/dt = 8/3 ft/s is how fast the shadow lengthens, not how fast its tip moves; the tip adds the walker's own 4 ft/s.

cards.q: Find how fast the distance between two cars is changing at the instant car A is 8 miles north of an intersection, driving north at 60 mph, and car B is 6 miles east of it, driving east at 30 mph.
cards.a: The distance is increasing at 66 mph. With x east and y north, z² = x² + y², and at the instant z = √(36 + 64) = 10. Then 2z(dz/dt) = 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt), so 10(dz/dt) = 6(30) + 8(60) = 180 + 480 = 660 and dz/dt = 66 mi/hr.
cards.h: → Pythagorean relation, find z, differentiate, solve
cards.n: Adding the speeds (90 mph) treats the cars as moving apart along one line; at a right angle the rates combine through z.

cards.q: Find the rate at which the angle of elevation from an observer to a balloon is changing when the balloon is 100 m high, if it rises vertically at 5 m/s from a point on level ground 100 m from the observer.
cards.a: dθ/dt = 0.025 radian per second. With h the height, tan θ = h/100, so sec²θ(dθ/dt) = (1/100)(dh/dt). At h = 100, θ = π/4 and sec²θ = 2, so 2(dθ/dt) = 5/100 and dθ/dt = 0.025 rad/s.
cards.h: → tan θ = h/100, differentiate, evaluate sec²θ
cards.n: The rule d/dθ(tan θ) = sec²θ holds in radians only, so the rate is in rad/s; sec²θ must be evaluated at the instant, not left as a symbol.

cards.q: Find the rate at which the angle between a 13-ft ladder and the ground is changing when the base is 5 ft from the wall, if the base slides away from the wall at 2 ft/s.
cards.a: dθ/dt = −1/6 radian per second: the angle is decreasing. With x the distance of the base from the wall, cos θ = x/13, so −sin θ(dθ/dt) = (1/13)(dx/dt). At x = 5 the height is 12, so sin θ = 12/13, and −(12/13)(dθ/dt) = 2/13, giving dθ/dt = −1/6.
cards.h: → cos θ = x/13, differentiate, sin θ at the instant
cards.n: Dropping the minus sign from d/dt(cos θ) makes the angle grow while the ladder slides down; the angle with the ground must shrink.

cards.q: Find how fast the water level rises in a cylindrical tank of radius 2 m when water is poured in at 3 m³/min.
cards.a: dh/dt = 3/(4π) ≈ 0.239 m/min, at every depth. V = πr²h = 4πh with the radius fixed at 2, so dV/dt = 4π(dh/dt), and 3 = 4π(dh/dt) gives dh/dt = 3/(4π) meter per minute.
cards.h: → V with the fixed radius, differentiate, solve
cards.n: Carrying a dr/dt term treats the fixed radius as a variable; unlike a cone's water surface, a cylinder's radius really is constant.

cards.q: Find the rate at which a runner's distance to second base is changing when the runner is halfway from home plate to first base, running at 24 ft/s. A baseball diamond is a square 90 ft on a side.
cards.a: dD/dt = −24/√5 ≈ −10.7 ft/s: the distance to second base is decreasing at about 10.7 ft/s. With x the distance from home, first base is 90 − x away and second base 90 ft beyond it at a right angle, so D² = (90 − x)² + 90². At x = 45, D = √10125 = 45√5. Then 2D(dD/dt) = −2(90 − x)(dx/dt), so dD/dt = −45(24)/(45√5) = −24/√5.
cards.h: → right triangle to second base, differentiate, substitute
cards.n: D² = x² + 90² measures the distance to third base, not second; the leg along the base path is the 90 − x still to run.

cards.q: Find how fast the length of a 6-ft person's shadow changes as the person walks toward a 15-ft lamppost at 3 ft/s.
cards.a: ds/dt = −2 ft/s: the shadow is shrinking at 2 feet per second. With x the distance to the post and s the shadow length, similar triangles give 15/(x + s) = 6/s, so s = (2/3)x. Walking toward the post, dx/dt = −3, so ds/dt = (2/3)(−3) = −2 ft/s.
cards.h: → similar triangles, s in terms of x, signed rate
cards.n: Walking toward the post makes x decrease, so dx/dt = −3; using +3 says the shadow grows as the person nears the light.

cards.q: Interpret dh/dt = −25/(72π) m/min, found when the water in a draining conical tank is 4 m deep, in the context of the problem.
cards.a: At the instant the water is 4 m deep, the depth of the water is decreasing at 25/(72π) ≈ 0.111 meter per minute. The minus sign is the word decreasing, the units are meters per minute, and the statement holds at that instant only, because dh/dt changes as the tank drains.
cards.h: → instant, quantity, decreasing, rate, units
cards.n: 'The water drops 0.111 m' gives neither 'per minute' nor the instant h = 4; an interpretation needs both, with the sign read as decreasing.

cards.q: Find the rate of change of the area of a triangle with sides 4 m and 5 m when the angle θ between them is π/3 and is increasing at 0.06 radian per second.
cards.a: dA/dt = 0.3 m²/s. A = (1/2)(4)(5)sin θ = 10 sin θ, so dA/dt = 10cos θ(dθ/dt) = 10(1/2)(0.06) = 0.3 square meter per second.
cards.h: → A = ½ab sin θ, differentiate, evaluate cos θ
cards.n: The sides are fixed, so only θ varies; evaluating sin(π/3) instead of cos(π/3) after differentiating gives about 0.52.

cards.q: Explain why you must not substitute the instantaneous values before differentiating.
cards.a: Before differentiating, the equation must hold at every time, so each changing quantity stays a variable. Substituting its value at the instant makes it a constant, whose derivative is 0, so its rate term vanishes. Substitute the instant's values only after differentiating.
cards.h: → the equation must hold for all t → a substituted value is constant → its rate term becomes 0
cards.n: Fixed quantities, such as a ladder's length or a cone's r/h ratio, may go in early; the instant's values of changing quantities may not.
o: Putting x = 5 into x² + y² = 169 first gives 25 + y² = 169, whose derivative 2y(dy/dt) = 0 forces dy/dt = 0, which is false.
An equation true at only one instant cannot be differentiated with respect to t, because a derivative compares values at nearby times.

w.a: You can substitute first because the numbers are the same either way.
w.why: a substituted variable loses its rate term

w.a: Substituting first just makes the algebra easier.
w.why: it changes the equation being differentiated

w.a: Only the rates must wait until the end; lengths can go in any time.
w.why: changing lengths are variables too

cards.q: Explain why the top of a sliding ladder falls faster and faster even though its base moves away from the wall at a constant rate.
cards.a: From x² + y² = L², dy/dt = −(x/y)(dx/dt). As the base moves out, x increases and y decreases, so x/y increases, and with dx/dt constant the speed of the top, (x/y)|dx/dt|, increases.
cards.h: → dy/dt = −(x/y)·dx/dt → x grows, y shrinks → x/y grows → the top falls faster
cards.n: 'Both ends move at the same speed' ignores the factor x/y; the two speeds match only at the instant x = y.
o: For a 13-ft ladder with dx/dt = 2, the top falls at 5/6 ft/s when x = 5 and y = 12, but at 24/5 ft/s when x = 12 and y = 5.
The length is fixed, so as the ladder flattens each foot the base moves out costs the top more height.

w.a: The top falls at 2 ft/s, the same rate as the base, because the ladder is rigid.
w.why: the rates differ by the factor x/y

w.a: The top falls more slowly near the ground because it has less distance left.
w.why: x/y grows, so the top speeds up

w.a: The top's speed is constant because the ladder's length is constant.
w.why: a constant L does not make dy/dt constant

cards.q: Explain why the depth of water in a vertex-down conical tank rises more and more slowly when water is poured in at a constant rate.
cards.a: With r = kh, V = (π/3)k²h³, so dV/dt = πk²h²(dh/dt) = πr²(dh/dt): the inflow spreads over the water surface, a circle of area πr². As the tank fills, r grows, so for a fixed dV/dt the rate dh/dt = (dV/dt)/(πr²) decreases.
cards.h: → dV/dt = (surface area)·dh/dt → surface widens as h grows → dh/dt shrinks
cards.n: 'Constant inflow means the level rises steadily' holds for a cylinder, not for a cone, whose cross-section widens with depth.
o: For the cone with r = 3h/5, dh/dt = 25(dV/dt)/(9πh²), which decreases as h increases.
A centimeter of depth near the top holds far more water than one near the vertex, so it takes longer to fill.

w.a: The level rises at a constant rate because water is added at a constant rate.
w.why: true for a cylinder, not a widening cone

w.a: The level rises faster as the tank fills because there is more water pushing up.
w.why: dh/dt decreases as h increases

w.a: dh/dt equals dV/dt because both measure the water.
w.why: different units; they differ by the surface area

cards.q: Explain why the tip of the shadow of a 6-ft person walking away from a 15-ft lamppost at a constant 4 ft/s moves at a constant rate, however far the person is from the post.
cards.a: Similar triangles give the shadow length s = (2/3)x, so the tip is at x + s = (5/3)x from the post. That is a constant multiple of x, so the tip's rate is (5/3)(dx/dt) = 20/3 ft/s at every distance x.
cards.h: → similar triangles → tip at (5/3)x → linear in x → rate (5/3)·dx/dt, constant
cards.n: Expecting the tip to speed up as the person walks away confuses this linear relation with one like the ladder's, where the ratio x/y varies.
o: The ratio s/x = 2/3 is fixed by the two heights, so the shadow grows in fixed proportion to the walker's distance.
d(x + s)/dt = dx/dt + ds/dt = 4 + 8/3, and neither term depends on x.

w.a: The tip moves faster as the person gets farther away because the shadow gets longer.
w.why: the shadow grows at a constant 8/3 ft/s

w.a: The tip moves at 4 ft/s, the same as the person.
w.why: the shadow's growth adds 8/3 ft/s

w.a: The tip moves at 8/3 ft/s.
w.why: that is the rate of the shadow's length, not the tip

cards.q: Explain why the rate of change of an angle in a related rates problem is found in radians per unit of time.
cards.a: The derivative rules d/dθ(sin θ) = cos θ and d/dθ(tan θ) = sec²θ hold only when θ is in radians. Differentiating tan θ = h/100 with respect to t therefore gives dθ/dt in radians per second; degrees would need an extra factor of 180/π.
cards.h: → trig derivatives assume radians → the chain rule gives dθ/dt in rad per unit time → degrees need a conversion
cards.n: Answering in degrees per second without converting, or with a calculator in degree mode, gives a number off by the factor 180/π.
o: If θ were measured in degrees, d/dθ(sin θ) would be (π/180)cos θ, so the standard rules would change.
The limit sin θ/θ → 1, on which the trig derivatives rest, is true only for θ in radians.

w.a: The rate is in degrees per second because angles of elevation are measured in degrees.
w.why: the derivative rules assume radians

w.a: Units do not matter for an angle's rate because angles have no units.
w.why: radians versus degrees changes the number

w.a: dθ/dt is in meters per second because the balloon rises in meters.
w.why: an angle's rate is in radians per unit of time

cards.q: Explain why a bare answer of −0.111 does not earn the interpretation point when a related rates question asks how fast the depth of a draining tank is changing when the depth is 4 m.
cards.a: An interpretation must tie the number to the context: the quantity (the depth), the direction (decreasing, carried by the minus sign), the size of the rate, the units (meters per minute) and the instant (when the depth is 4 m). A bare −0.111 states none of these.
cards.h: → a number alone → no quantity, direction, units or instant → no interpretation
cards.n: Units are the usual lost point: 0.111 m or m² per minute is wrong; a depth rate is in meters per minute.
o: 'When the water is 4 m deep, the depth is decreasing at about 0.111 m/min' supplies every missing piece in one sentence.
Without the instant, a reader cannot tell which moment the rate describes, since dh/dt changes as the tank drains.

w.a: dh/dt = −0.111, so the water is going down.
w.why: no units and no instant

w.a: The depth is decreasing at −0.111 meters per minute.
w.why: 'decreasing' and the minus sign together reverse it

w.a: The water drops 0.111 meters when it is 4 m deep.
w.why: a change is not a rate; 'per minute' is missing

cards.q: Explain why the distance between two cars, one driving north and one driving east away from the same intersection, increases at a rate less than the sum of their speeds.
cards.a: The distance is z = √(x² + y²), so dz/dt = (x/z)(dx/dt) + (y/z)(dy/dt): each speed is weighted by x/z or y/z. Both weights are less than 1, so dz/dt is less than the sum of the speeds; at x = 6, y = 8 with speeds 30 and 60 mph it is 66 mph, not 90.
cards.h: → z² = x² + y² → dz/dt weights each speed by x/z or y/z → weights < 1 → less than the sum
cards.n: Adding the speeds treats the cars as moving apart along one line; at a right angle the rates combine through z.
o: Speeds add directly only for motion along one line; perpendicular motions combine through the Pythagorean relation.
x/z and y/z are the cosines of the angles between the line joining the cars and each road, and a cosine is at most 1.

w.a: The distance grows at 90 mph because 60 + 30 = 90.
w.why: the motions are perpendicular, not opposite

w.a: The distance grows at √(60² + 30²) ≈ 67.1 mph.
w.why: true only if both cars left the intersection together

w.a: The distance grows at 60 mph, the faster car's speed.
w.why: both cars contribute

cards.q: State the linearization of f at x = a and what it is used for.
cards.a: L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x − a), the equation of the line tangent to f at x = a. For x near a, f(x) ≈ L(x): the tangent line approximation (linearization) estimates values of f that are hard or impossible to compute exactly, from one known point and the slope there.
cards.h: → formula, then its use
cards.n: Writing f(a) + f'(x)(x − a), with the slope at x instead of at a, is not a line; the slope must be the number f′(a).

cards.q: Decide whether a tangent line approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate.
cards.a: Decide by the concavity of f between a and x. If f''(x) > 0 there (concave up), the graph lies above its tangent line, so L underestimates f. If f''(x) < 0 (concave down), the graph lies below the tangent, so L overestimates. If f'' changes sign between a and x, this test gives no conclusion.
cards.h: → sign of f″ on the interval → above or below the tangent
cards.n: 'f is increasing, so it is an underestimate' uses f′, which says nothing about which side of the tangent the graph is on; concavity decides.

cards.q: Explain the justification language required for an over- or underestimate claim.
cards.a: Name the sign of f'' on the interval between a and the point estimated, the concavity it gives, where the tangent line sits, and the conclusion: 'Since f''(x) < 0 for 2 < x < 2.1, f is concave down there, so the tangent line lies above the graph and L(2.1) is an overestimate of f(2.1).'
cards.h: → sign of f″ on the interval → concavity → conclusion
cards.n: Citing only f″(a) < 0 does not show the concavity on the whole interval from a to x, which is what the claim needs.

cards.q: Describe how to use linearization to estimate √4.1.
cards.a: √4.1 ≈ 2.025. Take f(x) = √x and a = 4, where f(4) = 2 and f'(x) = 1/(2√x) gives f'(4) = 1/4. Then L(x) = 2 + (1/4)(x − 4), so L(4.1) = 2 + 0.25(0.1) = 2.025. Since f''(x) = −1/(4x√x) < 0, √x is concave down and 2.025 is an overestimate.
cards.h: → choose a = 4, tangent line, evaluate
cards.n: Choosing a = 4.1, where √a is the unknown, defeats the purpose; the true value is 2.02485 to five decimal places, just below the estimate.

cards.q: Define local linearity and connect it to tangent line approximation.
cards.a: A function is locally linear at x = a when it is differentiable there: zooming in on the point, the graph becomes indistinguishable from its tangent line. That is why the tangent line L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x − a) approximates f(x) for x near a, and why the approximation worsens as x moves away from a.
cards.h: → definition, then the link to the tangent line
cards.n: A corner or cusp, such as |x| at 0, never straightens out under zooming, so there is no tangent line and no linearization there.

cards.q: Use linearization to approximate $\sqrt[3]{8.06}$.
cards.a: ∛8.06 ≈ 2.005. Take f(x) = x^(1/3) and a = 8, where f(8) = 2 and f'(x) = (1/3)x^(−2/3) gives f'(8) = 1/12. Then L(8.06) = 2 + (1/12)(0.06) = 2.005. Since f''(x) = −(2/9)x^(−5/3) < 0 for x > 0, the estimate is an overestimate.
cards.h: → nearest perfect cube, tangent line, evaluate
cards.n: Using 0.6 for 8.06 − 8, or dropping the 1/3 from f′, are the usual slips; the true value, about 2.00499, is just below the estimate.

cards.q: For $y=x^{2}$ at x=3 with dx=0.1, compute the differential dy and compare it to the actual change $\Delta y$.
cards.a: dy = 0.6 and Δy = 0.61. The differential is dy = f'(3)dx = 6(0.1) = 0.6, the change along the tangent line. The actual change is Δy = (3.1)² − 3² = 9.61 − 9 = 0.61. dy is slightly smaller because y = x² is concave up, so the curve rises above its tangent line.
cards.h: → tangent-line change, then actual change
cards.n: dy only estimates Δy; here they differ by (dx)² = 0.01, a gap that shrinks faster than dx as dx → 0.

cards.q: $f(x) = \ln x$ is approximated near x=1 by its tangent line. Since f''(x) < 0 for x>0, decide whether the tangent approximation of f(1.2) over- or underestimates f.
cards.a: Overestimate. f''(x) = −1/x² < 0 for x > 0, so f is concave down between 1 and 1.2, and a concave-down graph lies below its tangent line. The tangent line L(x) = x − 1 gives L(1.2) = 0.2, above ln 1.2 ≈ 0.182.
cards.h: → sign of f″, concavity, tangent above or below
cards.n: 'Overestimate because ln x is increasing' cites f′ > 0, which does not decide the side; the concavity between 1 and 1.2 does.

cards.q: $g(x) = e^{x}$ is approximated near x=0 by its tangent line. Since g''(x) > 0 for all x, decide whether the tangent approximation of g(0.3) over- or underestimates g.
cards.a: Underestimate. g''(x) = eˣ > 0 for all x, so g is concave up between 0 and 0.3, and a concave-up graph lies above its tangent line. The tangent line L(x) = 1 + x gives L(0.3) = 1.3, below e^0.3 ≈ 1.350.
cards.h: → sign of g″, concavity, tangent above or below
cards.n: Concave up puts the tangent below the curve, so the estimate is under; a memorized 'up means over' reverses it.

cards.q: Approximate W(12) using the tangent line to W at t = 10, where W(t) is the amount of water, in millions of gallons, in a reservoir t days after a drought begins, with W(10) = 250 and W'(10) = −4. Given that W''(t) > 0 for 8 < t < 14, decide whether the approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate.
cards.a: W(12) ≈ 242 million gallons, an underestimate. The tangent line is L(t) = 250 − 4(t − 10), so L(12) = 250 − 8 = 242. Since W''(t) > 0 for 10 < t < 12, W is concave up there, its graph lies above the tangent line, and L(12) is below W(12).
cards.h: → tangent line, evaluate, concavity decides
cards.n: 'Underestimate because W is decreasing' cites W′, which does not decide the side; and 242 needs its units, millions of gallons.

cards.q:
Approximate f(1.8) using the line tangent to the graph of f at x = 2. The table gives values of a differentiable function f and its derivative.
x · f(x) · f′(x)
0 · 5 · −3
2 · 1 · 1.5
5 · 7 · 2
cards.h: → tangent line at the nearest row, then evaluate
cards.n: Using +0.2 for 1.8 − 2 gives 1.3, the estimate for f(2.2); to the left of 2 the step is negative.

cards.q: Approximate f(2.1) using the tangent line to f at x = 2, where f(2) = 5 and f'(x) = √(x³ + 1). Then decide whether the approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate.
cards.a: f(2.1) ≈ 5.3, an underestimate. f'(2) = √9 = 3, so L(x) = 5 + 3(x − 2) and L(2.1) = 5.3. f''(x) = 3x²/(2√(x³ + 1)) > 0 for 2 ≤ x ≤ 2.1, so f is concave up there and its graph lies above the tangent line.
cards.h: → f′(2), tangent line, sign of f″ on [2, 2.1]
cards.n: With f unknown the tangent line is the only tool; concluding from f′ > 0 ('f is increasing') gives no information about over or under.
