cards.q: Approximate f(1.4) using the tangent line at x = 1, and decide whether it is an overestimate or an underestimate, given that f(1) = 2, f'(1) = −0.5, and the graph of f′ is a curve that decreases throughout the interval 0 < x < 3.
cards.a: f(1.4) ≈ 1.8, an overestimate. L(x) = 2 − 0.5(x − 1), so L(1.4) = 2 − 0.2 = 1.8. The graph of f′ is decreasing on 1 < x < 1.4, so f is concave down there, and a concave-down graph lies below its tangent line.
cards.h: → tangent line, then f′ decreasing ⇒ concave down
cards.n: 'f′ is negative, so f is decreasing, so overestimate' reaches the right word for the wrong reason; the reason is that f′ is decreasing.

cards.q: Approximate f(2.9) using the tangent line at x = 3, given that f(3) = 10, f'(3) = 4 and f is concave up on 0 < x < 4. Decide whether the approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate.
cards.a: f(2.9) ≈ 9.6, an underestimate. L(2.9) = 10 + 4(2.9 − 3) = 10 − 0.4 = 9.6. A concave-up graph lies above its tangent lines on both sides of the point of tangency, so the tangent line value is below f(2.9) even though 2.9 is to the left of 3.
cards.h: → tangent line, then concavity on the left side too
cards.n: Flipping the conclusion for points left of a is the trap; which side of the tangent the curve lies on depends only on concavity.

cards.q: Approximate the y-coordinate of the point on the curve x² + xy + y² = 7 with x = 1.1 near (1, 2), using the line tangent to the curve at (1, 2).
cards.a: y ≈ 1.92. Implicit differentiation gives 2x + y + x(dy/dx) + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y), which is −4/5 at (1, 2). The tangent line is y = 2 − 0.8(x − 1), and at x = 1.1 it gives 2 − 0.08 = 1.92 (the true value is about 1.918).
cards.h: → implicit dy/dx at (1, 2), tangent line, evaluate
cards.n: Borrows implicit differentiation from Unit 3: dropping the y from d(xy)/dx = x(dy/dx) + y gives slope −2/5 and the wrong estimate 1.96.

cards.q: Explain why a tangent line approximation of f(x) is an underestimate when f'' > 0 between the point of tangency a and x.
cards.a: f'' > 0 there means f′ is increasing, so f is concave up. To the right of a the curve's slope exceeds the tangent's slope f'(a); to the left it is smaller. Either way the curve bends upward away from the line, so f(x) > L(x) and L underestimates.
cards.h: → f″ > 0 → f′ increasing → the curve bends up away from the tangent on both sides → L below f
cards.n: 'Underestimate because f is increasing' cites f′, which never decides the side; the sign of f″ between a and x does.
o: A concave-up graph lies above each of its tangent lines, so any tangent line value is below the function value.
For f(x) = x² at a = 1, L(x) = 2x − 1 and f(x) − L(x) = (x − 1)² > 0 for every x ≠ 1.

w.a: It is an underestimate because f is increasing.
w.why: f′ says nothing about which side of the tangent

w.a: It is an underestimate because f'' > 0 means the tangent line is above the curve.
w.why: concave up puts the tangent below the curve

w.a: Tangent line approximations are always underestimates.
w.why: concave down gives overestimates

cards.q: Explain why the tangent line approximation to √x at x = 4 is very accurate at x = 4.1 but poor at x = 9.
cards.a: √x is differentiable at 4, so near 4 its graph is nearly straight and hugs the tangent L(x) = 2 + (x − 4)/4. Farther away the bending adds up: L(4.1) = 2.025 is off by about 0.00015, but L(9) = 3.25 is off by 0.25, since √9 = 3.
cards.h: → locally linear near 4 → the gap between the curve and the tangent grows with the distance from 4
cards.n: 'The tangent line gives the exact value near a' overstates it; the error is small near a but never zero unless f is linear.
o: The gap between √x and L(x) shrinks faster than |x − 4| as x → 4, which is what local linearity means.
√x is concave down, so it falls farther below the tangent line the farther x is from 4.

w.a: The tangent line is equally accurate everywhere because it has the right slope.
w.why: the slope matches only at x = 4

w.a: L(9) must be accurate because 9 is a perfect square.
w.why: being a perfect square does not help the line

w.a: The approximation at 4.1 is exact because 4.1 is so close to 4.
w.why: the error is small, not zero

cards.q: Explain why the sign of f'' at x = a alone cannot settle whether a tangent line approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate.
cards.a: What matters is the concavity on the whole interval from a to x. If f'' changes sign in between, the graph can cross the tangent line. For f(x) = x³ at a = −1, L(x) = 3x + 2 overestimates f(0.5) (3.5 against 0.125) but underestimates f(3) (11 against 27), although f''(−1) < 0.
cards.h: → over or under depends on concavity between a and x → f″ can change sign → the curve can cross the tangent
cards.n: A justification that checks f″ only at a, not on the interval, supports nothing when the interval contains an inflection point.
o: x³ has an inflection point at 0, so between −1 and 0.5 it switches from concave down to concave up.
If f'' is continuous, f''(a) < 0 gives concavity only on some interval around a, which may not reach x.

w.a: f''(−1) < 0, so every tangent line estimate from x = −1 is an overestimate.
w.why: f″ changes sign before x = 3

w.a: The estimate of f(3) must be an overestimate because the tangent was drawn where f is concave down.
w.why: concavity at a need not last out to 3

w.a: Over or under depends on whether x is to the left or right of a.
w.why: it depends on concavity between a and x

cards.q: Explain why the tangent line approximation of f(1.4) at x = 1 is an overestimate when the graph of f′ is decreasing on 0 < x < 3.
cards.a: A decreasing f′ means f is concave down on 0 < x < 3, including between 1 and 1.4. A concave-down graph lies below its tangent lines, so the tangent line value L(1.4) is greater than f(1.4): an overestimate.
cards.h: → f′ decreasing → f concave down → graph below the tangent → L overestimates
cards.n: Reading the sign of f′ (negative, so f is decreasing) instead of the direction of f′ (decreasing) is the trap; concavity comes from how f′ changes.
o: f'' is the slope of the graph of f′, and a decreasing f′ graph has f'' < 0 wherever f'' exists.
Moving right from x = 1, the slope of f keeps dropping below f'(1), so f falls below the tangent line.

w.a: It is an overestimate because f′ is negative, so f is decreasing.
w.why: the sign of f′ does not decide the side

w.a: It is an underestimate because the graph of f′ is decreasing, so f is concave up.
w.why: a decreasing f′ means concave down

w.a: It cannot be decided without a formula for f.
w.why: the behavior of f′ is enough

cards.q: Explain why a = 4 is chosen, rather than a = 4.1, to approximate √4.1 by a tangent line.
cards.a: The tangent line needs exact values of f(a) and f'(a). At a = 4, f(4) = 2 and f'(4) = 1/4 are exact; at a = 4.1 they involve √4.1 itself, the unknown. The nearest point where both values are known exactly, 4, gives the most accurate usable line.
cards.h: → need exact f(a) and f′(a) → √4 = 2 is known, √4.1 is not → take the nearest such point
cards.n: A far point such as a = 9 also has exact values but gives 2.183, a much worse estimate; choose the nearest convenient point.
o: Accuracy falls with the distance from a, so among points with known values the closest one is best, here 4, only 0.1 away.
Using a = 4.1 would need √4.1 to build the line, which is circular.

w.a: a = 4.1 is best because the tangent line is exact there.
w.why: f(4.1) is the unknown being estimated

w.a: Any a works equally well as long as f is differentiable there.
w.why: accuracy falls with the distance from a

w.a: a = 0 is best because √0 = 0 is the easiest value.
w.why: √x has no derivative at 0, and 0 is far from 4.1

cards.q: Explain why f(x) = |x| has no tangent line approximation at x = 0.
cards.a: The approximation needs f'(0), and |x| is not differentiable at 0: its slope is −1 on the left and 1 on the right. Zooming in never makes the graph look like one line, because the corner stays, so no single line approximates |x| on both sides of 0.
cards.h: → corner → no derivative at 0 → not locally linear → no tangent line to approximate with
cards.n: Using a one-sided slope as f′(0) gives a line that fits one side only; there is no tangent line approximation at a corner.
o: Local linearity means the graph becomes indistinguishable from a line under zooming, and |x| looks like the same V at every scale.
Every line through (0, 0) misses |x| by at least |x| on one side, while a true tangent line's error shrinks faster than |x|.

w.a: The tangent line at x = 0 is y = 0 because |0| = 0.
w.why: passing through the point is not tangency

w.a: The tangent line at 0 has slope 1 because |x| = x.
w.why: |x| = −x for x < 0

w.a: Every continuous function has a tangent line approximation.
w.why: continuity does not give a derivative

cards.q: State L'Hospital's Rule with its hypotheses.
cards.a: If f and g are differentiable near a (except possibly at a), g′(x) ≠ 0 near a, and either lim f(x) = lim g(x) = 0 or both limits are infinite as x → a, then lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f′(x)/g′(x), provided the limit of f′/g′ exists (or is ±∞). It also holds for one-sided limits and for x → ±∞.
cards.h: → hypotheses (form, differentiability), then conclusion
cards.n: The conclusion uses f′/g′, the ratio of the derivatives, not (f/g)′, the derivative of the ratio; and the form must be checked first.

cards.q: Identify the indeterminate forms to which L'Hospital's Rule applies directly.
cards.a: Only 0/0 and ∞/∞: lim f(x) = 0 and lim g(x) = 0, or f(x) and g(x) both unbounded (with any signs, ±∞/±∞). These are the forms the CED assesses; other indeterminate forms are not assessed on the AP exam.
cards.h: → two forms, stated as limits
cards.n: Show the form as two limits, lim f(x) = 0 and lim g(x) = 0; writing 'lim f(x)/g(x) = 0/0' treats a label as a value, which the CED calls incorrect.

cards.q: Explain the two most common errors when applying L'Hospital's Rule.
cards.a: 1) Differentiating the quotient with the quotient rule, (f/g)′, instead of differentiating the numerator and denominator separately, f′/g′. 2) Applying the rule when the limit is not 0/0 or ∞/∞: lim (x + 1)/x as x → 0 has the form 1/0, where the rule would give 1/1 = 1, but the one-sided limits are −∞ and +∞, so the limit does not exist.
cards.h: → two errors, each with its fix
cards.n: Verifying the form is part of showing the rule applies, so skipping it can cost the point even when the numerical answer happens to be right.

cards.q: Describe what to do when one application of L'Hospital's Rule still yields 0/0.
cards.a: Check that the new quotient f′(x)/g′(x) still has the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, say so, and apply the rule again to get f″(x)/g″(x), simplifying between steps. For lim (1 − cos x)/x² as x → 0: 0/0 gives sin x/(2x), still 0/0, which gives cos x/2 → 1/2.
cards.h: → recheck the form, apply again, simplify
cards.n: A second pass without rechecking fails once the form is no longer indeterminate; some limits, like x/√(x² + 1) at ∞, cycle forever and need algebra.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x}$ and state the growth ranking it illustrates.
cards.a: 0. As x → ∞, ln x → ∞ and x → ∞, so the form is ∞/∞ and L'Hospital's Rule gives lim (1/x)/1 = lim 1/x = 0. The ranking it shows: ln x grows more slowly than any positive power of x, and powers grow more slowly than exponentials such as eˣ.
cards.h: → form, rule, value, ranking
cards.n: Writing lim ln x/x = ∞/∞ = 1 treats the label as a value; ∞/∞ says only that more work is needed, and the limit turns out to be 0.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{2x}-1}{\sin x}$.
cards.a: 2. As x → 0, $e^{2x}-1 \to 0$ and sin x → 0, so the form is 0/0 and L'Hospital's Rule applies: the limit equals lim $\frac{2e^{2x}}{\cos x}$ = 2(1)/1 = 2.
cards.h: → state both limits are 0, differentiate separately
cards.n: Dropping the chain-rule factor 2 from the derivative of $e^{2x}$ gives 1; the 2 comes from the inner function 2x.

cards.q: Explain why L'Hôpital's Rule fails to help on $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x+\sin x}{x}$, and evaluate the limit a different way.
cards.a: The limit is 1. The form is ∞/∞, but the rule gives lim (1 + cos x)/1, which oscillates between 0 and 2 and has no limit, so the rule gives no information. Dividing through by x instead: 1 + (sin x)/x → 1 + 0 = 1, since |sin x/x| ≤ 1/x → 0.
cards.h: → rule inconclusive, then algebra
cards.n: Concluding 'the limit does not exist' because lim f′/g′ does not exist is the trap; the rule says nothing when that limit fails to exist.

cards.q: A student applies L'Hopital's Rule to $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^{2}}{\sin x}$ with no comment on the form. Decide whether this earns full credit, and explain what's missing.
cards.a: No. The response must first show that the rule applies: lim x² = 0 and lim sin x = 0 as x → 0, so the limit has the indeterminate form 0/0. Only then may it write lim 2x/cos x = 0/1 = 0. A correct 0 without that verification can lose the point for showing the rule applies.
cards.h: → no, then the missing statement
cards.n: The CED says students must show that the rule applies; a bare 'by L'Hospital' followed by derivatives skips that step.

cards.q:
Evaluate each limit. Each has the form 0/0 or ∞/∞: say which, then apply L'Hospital's Rule as many times as needed.
1. $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\ln x}{x-1}$
2. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan(3x)}{x}$
3. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^{2}}{e^{x}}$
4. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x-\sin x}{x^{3}}$
5. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x^{2}+1}{5x^{2}-x}$
6. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\arctan x}{x}$
7. $\lim_{x \to \pi} \frac{\sin x}{x-\pi}$
8. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{x}-1-x}{x^{2}}$
9. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln(x^{2}+1)}{\ln x}$
10. $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^{3}-8}{x^{2}-4}$
cards.h: → form, derivatives, value, one line each
cards.n: Each repeated application needs the form rechecked (items 3, 4, 5, 8); 5 and 10 also yield to algebra, which is equally valid.

cards.q:
Decide whether L'Hospital's Rule applies to each limit as written, and give the limit.
1. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos x}{x}$
2. $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \frac{\ln x}{x}$
3. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x+1}$
4. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{e^{x}}{x^{3}}$
5. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{x}-1}{x^{2}}$
6. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{2x+1}{x-3}$
cards.a:
1 → no: the form is 1/0. The limit does not exist (−∞ from the left, +∞ from the right).
2 → no: the form is −∞/0⁺. The limit is −∞; the rule, misapplied, gives lim (1/x)/1 = +∞.
3 → no: the form is 0/1. The limit is 0 by direct substitution.
4 → yes, ∞/∞, three times: eˣ/(3x²), eˣ/(6x), eˣ/6 → ∞. The quotient grows without bound.
5 → yes, 0/0 once: eˣ/(2x) has the form 1/0, so stop; the limit does not exist (−∞ from the left, +∞ from the right). A second application, giving 1/2, is invalid.
6 → yes, ∞/∞: 2/1 → 2.
cards.h: → form first, then yes or no, then the limit
cards.n: Item 5 is the trap: after one valid step the form is 1/0, and a second application wrongly gives 1/2.

cards.q: Find $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$, where f and g are twice-differentiable functions with f(3) = 0, g(3) = 0, f'(3) = 4 and g'(3) = −2.
cards.a: −2. f and g are differentiable, hence continuous, so lim f(x) = f(3) = 0 and lim g(x) = g(3) = 0 as x → 3: the form is 0/0, and L'Hospital's Rule applies. Since f′ and g′ are continuous and g′(3) ≠ 0, the limit is lim f′(x)/g′(x) = f′(3)/g′(3) = 4/(−2) = −2.
cards.h: → limits of f and g are 0, rule, evaluate f′/g′ at 3
cards.n: Writing f(3)/g(3) = 0/0 and stopping earns nothing; the limits of f and g must be stated as 0, which continuity supplies.

cards.q: Find the value of k for which $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{kx}-1}{3x} = 2$.
cards.a: k = 6. As x → 0, $e^{kx}-1 \to 0$ and 3x → 0, so the form is 0/0 and L'Hospital's Rule gives lim $\frac{ke^{kx}}{3}$ = k/3. Setting k/3 = 2 gives k = 6.
cards.h: → check 0/0, apply the rule, solve for k
cards.n: Differentiating $e^{kx}$ as $e^{kx}$, without the factor k, gives 1/3 = 2 with no solution; the chain rule brings down k.

cards.q: Find $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{f(x)-3}{x^{2}-1}$, where f is twice differentiable with f(1) = 3 and f'(1) = 4.
cards.a: 2. f is continuous at 1, so lim (f(x) − 3) = f(1) − 3 = 0, and lim (x² − 1) = 0 as x → 1: the form is 0/0. By L'Hospital's Rule the limit is lim f′(x)/(2x) = f′(1)/2 = 4/2 = 2, using the continuity of f′.
cards.h: → check 0/0, differentiate top and bottom, evaluate
cards.n: Writing the new numerator as f′(x) − 3 keeps the constant; the derivative of 3 is 0, so the numerator's derivative is just f′(x).

cards.q: Write the statement that shows L'Hospital's Rule applies to $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{x}-\cos x}{x}$, then evaluate the limit.
cards.a: Since lim (eˣ − cos x) = 1 − 1 = 0 and lim x = 0 as x → 0, the limit has the indeterminate form 0/0, so L'Hospital's Rule applies. Then the limit is lim (eˣ + sin x)/1 = 1 + 0 = 1.
cards.h: → two limits, the form named, then the rule
cards.n: Writing lim (eˣ − cos x)/x = 0/0 uses the label as a value, which the CED calls incorrect; state the two limits separately.

cards.q: Identify the errors in this work: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(2x)}{x} = \frac{\lim_{x \to 0} \sin(2x)}{\lim_{x \to 0} x} = \frac{0}{0}$, so the limit does not exist.
cards.a: Two errors. The limit of a quotient is not the quotient of the limits when the denominator's limit is 0, and 0/0 is a label for an indeterminate form, not a value, so it says nothing about existence. Correctly: lim sin(2x) = 0 and lim x = 0, so L'Hospital's Rule gives lim 2cos(2x)/1 = 2. The limit is 2.
cards.h: → two errors named, then the correct limit
cards.n: '0/0 means undefined, so no limit' is the trap; an indeterminate form is a signal to do more work, not a verdict.

cards.q: Explain why applying L'Hospital's Rule to $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \frac{\ln x}{x}$ gives a wrong answer.
cards.a: The rule needs the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, but here ln x → −∞ while x → 0⁺: the form is −∞/0⁺, which is not indeterminate. A large negative number over a tiny positive one gives a limit of −∞. The rule, misapplied, gives lim (1/x)/1 = +∞, the wrong sign.
cards.h: → form is −∞/0⁺ → not 0/0 or ∞/∞ → rule does not apply → limit is −∞
cards.n: Differentiating top and bottom before checking the form is the trap; the check is the first line of any L'Hospital solution.
o: Written as (ln x)·(1/x), the factors head to −∞ and +∞, so the product heads to −∞.
At x = 0.01, ln x/x ≈ −4.6/0.01 = −460, already large and negative.

w.a: By L'Hospital's Rule the limit is lim (1/x)/1 = +∞.
w.why: the form is not indeterminate

w.a: The limit is 0 because the numerator and denominator both go to 0.
w.why: ln x → −∞, not 0

w.a: The form is ∞/0, which is indeterminate, so the rule applies.
w.why: ∞/0 is not one of the two forms

cards.q: Explain why $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{f'(3)}{g'(3)}$ when f and g are twice differentiable, f(3) = g(3) = 0 and g'(3) ≠ 0.
cards.a: Differentiable functions are continuous, so lim f(x) = f(3) = 0 and lim g(x) = g(3) = 0: the form is 0/0 and L'Hospital's Rule applies. Twice differentiable makes f′ and g′ continuous, so lim f′(x)/g′(x) = f′(3)/g′(3), with g′(3) ≠ 0.
cards.h: → differentiable ⇒ continuous ⇒ both limits 0 → rule applies → f′, g′ continuous → evaluate at 3
cards.n: Stating f(3) = g(3) = 0 without continuity leaves a gap: the rule needs the limits of f and g, not only their values at 3.
o: By local linearity f(x) ≈ f'(3)(x − 3) and g(x) ≈ g'(3)(x − 3) near 3, so the ratio is close to f'(3)/g'(3).
Dividing top and bottom by x − 3 gives [(f(x) − f(3))/(x − 3)]/[(g(x) − g(3))/(x − 3)], whose limit is f'(3)/g'(3) by the definition of the derivative.

w.a: The limit is 0/0, so it does not exist.
w.why: 0/0 is a label, not a value

w.a: The limit is f(3)/g(3) = 0 because both functions are 0 there.
w.why: 0/0 cannot be evaluated by substitution

w.a: By the quotient rule the limit is (f′g − fg′)/g² at x = 3.
w.why: the rule uses f′/g′, not the derivative of f/g

cards.q: Explain why writing $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 3x}{x} = \frac{0}{0}$ is incorrect, even as a first step.
cards.a: An equals sign asserts a value, but 0/0 is not a number: it is a label saying both limits are 0 and the limit is still undetermined. The correct first step states lim sin 3x = 0 and lim x = 0, so the form is 0/0; L'Hospital's Rule then gives lim 3cos 3x/1 = 3.
cards.h: → '=' claims a value → 0/0 labels a form, not a number → state the two limits instead
cards.n: The CED names writing a limit equal to 0/0 as incorrect; report the form in words or as two separate limits.
o: Different 0/0 limits have different values, such as sin 3x/x → 3 and sin x/x → 1, so 0/0 cannot equal any one number.
Saying 'the limit has the indeterminate form 0/0' describes the quotient without claiming a value for it.

w.a: It is fine to write = 0/0 because both parts are zero.
w.why: the equation claims a value that does not exist

w.a: 0/0 = 1, so the limit is 1.
w.why: 0/0 has no value, and this limit is 3

w.a: 0/0 means the limit is undefined.
w.why: an indeterminate form can still have a limit

cards.q: Explain why, when f(a) = g(a) = 0 and g'(a) ≠ 0 for differentiable f and g, the ratio f(x)/g(x) is close to f'(a)/g'(a) for x near a.
cards.a: By local linearity, near a, f(x) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)(x − a) = f'(a)(x − a) and g(x) ≈ g'(a)(x − a). The factors x − a cancel in the ratio, leaving f'(a)/g'(a). This is the idea behind L'Hospital's Rule: the ratio of the functions is governed by the ratio of their slopes.
cards.h: → near a both functions look like their tangent lines → f ≈ f′(a)(x − a), g ≈ g′(a)(x − a) → ratio of slopes
cards.n: This explains the rule; on the exam the justification still states lim f(x) = lim g(x) = 0 before the rule is applied.
o: Zoomed in at (a, 0), both graphs look like lines through the same point, and the ratio of their heights is the ratio of their slopes.
f(x)/g(x) = [(f(x) − f(a))/(x − a)] ÷ [(g(x) − g(a))/(x − a)], and each difference quotient tends to its derivative.

w.a: The ratio is close to 0/0 because both functions are near 0.
w.why: 0/0 is not a value

w.a: The ratio is close to f(a)/g(a) because the functions are continuous.
w.why: f(a)/g(a) = 0/0 is undefined

w.a: The ratio is close to (f/g)′(a) by the quotient rule.
w.why: the rule uses the ratio of the derivatives

cards.q: Explain why applying L'Hospital's Rule twice to $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{x}-1}{x^{2}}$ gives the wrong answer 1/2.
cards.a: The first application is valid (0/0) and gives lim eˣ/(2x). That quotient has the form 1/0, which is not indeterminate, so the rule cannot be applied again. Since eˣ/(2x) → −∞ from the left and +∞ from the right, the limit does not exist; 1/2 comes from misusing the rule.
cards.h: → first step valid (0/0) → new form 1/0 → not indeterminate → the rule stops → the limit does not exist
cards.n: Recheck the form after every application; a second pass without the check is the classic error.
o: Near 0, eˣ − 1 ≈ x, so the quotient behaves like x/x² = 1/x, which is unbounded.
At x = 0.01 the quotient is about 100.5 and at x = −0.01 about −99.5, nowhere near 1/2.

w.a: Applying the rule twice gives eˣ/2 → 1/2, so the limit is 1/2.
w.why: the second application is on a 1/0 form

w.a: The limit is 0 because eˣ − 1 → 0.
w.why: the denominator also → 0, and faster

w.a: You can keep applying the rule until you get a number.
w.why: each application needs a 0/0 or ∞/∞ form

cards.q: Explain why $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^{2}}{e^{x}} = 0$ shows that eˣ grows faster than x².
cards.a: Both grow without bound, so the form is ∞/∞, and L'Hospital's Rule gives lim 2x/eˣ, again ∞/∞, then lim 2/eˣ = 0. A ratio tending to 0 means the denominator eventually dwarfs the numerator: eˣ grows faster than x².
cards.h: → ∞/∞ → rule twice, form checked each time → ratio → 0 → the denominator dominates
cards.n: 'Both go to ∞, so the ratio is 1' treats ∞/∞ as a value; the rule, with the form checked, shows the ratio → 0.
o: At x = 20, x²/eˣ = 400/(4.85 × 10⁸) ≈ 8 × 10⁻⁷, already tiny.
The same argument, applied n times, shows xⁿ/eˣ → 0 for every positive integer n.

w.a: The limit is 1 because both go to infinity.
w.why: ∞/∞ is a form, not the value 1

w.a: x² grows faster because it is a power and eˣ is only e to a power.
w.why: exponentials outgrow every power

w.a: The limit is ∞/∞, so the two grow at the same rate.
w.why: the form says nothing until the limit is found

cards.q: State the Mean Value Theorem with its hypotheses.
cards.a: If f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] and differentiable on the open interval (a, b), then there is at least one c in (a, b) with $f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. In words: somewhere strictly inside the interval, the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change over [a, b].
cards.h: → two hypotheses, then the conclusion about c
cards.n: Dropping either hypothesis, or putting c in the closed interval [a, b], misstates it: the guarantee is an interior c, and only when both conditions hold.

cards.q: Explain the geometric meaning of the Mean Value Theorem.
cards.a: At least one point strictly between a and b has a tangent line parallel to the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)). Parallel lines have equal slopes, so the tangent slope f'(c) equals the secant slope $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, the average rate of change on [a, b].
cards.h: → tangent parallel to secant, so equal slopes
cards.n: 'The tangent line equals the secant line' is wrong: the lines are parallel (equal slopes) and usually distinct.

cards.q: Explain how to write an MVT justification that earns full credit.
cards.a: Three moves. Check the hypotheses with a reason: 'f is differentiable, so it is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)' (or cite the given information). Compute the average rate of change $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ with the numbers shown. Conclude by name: 'By the Mean Value Theorem, there is a c in (a, b) with f'(c) = [that value].'
cards.h: → hypotheses, the number, the named conclusion
cards.n: 'By MVT, yes' with no hypothesis check earns nothing, and 'f is continuous' alone misses differentiability; name the theorem and both conditions.

cards.q: State Rolle's Theorem and relate it to the Mean Value Theorem.
cards.a: If f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then there is at least one c in (a, b) with f'(c) = 0. It is the Mean Value Theorem in the case where the secant slope $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ is 0, so the tangent line at c is horizontal.
cards.h: → three hypotheses, the conclusion, then the link
cards.n: Forgetting f(a) = f(b) makes Rolle's claim false; the CED's EK names only the MVT, and citing it with average rate 0 is always acceptable.

cards.q: State the consequence of the MVT about a function whose derivative is identically zero.
cards.a: If f'(x) = 0 for every x in an interval, then f is constant on that interval. For any x₁ < x₂ there, the MVT gives a c between them with f(x₂) − f(x₁) = f'(c)(x₂ − x₁) = 0. Consequently, if f' = g' on an interval, then f − g is constant there.
cards.h: → the conclusion, then the MVT argument in one line
cards.n: The result needs an interval: f(x) = |x|/x has derivative 0 wherever it is defined, yet it is not constant, because its domain skips x = 0.

cards.q: Find the value of c guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem for $f(x)=x^{2}-4x$ on [1,5].
cards.a: c = 3. f is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [1, 5] and differentiable on (1, 5). The average rate of change is $\frac{f(5)-f(1)}{5-1} = \frac{5-(-3)}{4} = 2$. Setting f'(c) = 2c − 4 = 2 gives c = 3, which lies in (1, 5).
cards.h: → check hypotheses, average rate, solve f′(c) = it
cards.n: Solving f'(c) = 0 instead of f'(c) = average rate, or not checking that c lies inside (1, 5), are the two usual slips.

cards.q: Find the value(s) of c guaranteed by Rolle's Theorem for $f(x)=x^{3}-3x$ on $\left[-\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3}\right]$.
cards.a: c = −1 and c = 1. f is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable everywhere, and $f(-\sqrt{3}) = -3\sqrt{3} + 3\sqrt{3} = 0 = f(\sqrt{3})$. Then $f'(c) = 3c^{2} - 3 = 0$ gives c = ±1, and both lie in $\left(-\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{3}\right)$ since √3 ≈ 1.73.
cards.h: → verify f(a) = f(b), solve f′(c) = 0, keep interior c
cards.n: Reporting only c = 1 loses half the answer: Rolle's Theorem guarantees at least one c, and here both roots lie inside the interval.

cards.q: A differentiable function f has table values f(1) = 4 and f(5) = 16. Compute the average rate of change of f on [1,5], and state what the Mean Value Theorem guarantees.
cards.a: The average rate of change is $\frac{16-4}{5-1} = 3$. Because f is differentiable, it is continuous on [1, 5] and differentiable on (1, 5), so the Mean Value Theorem guarantees at least one c with 1 < c < 5 and f'(c) = 3. The table cannot say where c is or whether there is more than one.
cards.h: → one quotient, then the named guarantee
cards.n: Claiming f'(3) = 3 (the midpoint) or f' = 3 throughout invents information; the theorem gives the existence of some c, not its location.

cards.q:
Determine whether there must be a time t with 2 < t < 8 at which H′(t) = −1.5, and justify your answer. H(t) is the depth of snow, in centimeters, t hours after midnight; H is differentiable.
t (hours) · H(t) (cm)
0 · 40
2 · 46
5 · 44
8 · 37
12 · 31
cards.a: Yes. H is differentiable, so it is continuous on [2, 8] and differentiable on (2, 8). $\frac{H(8)-H(2)}{8-2} = \frac{37-46}{6} = -1.5$. By the Mean Value Theorem there is a time t in (2, 8) with H'(t) = −1.5 cm per hour: at that instant the snow depth is decreasing at 1.5 cm per hour.
cards.h: → yes or no, hypotheses, quotient, MVT by name
cards.n: Using H(5) or the whole table instead of the endpoints 2 and 8, or omitting 'H is differentiable, so continuous', loses the point.

cards.q:
Decide whether the Mean Value Theorem applies to each function on the given interval, and give the reason.
(a) $x^{2/3}$ on [−1, 8]
(b) √x on [0, 4]
(c) 1/x on [−1, 2]
(d) |x − 1| on [2, 5]
(e) tan x on [0, π]
(f) ln x on [1, e]
(g) $x^{1/3}$ on [−1, 1]
(h) f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 2x − 1 for x > 1, on [0, 3]
cards.a:
(a) → no: continuous, but f'(0) does not exist (cusp at 0, inside the interval)
(b) → yes: continuous on [0, 4], differentiable on (0, 4); f'(0) failing at the endpoint does not matter
(c) → no: 1/x is undefined, so not continuous, at x = 0
(d) → yes: on [2, 5], f(x) = x − 1; the corner at x = 1 is outside the interval
(e) → no: tan x is undefined at x = π/2
(f) → yes: ln x is continuous and differentiable for x > 0
(g) → no: vertical tangent at 0, so f'(0) does not exist (a c happens to exist anyway, but nothing guaranteed it)
(h) → yes: both pieces give 1 at x = 1 and both slopes are 2 there, so f is differentiable on (0, 3)
cards.h: → yes or no per line, with the failing hypothesis
cards.n: Differentiability is needed only on the OPEN interval: √x on [0, 4] qualifies even though f'(0) does not exist.

cards.q: Find every c in (0, 3) guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem for f(x) = x² when x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 2x − 1 when x > 1.
cards.a: c = 5/6. The pieces agree at x = 1 (both give 1) and so do their slopes (2x gives 2, and 2), so f is continuous on [0, 3] and differentiable on (0, 3). Average rate = $\frac{f(3)-f(0)}{3-0} = \frac{5-0}{3} = \frac{5}{3}$. On (0, 1), f'(c) = 2c = 5/3 gives c = 5/6; on (1, 3), f' = 2 ≠ 5/3. So c = 5/6 is the only value.
cards.h: → check the join, average rate, solve on each piece
cards.n: Solving on one piece only, or skipping the check at x = 1 (the one place differentiability could fail; Unit 2's join test), leaves the answer unsupported.

cards.q: Determine the largest possible value of f(6) if f is differentiable, f(2) = 5, and f′(x) ≤ 3 for all x.
cards.a: 17. f is differentiable, so the Mean Value Theorem applies on [2, 6]: f(6) − f(2) = f'(c)(6 − 2) for some c in (2, 6). Since f'(c) ≤ 3, f(6) ≤ 5 + 3 · 4 = 17. The bound is reached by f(x) = 3x − 1, so no smaller bound is possible.
cards.h: → MVT turns a derivative bound into a value bound
cards.n: Reporting 'f(6) = 17' as a fact misreads the task: the MVT gives f(6) ≤ 17, with equality only if f' = 3 on the whole interval.

cards.q: Decide whether the Mean Value Theorem applies to f(x) = |x| on [-1, 2].
cards.a: It does not apply. f is continuous on [−1, 2], but not differentiable at x = 0, which lies in (−1, 2): the slope is −1 on the left and 1 on the right. So nothing is guaranteed, and in fact no c works: the average rate is (2 − 1)/3 = 1/3, while f' is only ±1.
cards.h: → continuous, yes → corner at 0 inside (−1, 2) → not differentiable → no guarantee (and no c exists)
cards.n: 'The MVT applies because |x| is continuous' checks one hypothesis only; the corner at 0 lies inside the interval, so differentiability fails.
o: The left and right derivatives at 0 are −1 and 1, so f'(0) does not exist and the open-interval hypothesis fails.
Check the conclusion directly: the secant slope is 1/3, but every tangent slope is −1 or 1, so no c can exist.

w.a: The MVT applies because |x| is continuous on [−1, 2].
w.why: continuity alone is not enough; differentiability on (−1, 2) is also required

w.a: It does not apply because f(−1) ≠ f(2).
w.why: equal endpoint values are Rolle's extra hypothesis, not the MVT's

w.a: It applies with c = 0, where the graph has its minimum.
w.why: f'(0) does not exist, so c = 0 cannot satisfy f'(c) = 1/3

cards.q: Explain why a driver who covers 150 miles in 2.5 hours must at some instant have been driving at exactly 60 miles per hour, assuming the position function is differentiable.
cards.a: Let s(t) be the distance traveled, in miles, at t hours. s is differentiable, so it is continuous on [0, 2.5] and differentiable on (0, 2.5). The average velocity is $\frac{150-0}{2.5-0} = 60$ mph. By the Mean Value Theorem, s'(t) = 60 mph for some t in (0, 2.5).
cards.h: → s differentiable → average velocity 60 mph → MVT → s′(t) = 60 at some interior t
cards.n: 'The average was 60, so the driver went 60 the whole time' confuses average and instantaneous; the MVT promises at least one instant, not every instant.
o: The secant line of the position graph from (0, 0) to (2.5, 150) has slope 60, and the MVT gives a tangent line of the same slope at some interior time.
If the velocity were below 60 mph at every instant, less than 150 miles would be covered in 2.5 hours; the MVT turns that intuition into a guarantee.

w.a: The driver averaged 60 mph, so the speedometer read 60 the whole trip.
w.why: an average does not fix the speed at every instant

w.a: 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60, so the driver was going 60.
w.why: computes the average but never invokes the MVT or its hypotheses

w.a: By the Intermediate Value Theorem the speed must hit 60.
w.why: names the wrong theorem; the data are positions, and the MVT links them to a velocity

cards.q: Explain why no c in (−1, 8) satisfies $f'(c) = \frac{f(8)-f(-1)}{9}$ for $f(x) = x^{2/3}$, and why this does not contradict the Mean Value Theorem.
cards.a: The average rate is (4 − 1)/9 = 1/3. $f'(x) = \frac{2}{3}x^{-1/3}$ is negative for x < 0, and for x > 0 it equals 1/3 only at x = 8, an endpoint. No contradiction: f'(0) does not exist, so f is not differentiable on (−1, 8) and the MVT promises nothing.
cards.h: → average rate 1/3 → f′ = 1/3 only at the endpoint 8 → f′(0) undefined → hypothesis fails → no promise
cards.n: 'The MVT is false here' misreads a conditional theorem: when a hypothesis fails, the conclusion may fail too.
o: The graph has a cusp at the origin, so the differentiability hypothesis on the open interval is not met, and the theorem makes no claim.
A statement 'if P then Q' is contradicted only when P holds and Q fails; here P fails.

w.a: The MVT fails because $x^{2/3}$ is not continuous at 0.
w.why: $x^{2/3}$ is continuous at 0; it is the derivative that fails to exist

w.a: c = 8 works, so the MVT is satisfied.
w.why: 8 is an endpoint, and the MVT's c must lie in the open interval

w.a: There must be an arithmetic mistake, since the MVT always gives a c.
w.why: the MVT gives a c only when both hypotheses hold

cards.q: Explain why the Mean Value Theorem requires continuity on the closed interval [a, b], using f(x) = x for 0 ≤ x < 1 with f(1) = 0.
cards.a: This f is differentiable on (0, 1) with f'(x) = 1, and f(0) = f(1) = 0, so the average rate on [0, 1] is 0. Yet f' = 1 ≠ 0 everywhere inside. The failure is at x = 1: $\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} f(x) = 1 \ne f(1)$, so f is not continuous on [0, 1], and nothing is guaranteed.
cards.h: → differentiable inside, but a jump at the endpoint → secant slope 0 → every tangent slope 1 → no c
cards.n: Checking differentiability on (a, b) alone is not enough: continuity at the endpoints themselves is a separate hypothesis that must be stated.
o: A jump at an endpoint changes the secant slope without changing any tangent slope, so the two need not match.
Differentiability on (a, b) says nothing about the endpoints; continuity on [a, b] is what ties f(a) and f(b) to the interior behavior.

w.a: The MVT fails because f is not differentiable on (0, 1).
w.why: f is differentiable on (0, 1), with f'(x) = 1

w.a: Differentiability implies continuity, so continuity never needs checking.
w.why: differentiability on the open interval says nothing about the endpoints

w.a: The MVT works here with c = 1.
w.why: c must lie inside (0, 1), and f'(1) does not exist

cards.q: State the Extreme Value Theorem with its hypotheses.
cards.a: If f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b], then f has at least one absolute maximum value and at least one absolute minimum value on [a, b]. Both hypotheses matter: the interval must be closed and bounded, and f must be continuous on all of it.
cards.h: → one hypothesis on f, one on the interval, the conclusion
cards.n: Adding 'differentiable' is harmless but unnecessary; omitting 'closed interval', or saying 'f has a maximum' with no interval, misstates the theorem.

cards.q: Define a critical point of f.
cards.a: An interior point c of the domain of f at which f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) does not exist. f(c) itself must be defined: x = 0 is not a critical point of f(x) = 1/x, although it still splits a sign chart.
cards.h: → two conditions on f′, one on f
cards.n: Calling the zeros of f (its x-intercepts) critical points confuses f with f'; the definition is about f' being 0 or undefined.

cards.q: Contrast relative (local) extrema and absolute (global) extrema.
cards.a: A relative maximum at c means f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x in some open interval around c; an absolute maximum means f(c) ≥ f(x) for every x in the whole domain or stated interval (minima likewise, with ≤). An absolute extremum at an interior point is also relative, but a relative extremum need not be absolute.
cards.h: → neighborhood versus whole interval, then how they relate
cards.n: Reporting the location x = c when the question asks for the extreme VALUE f(c), or the reverse, is the classic slip: 'the maximum is 5, at x = 2'.

cards.q: Describe how to find the critical points of a function whose derivative is a fraction or contains a radical.
cards.a: Rewrite f' as one fraction with no negative exponents. Zeros of the numerator give f' = 0; zeros of the denominator give f' undefined. Keep a value only if f itself is defined there: a zero of the denominator where f is also undefined, such as x = 0 for x + 4/x, is not a critical point.
cards.h: → one fraction; numerator, denominator, domain check
cards.n: Setting only the numerator equal to 0 misses the points where f' does not exist, and cusps and corners are often where the extrema are.

cards.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of $f(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}$ on [−1,3].
cards.a: Absolute maximum 0, at x = 0 and x = 3; absolute minimum −4, at x = −1 and x = 2. f is a polynomial, continuous on the closed interval, so both extremes exist (EVT). f'(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2) = 0 at x = 0, 2. Values: f(−1) = −4, f(0) = 0, f(2) = −4, f(3) = 0.
cards.h: → EVT, critical points, table of four values
cards.n: Each extreme value here is attained twice; naming only one location, or answering with points when the question asks for values, loses credit.

cards.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of $f(x) = x^{4}-4x^{2}$ on [−2,3].
cards.a: Absolute maximum 45, at x = 3; absolute minimum −4, at x = −√2 and x = √2. f is continuous on [−2, 3], so both exist (EVT). f'(x) = 4x³ − 8x = 4x(x² − 2) = 0 at x = 0, ±√2, all in the interval. Values: f(−2) = 0, f(−√2) = −4, f(0) = 0, f(√2) = −4, f(3) = 81 − 36 = 45.
cards.h: → EVT, three critical points, five values compared
cards.n: Discarding x = −√2 as 'extraneous' loses a tie for the minimum; every critical point inside [−2, 3] is a candidate.

cards.q: Identify all critical points of $f(x) = x^{2/3}(x-4)$ on its domain.
cards.a: x = 0 and x = 8/5. $f(x) = x^{5/3} - 4x^{2/3}$, so $f'(x) = \frac{5}{3}x^{2/3} - \frac{8}{3}x^{-1/3} = \frac{5x-8}{3x^{1/3}}$. The numerator is 0 at x = 8/5. The denominator is 0 at x = 0, where f(0) = 0 is defined, so f' fails to exist at a point of the domain.
cards.h: → expand, differentiate, one fraction, both zeros
cards.n: Missing x = 0 is the trap: f'(0) does not exist but f(0) does, so 0 is a critical point (a cusp, and in fact a relative maximum).

cards.q:
Identify every critical point of each function, and say whether f′ is 0 or undefined there.
(a) f(x) = x³ − 12x
(b) f(x) = x eˣ
(c) f(x) = x + 4/x
(d) f(x) = |x − 3|
(e) $f(x) = x^{1/3}$
(f) f(x) = sin x + cos x on (0, 2π)
(g) f(x) = x ln x
(h) $f(x) = \frac{x}{x^{2}+1}$
(i) $f(x) = (x^{2}-1)^{2/3}$
cards.a:
(a) f' = 3x² − 12 → x = ±2, f' = 0
(b) f' = eˣ(x + 1) → x = −1, f' = 0
(c) f' = 1 − 4/x² → x = ±2, f' = 0; x = 0 is not in the domain, so it is not critical
(d) corner → x = 3, f' undefined (slopes −1 and 1)
(e) $f' = \frac{1}{3x^{2/3}}$ → x = 0, f' undefined (vertical tangent)
(f) f' = cos x − sin x → x = π/4 and 5π/4, f' = 0
(g) f' = ln x + 1 → x = 1/e, f' = 0 (domain x > 0)
(h) $f' = \frac{1-x^{2}}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}$ → x = ±1, f' = 0
(i) $f' = \frac{4x}{3(x^{2}-1)^{1/3}}$ → x = 0 (f' = 0) and x = ±1 (f' undefined)
cards.h: → one line per function: the values, then 0 or undefined
cards.n: In (c), f' is undefined at 0 only because f is, so 0 is not critical; in (e) and (i), f is defined where f' fails, so those points count.

cards.q:
Decide whether the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum for each function on the interval, and give the reason.
(a) 1/x on [1, 3]
(b) 1/x on [−1, 1]
(c) x² on (−1, 2)
(d) tan x on [0, π/4]
(e) √x on [0, 4]
(f) eˣ on [0, ∞)
(g) f(x) = x for 0 ≤ x < 2 and f(2) = 0, on [0, 2]
cards.a:
(a) → yes: continuous on a closed interval (max 1 at x = 1, min 1/3 at x = 3)
(b) → no: undefined, so not continuous, at x = 0 (and it has neither extreme)
(c) → no: open interval (a minimum 0 at x = 0 happens to exist; values approach 4 but no maximum is attained)
(d) → yes: continuous on [0, π/4] (max 1, min 0)
(e) → yes: continuous on [0, 4] (max 2, min 0)
(f) → no: the interval is unbounded (min 1 at x = 0, no maximum)
(g) → no: discontinuous at x = 2; values approach 2 but never reach it, so there is no maximum (the minimum 0 exists)
cards.h: → yes or no per line, with the failing hypothesis
cards.n: 'Not guaranteed' does not mean 'does not exist': in (c), x² still has an absolute minimum at x = 0 even though the EVT is silent.

cards.q: Identify the relative extrema of f on the open interval (0, 8) and the absolute extrema of f on [0, 8], where the graph of f on [0, 8] consists of line segments joining (0, 2), (2, 5), (4, 1), (6, 4), and (8, −1).
cards.a: Relative maxima f(2) = 5 and f(6) = 4; relative minimum f(4) = 1. Absolute maximum 5, at x = 2; absolute minimum −1, at x = 8. The critical points are the corners x = 2, 4, 6, where f' does not exist and the graph switches between rising and falling. The absolute minimum comes from the endpoint, since −1 < 1.
cards.h: → list the turning points, then compare with the endpoints
cards.n: 'The absolute minimum is 1' misses the endpoint value f(8) = −1; and these extrema sit at corners, where f' does not exist, not where f' = 0.

cards.q:
Classify the critical point x = 0 of each function as a relative maximum, a relative minimum, or neither, and say whether f′(0) is 0 or undefined.
(a) x²
(b) x³
(c) |x|
(d) $x^{1/3}$
(e) −x⁴
(f) $x^{2/3}$
cards.a:
(a) f'(0) = 0 → relative minimum (f' changes − to +)
(b) f'(0) = 0 → neither (f' > 0 on both sides)
(c) f'(0) undefined (corner) → relative minimum
(d) f'(0) undefined (vertical tangent) → neither (f' > 0 on both sides)
(e) f'(0) = 0 → relative maximum (f' changes + to −)
(f) f'(0) undefined (cusp) → relative minimum
cards.h: → one line each: type of critical point, then the verdict
cards.n: (b) and (d) are the classic critical points that are not extrema: f' keeps its sign, whether f'(0) is 0 or undefined.

cards.q: Explain why the Extreme Value Theorem can fail on an open interval.
cards.a: On an open interval f can approach a value at a missing endpoint without ever reaching it. f(x) = x on (0, 1) is continuous, but it takes values arbitrarily close to 0 and to 1 and never equals either, so it has no absolute maximum or minimum. The EVT needs the endpoints included.
cards.h: → open interval → endpoints missing → values approach a bound never reached → no extremum guaranteed
cards.n: 'It fails because f is not continuous' misdiagnoses: f(x) = x is continuous; the missing hypothesis is the closed interval.
o: On [0, 1] the same function attains 0 and 1 at the endpoints; removing the endpoints removes exactly the points where the extremes were attained.
f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1) is continuous yet unbounded above, so there is not even a finite value to be the maximum.

w.a: The EVT fails on open intervals because every function is discontinuous at open endpoints.
w.why: the function can be continuous at every point of the open interval

w.a: f(x) = x on (0, 1) has maximum 1 at x = 1.
w.why: x = 1 is not in the interval, so the value 1 is never attained

w.a: On an open interval a function never has extrema.
w.why: the EVT merely stops guaranteeing them; x² on (−1, 1) has a minimum

cards.q: Identify why an endpoint of a closed interval is not counted as a relative extremum.
cards.a: A relative extremum at c compares f(c) with the values of f on an open interval around c, and at an endpoint no such interval lies inside the domain: only one side exists. Endpoints are still candidates for absolute extrema, which is why the Candidates Test checks them.
cards.h: → relative needs an open interval around c → an endpoint has one side only → not relative → still an absolute candidate
cards.n: Textbooks differ on this convention; the safe habit is to report endpoint extremes as absolute and to classify only interior critical points as relative.
o: The First Derivative Test needs the sign of f' on both sides of c; at an endpoint there is only one side, so the sign-change argument cannot be made.

w.a: Endpoints can never be extrema of any kind.
w.why: endpoints are often where the absolute extrema occur

w.a: An endpoint is not an extremum because f' is not zero there.
w.why: extrema need not have f' = 0, and endpoints can be absolute extrema

cards.q: Explain why x = 0 is a critical point of f(x) = x³ but not a relative extremum.
cards.a: f'(x) = 3x², so f'(0) = 0 and x = 0 is a critical point. But f'(x) > 0 on both sides of 0, so f increases through 0: f(x) < 0 = f(0) for x < 0 and f(x) > 0 for x > 0. f' does not change sign, so there is no relative extremum.
cards.h: → f′(0) = 0, so critical → f′ > 0 on both sides → f rises through 0 → no max or min
cards.n: 'f'(0) = 0, so it is a maximum or minimum' is the error: a critical point is only a candidate (FUN-1.C.3).
o: Every interval around 0 contains points with f(x) > f(0) and points with f(x) < f(0), so f(0) is neither the largest nor the smallest nearby value.
The Second Derivative Test is inconclusive (f''(0) = 0), and the First Derivative Test shows no sign change.

w.a: f'(0) = 0, so f has a relative minimum at 0.
w.why: a zero derivative only makes x = 0 a candidate

w.a: x = 0 is not a critical point because f(0) = 0.
w.why: the definition concerns f'(0), not f(0)

w.a: It is not an extremum because f''(0) = 0.
w.why: f''(0) = 0 only makes the Second Derivative Test inconclusive; x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 and a minimum

cards.q: Explain why x = 0 is not a critical point of f(x) = x + 4/x even though f′(0) does not exist.
cards.a: A critical point must be a point of the domain where f' is 0 or undefined, and f(0) is not defined, so x = 0 cannot be one: there is no point of the graph there to be a maximum or minimum. The critical points are x = ±2, where f'(x) = 1 − 4/x² = 0; x = 0 only splits the sign chart.
cards.h: → critical points need f defined → f(0) undefined → not critical → still a break on the sign chart
cards.n: Listing x = 0 as a critical point, and then as an extremum, is the trap: f' undefined because f itself is undefined does not count.
o: The graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 0, so no point of the graph sits at x = 0 to be an extremum.

w.a: x = 0 is a critical point because f'(0) is undefined.
w.why: f(0) is undefined too, so 0 is not in the domain

w.a: Critical points are where f(x) = 0, and x + 4/x is never 0, so there are none.
w.why: critical points come from f', and f'(±2) = 0

cards.q: State the test for intervals on which f is increasing or decreasing.
cards.a: If f'(x) > 0 for every x in an open interval, then f is increasing on that interval; if f'(x) < 0 for every x in it, then f is decreasing there. To use it: find where f' = 0 or is undefined, make a sign chart of f', and report x-intervals by sign.
cards.h: → sign of f′ ⇒ direction of f, on an interval
cards.n: 'f is increasing because f is positive' confuses f with f'; the test reads the sign of the derivative, and the answer is an interval of x-values.

cards.q: Explain how to build a sign chart for f'.
cards.a: Mark on a number line every x where f' = 0, where f' is undefined, and where f is undefined, plus any domain endpoints. f' keeps one sign between consecutive marks, so test one value in each subinterval and record only the sign of f' there: + means f is increasing, − means decreasing.
cards.h: → marks, one test value per piece, signs
cards.n: A sign chart by itself is not accepted as a justification; the written answer must say, for example, 'f'(x) > 0 on (2, 5)'.

cards.q: Describe how to report intervals of increase when f has a hole or a vertical asymptote.
cards.a: Break the number line at every x where f is undefined as well as at the critical points, and report each piece as its own interval. For f(x) = 1/x, f is decreasing on (−∞, 0) and on (0, ∞), but not on one interval containing both: f(−1) = −1 < f(1) = 1.
cards.h: → split at undefined points, one interval per piece
cards.n: Writing one interval that runs across the asymptote or hole (such as 'decreasing for all x ≠ 0' as a single interval) is wrong; f(−1) < f(1) disproves it for 1/x.

cards.q: Find the intervals where $f(x)=x^{3}-12x$ is increasing.
cards.a: (−∞, −2) and (2, ∞). f'(x) = 3x² − 12 = 3(x − 2)(x + 2), which is 0 at x = ±2. f'(x) > 0 for x < −2 (for example f'(−3) = 15) and for x > 2, while f'(x) < 0 on (−2, 2). f is increasing where f' > 0.
cards.h: → factor f′, sign on each piece, report intervals
cards.n: Answering 'x > 2' alone drops the left interval; 'f is increasing at x = ±2' confuses the break points with the intervals.

cards.q: The graph of f' falls from (-1,4) to (3,-4), then stays constant at -4 until x=5. Identify the interval(s) where f is increasing and where f is decreasing.
cards.a: Increasing on (−1, 1); decreasing on (1, 5). The first piece of f' is the line through (−1, 4) and (3, −4): f'(x) = 2 − 2x, which is 0 at x = 1, positive for x < 1 and negative for 1 < x < 3. On (3, 5), f' = −4 < 0. f is increasing where f' > 0 and decreasing where f' < 0.
cards.h: → find where f′ crosses 0, then read signs
cards.n: Reading 'the graph of f' is falling' as 'f is decreasing' is the trap: on (−1, 1) f' falls but is still positive, so f increases.

cards.q: Find the intervals where $f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$ is decreasing.
cards.a: (−∞, 3). f'(x) = 4x³ − 12x² = 4x²(x − 3). The factor 4x² is never negative, so f' < 0 for every x < 3 except x = 0, where f'(0) = 0, and f' > 0 for x > 3. An isolated zero of f' with no sign change does not interrupt decreasing; listing (−∞, 0) and (0, 3) is also correct.
cards.h: → factor out x², sign of the remaining factor
cards.n: Splitting at x = 0 is harmless, but calling x = 0 an extremum is wrong: f' is negative on both sides, so there is no sign change.

cards.q:
Determine the intervals on which each function is increasing and on which it is decreasing.
(a) f(x) = x³ − 3x²
(b) f(x) = eˣ − x
(c) $f(x) = \frac{x}{x^{2}+1}$
(d) f(x) = x + 1/x
(e) f(x) = (ln x)/x
(f) f(x) = x − 2 sin x on (0, 2π)
(g) f(x) = x² eˣ
(h) f(x) = x − ln x
cards.a:
(a) f' = 3x(x − 2) → increasing (−∞, 0) and (2, ∞); decreasing (0, 2)
(b) f' = eˣ − 1 → decreasing (−∞, 0); increasing (0, ∞)
(c) $f' = \frac{1-x^{2}}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}$ → increasing (−1, 1); decreasing (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞)
(d) f' = (x² − 1)/x² → increasing (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞); decreasing (−1, 0) and (0, 1)
(e) f' = (1 − ln x)/x² → increasing (0, e); decreasing (e, ∞)
(f) f' = 1 − 2cos x, zero at π/3 and 5π/3 → decreasing (0, π/3) and (5π/3, 2π); increasing (π/3, 5π/3)
(g) f' = x eˣ (x + 2) → increasing (−∞, −2) and (0, ∞); decreasing (−2, 0)
(h) f' = 1 − 1/x → decreasing (0, 1); increasing (1, ∞)
cards.h: → f′ in factored form, then the intervals, per line
cards.n: In (d), (−1, 1) must be split at 0, where f is undefined; in (e) and (h) the domain is x > 0, so no interval reaches left of 0.

cards.q: Determine the intervals on which f is increasing and decreasing on [0, 2], given f′(x) = cos(x²).
cards.a: Increasing on (0, √(π/2)); decreasing on (√(π/2), 2), where √(π/2) ≈ 1.253. On [0, 2], x² runs from 0 to 4, and cos(x²) = 0 only where x² = π/2 ≈ 1.571 (the next zero, x² = 3π/2 ≈ 4.71, lies beyond 4). So f' > 0 for x² < π/2 and f' < 0 for π/2 < x² ≤ 4.
cards.h: → zeros of cos(x²) in range, then the signs
cards.n: Treating cos(x²) like cos x puts the zero at x = π/2 ≈ 1.571; the argument is x², so the zero is at x = √(π/2).

cards.q: Determine the intervals on which f is increasing and decreasing, given f′(x) = (x − 1)²(x + 2)(x − 4).
cards.a: Increasing on (−∞, −2) and (4, ∞); decreasing on (−2, 4). f' = 0 at x = −2, 1, 4. The factor (x − 1)² ≥ 0 never changes sign, so f' has the sign of (x + 2)(x − 4): positive for x < −2 and x > 4, negative for −2 < x < 4 (with f'(1) = 0 only for an instant).
cards.h: → sign of each factor; squared factors never flip
cards.n: Flipping the sign at x = 1 is the trap: the squared factor is zero there but never negative, so f keeps decreasing through x = 1.

cards.q: Find the intervals on which $f(x) = \frac{x^{2}}{x-1}$ is increasing and decreasing.
cards.a: Increasing on (−∞, 0) and (2, ∞); decreasing on (0, 1) and (1, 2). $f'(x) = \frac{2x(x-1) - x^{2}}{(x-1)^{2}} = \frac{x(x-2)}{(x-1)^{2}}$. The denominator is positive for x ≠ 1, so f' has the sign of x(x − 2): positive for x < 0 or x > 2, negative for 0 < x < 2 with x ≠ 1. The split at x = 1 is where f is undefined.
cards.h: → quotient rule, sign of the numerator, split at x = 1
cards.n: 'Decreasing on (0, 2)' crosses the vertical asymptote x = 1: f(0.5) = −0.5 but f(1.5) = 4.5, so the answer must be two intervals.

cards.q: Explain why f(x) = x³ is increasing on (−∞, ∞) even though f′(0) = 0.
cards.a: f'(x) = 3x² > 0 for every x ≠ 0, so f is increasing on (−∞, 0] and on [0, ∞). The pieces share x = 0, so for any a < b, f(a) < f(b): f(x) < 0 for x < 0, f(0) = 0, f(x) > 0 for x > 0. One zero of f' with no sign change does not stop f from increasing.
cards.h: → f′ > 0 except at one point → increasing on each side → the sides join at 0 → increasing everywhere
cards.n: 'Increasing on (−∞, 0) and (0, ∞)' is also correct, but saying f stops increasing, or has an extremum, at 0 is wrong.
o: For a < 0 < b, f(a) = a³ < 0 < b³ = f(b), and on each side f' > 0, so every pair a < b satisfies f(a) < f(b).

w.a: f is not increasing at x = 0 because f'(0) = 0.
w.why: one isolated zero of f' does not interrupt increasing

w.a: f has a relative minimum at 0 because f'(0) = 0.
w.why: f' does not change sign, so there is no extremum

w.a: f is increasing because x³ gets bigger.
w.why: restates the claim without using the sign of f'

cards.q: Explain whether f(x) = x³ − 12x should be reported as increasing on [2, ∞) or on (2, ∞).
cards.a: Either is correct. f is continuous at x = 2 and f'(x) > 0 for x > 2, so f(2) < f(x) for every x > 2, and f is increasing on [2, ∞) as well as on (2, ∞). What is never correct is an interval containing a point where f is undefined.
cards.h: → f continuous at 2 → f(2) < f(x) for x > 2 → both forms are true → never include an undefined point
cards.n: Brackets at a point of continuity cost nothing; an interval such as (0, 2) that crosses an asymptote does.
o: Increasing is a statement about pairs of points; every pair (2, x) with x > 2 satisfies f(2) < f(x), so the endpoint may be included.

w.a: It must be (2, ∞), because f'(2) = 0 means f is not increasing at 2.
w.why: f is increasing on an interval, not at a point, and f(2) < f(x) for x > 2

w.a: It must be [2, ∞), because intervals of increase always include the critical points.
w.why: the open interval is equally correct

cards.q: Explain why f(x) = 1/x is not decreasing on (−∞, 0) ∪ (0, ∞), even though f′(x) < 0 at every x in its domain.
cards.a: The test 'f' < 0 on an interval, so f is decreasing' needs an interval, and the domain has a gap at 0. On each piece f is decreasing, but across the gap f(−1) = −1 < f(1) = 1, so a larger x gives a larger value. f is decreasing on (−∞, 0) and on (0, ∞) separately.
cards.h: → the test needs an interval → the domain has a gap at 0 → f(−1) < f(1) → report two intervals
cards.n: Treating the whole domain as one interval of decrease ignores the gap; the pair f(−1) < f(1) disproves it.
o: The MVT, which underlies the test, needs f continuous on [a, b]; for a < 0 < b that fails, so no conclusion about f(a) and f(b) follows.

w.a: Since f' < 0 everywhere, f is decreasing everywhere.
w.why: the domain is not an interval, so the test does not apply across 0

w.a: f is decreasing on (−∞, ∞) except at x = 0.
w.why: f(−1) < f(1), so it is not decreasing across the gap

w.a: f increases at 0 because it jumps from −∞ to ∞.
w.why: f is undefined at 0; nothing happens there to call increasing

cards.q: State the First Derivative Test.
cards.a: Let c be a critical point of f, with f continuous at c. If f' changes from positive to negative at c, f has a relative maximum at c; if f' changes from negative to positive, a relative minimum; if f' does not change sign at c, f has no relative extremum there.
cards.h: → three cases by the sign change of f′
cards.n: 'f'(c) = 0, so there is an extremum' leaves out the test itself; the verdict comes only from how f' changes sign across c.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies a relative maximum on the AP exam.
cards.a: 'f has a relative maximum at x = c because f' changes from positive to negative at x = c.' The sign change of f' is the reason; f'(c) = 0 may be added but is not enough on its own. Name f' explicitly and the x-value, using the function names the question uses.
cards.h: → one sentence: claim, because, sign change of f′
cards.n: 'It changes from positive to negative' or 'the slope goes up then down' is ambiguous about which function; name f' and say where.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies a relative minimum.
cards.a: 'f has a relative minimum at x = c because f' changes from negative to positive at x = c.' Alternatively, by the Second Derivative Test: 'f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, so f has a relative minimum at x = c.' Either way the reason names f' or f'' and the point.
cards.h: → claim + sign change, or f′(c) = 0 with f″(c) > 0
cards.n: 'f''(c) > 0' without f'(c) = 0, or 'f' is negative then positive' with no x-value, is incomplete and loses the justification point.

cards.q: Use the First Derivative Test to classify the critical point of $f(x)=xe^{-x}$.
cards.a: Relative maximum at x = 1 (value 1/e). $f'(x) = e^{-x} - xe^{-x} = e^{-x}(1-x)$, and $e^{-x} > 0$, so f' has the sign of 1 − x: positive for x < 1, negative for x > 1. Since f' changes from positive to negative at x = 1, f has a relative maximum there.
cards.h: → product rule, factor, sign change at the one zero
cards.n: Skipping the product rule gives f' = −e⁻ˣ, which has no zero at all; and the answer needs the sign change, not just f'(1) = 0.

cards.q: The graph of f' is negative for 0<x<2 and positive for 2<x<6, crossing the x-axis at x=2. Identify the x-value of the local extremum of f and classify it.
cards.a: x = 2, a relative minimum. f' changes from negative to positive at x = 2, so f decreases on (0, 2) and increases on (2, 6), and f(2) is less than the nearby values. The graph shown is of f', so its crossing point, not its lowest point, locates the extremum of f.
cards.h: → where f′ crosses 0, and in which direction
cards.n: Reading the lowest point of the graph of f' as the minimum of f is the trap; that point is where f decreases fastest, not a minimum of f.

cards.q: A table gives f'(1)=3, f'(2)=0.5, f'(3)=-1, f'(4)=-4, f'(5)=2. Decide the most likely location of a local maximum of f, and explain your reasoning.
cards.a: Between x = 2 and x = 3. If f' is continuous, f'(2) = 0.5 > 0 and f'(3) = −1 < 0 force f' = 0 somewhere in (2, 3) by the IVT, and there f' changes from positive to negative: the pattern of a relative maximum. (Likewise f' changes from negative to positive in (4, 5): a relative minimum.)
cards.h: → find the + to − switch in the table, then IVT on f′
cards.n: Picking x = 2 (smallest positive f') or x = 4 (most negative f') misreads the table; the maximum sits where f' switches sign (the IVT step is Unit 1).

cards.q:
Classify each critical point of f as a relative maximum, a relative minimum, or neither, using the First Derivative Test.
(a) f′(x) = x²(x − 3)
(b) f′(x) = (x + 1)(x − 2)²
(c) f′(x) = x(x − 2)(x + 3)
(d) f′(x) = eˣ(x − 1)
(e) f′(x) = cos x on (0, 2π)
(f) f′(x) = −(x + 2)³
(g) $f'(x) = (x-1)^{1/3}$
(h) $f'(x) = \frac{x-4}{x^{2}}$, where f is undefined at x = 0
cards.a:
(a) x = 0 → neither (f' < 0 on both sides); x = 3 → minimum (− to +)
(b) x = −1 → minimum (− to +); x = 2 → neither (f' > 0 on both sides)
(c) signs −, +, −, + → x = −3 minimum; x = 0 maximum; x = 2 minimum
(d) eˣ > 0, so the sign is that of x − 1 → x = 1 minimum
(e) x = π/2 → maximum (+ to −); x = 3π/2 → minimum (− to +)
(f) x = −2 → maximum (+ to −)
(g) x = 1 → minimum (− to +)
(h) x = 4 → minimum (− to +); x = 0 is not a critical point, since f(0) is undefined
cards.h: → sign pattern of f′ per line, then the verdict
cards.n: Squared factors, as in (a) and (b), do not flip the sign; odd powers, as in (f) and (g), do.

cards.q: Classify both critical points of $f(x) = x^{2/3}(x-4)$ with the First Derivative Test.
cards.a: Relative maximum at x = 0 (f(0) = 0); relative minimum at x = 8/5 (f(8/5) ≈ −3.283). $f'(x) = \frac{5x-8}{3x^{1/3}}$. For x < 0 the numerator and denominator are both negative, so f' > 0; for 0 < x < 8/5, f' < 0; for x > 8/5, f' > 0. f is continuous at 0, and f' changes + to − there and − to + at 8/5.
cards.h: → signs of numerator and denominator on three pieces
cards.n: Skipping x = 0 because f'(0) does not exist misses the maximum; the First Derivative Test works at a cusp as long as f is continuous there.

cards.q: Determine the x-coordinate of each relative extremum of f, and classify it, given f′(x) = x² − 2ˣ. Use a calculator where needed.
cards.a: Relative maximum at x ≈ −0.767; relative minimum at x = 2; relative maximum at x = 4. f' = 0 at x = 2 and x = 4 (2² = 2², 4² = 2⁴) and, by calculator, at x ≈ −0.767. Test values: f'(−2) = 3.75 > 0, f'(0) = −1 < 0, f'(3) = 1 > 0, f'(5) = −7 < 0. So f' changes + to − at −0.767 and at 4, and − to + at 2.
cards.h: → all three zeros of f′, one test value per piece
cards.n: Finding only 2 and 4 by inspection misses the negative zero near −0.767; graph f' on the calculator before building the sign chart.

cards.q: Determine a and b so that f(x) = x³ + ax² + b has a relative minimum at the point (2, −3).
cards.a: a = −3, b = 1. f is differentiable, so a relative minimum at x = 2 needs f'(2) = 0: f'(x) = 3x² + 2ax gives 12 + 4a = 0, a = −3. The point is on the graph: f(2) = 8 − 12 + b = −3, so b = 1. Check: f'(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2) changes from negative to positive at x = 2, so it is a minimum.
cards.h: → f′(2) = 0 and f(2) = −3, then confirm the sign change
cards.n: Using only f(2) = −3 leaves two unknowns; and without the final check, f'(2) = 0 alone could be a maximum or neither.

cards.q: Explain why f has a relative maximum at x = 1, given that f is continuous on (0, 3), f′(1) does not exist, f′(x) > 0 on (0, 1), and f′(x) < 0 on (1, 3).
cards.a: x = 1 is a critical point: f is defined there and f'(1) does not exist. f' > 0 on (0, 1), so f increases up to x = 1, and f' < 0 on (1, 3), so f decreases after it. Since f is continuous at 1, f(1) is the largest value near 1: a relative maximum by the First Derivative Test.
cards.h: → critical point (f′ undefined) → f′ changes + to − → f continuous at 1 → relative maximum
cards.n: 'No maximum, because f'(1) does not exist' is the error; the test needs a sign change and continuity at c, not f'(c) = 0.
o: The graph rises to a corner or cusp at x = 1 and falls after it, so f(1) is greater than every nearby value.

w.a: f cannot have an extremum at x = 1 because f'(1) is undefined.
w.why: points where f' is undefined are critical points and can be extrema

w.a: f has a maximum at x = 1 because f'(1) = 0.
w.why: f'(1) does not exist, so the stated reason is false

w.a: f has a maximum at 1 because f' is positive.
w.why: one sign is not a sign change, and no interval is named

cards.q: Explain why f(x) = 1/x² has no relative extremum at x = 0, even though f′ changes from positive to negative there.
cards.a: f(0) is undefined, so there is no point of the graph at x = 0 to be a maximum, and x = 0 is not a critical point. The First Derivative Test applies only at a critical point where f is continuous. f' = −2/x³ is positive for x < 0 and negative for x > 0 because f rises toward a vertical asymptote and falls away from it.
cards.h: → f(0) undefined → not a critical point → the test needs continuity at c → an asymptote, not an extremum
cards.n: Reading a sign chart without checking the domain produces a 'maximum at x = 0' for a function that is not defined there.
o: f(x) → ∞ as x → 0 from either side, so f is unbounded near 0; there is no largest value for a maximum to be.

w.a: f has a relative maximum at x = 0 because f' changes from positive to negative.
w.why: f(0) does not exist, so there is no point to be a maximum

w.a: f has a relative minimum at 0 because f' is undefined there.
w.why: an undefined f' makes a critical point only where f is defined

w.a: There is no extremum because f'(0) is not 0.
w.why: the reason is that f is undefined at 0, not the value of f'

cards.q: Explain why 'f′(3) = 0, so f has a relative maximum at x = 3' earns no justification point.
cards.a: f'(3) = 0 only makes x = 3 a critical point, and x³ at 0 shows a critical point can be neither maximum nor minimum. A justification needs a test: 'f' changes from positive to negative at x = 3' (First Derivative Test), or 'f'(3) = 0 and f''(3) < 0' (Second Derivative Test).
cards.h: → f′(3) = 0 → only a candidate → no test named → add the sign change or f″(3) < 0
cards.n: Piling on more critical-point facts (f(3) exists, the tangent is horizontal) does not help; the missing piece is the sign change or the sign of f''(3).
o: A horizontal tangent can belong to a maximum, a minimum, or a point where f keeps increasing, so f'(3) = 0 cannot decide among them.

w.a: f'(3) = 0 and the graph has a horizontal tangent, so there is a maximum.
w.why: a horizontal tangent is the same fact restated

w.a: f'(3) = 0 and f(3) is the largest value.
w.why: asserts the conclusion without a reason

w.a: f'(3) = 0 and f' is positive before 3.
w.why: gives one side only; the sign after 3 decides between maximum and neither

cards.q: Explain the Candidates Test for absolute extrema on a closed interval.
cards.a: For f continuous on [a, b]: list every critical point in (a, b) and both endpoints, evaluate f at each, and compare the values. The largest value is the absolute maximum and the smallest the absolute minimum. The EVT guarantees both exist, and absolute extrema can occur only at critical points or endpoints, so the list is complete.
cards.h: → list candidates, evaluate f, compare values
cards.n: Comparing x-values, or values of f', instead of values of f is a common slip; the test compares the heights f(x) at the candidates.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies an absolute maximum on a closed interval.
cards.a: Show the table of candidate values, then write: 'f is continuous on [a, b]; the candidates are the critical points and the endpoints a and b; f(c) is the largest of these values, so the absolute maximum of f on [a, b] is f(c).' Continuity, a complete candidate list and the comparison each carry weight.
cards.h: → continuity, full candidate list, comparison of values
cards.n: Justifying an absolute maximum only with 'f' changes from + to − at c' is a relative argument; on a closed interval the endpoints must be compared too.

cards.q: Describe how to justify an absolute extremum on an open or unbounded interval.
cards.a: There are no endpoints to evaluate, so argue from f' across the whole interval: if f is continuous, f' > 0 for every x < c in the interval and f' < 0 for every x > c, then f increases up to c and decreases after it, so f(c) is the absolute maximum. If c is the only critical point, a relative extremum there is automatically absolute.
cards.h: → sign of f′ on each whole side of c
cards.n: Plugging in 'endpoints' that are not in the interval (such as f(0) for x > 0) uses values f never takes there; argue from signs or limits instead.

cards.q: Find the absolute minimum of $f(x)=\frac{1}{3}x^{3}-x$ on [0,3].
cards.a: −2/3, at x = 1. f is continuous on [0, 3]. f'(x) = x² − 1 = 0 at x = ±1, and only x = 1 lies in [0, 3]. Candidates: f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1/3 − 1 = −2/3, f(3) = 9 − 3 = 6. The smallest value is −2/3.
cards.h: → critical points in the interval, three values
cards.n: Including x = −1, which lies outside [0, 3], is harmless here but wrong in principle; only candidates in the interval count.

cards.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x) = |x−2|+3 on [−1,5].
cards.a: Absolute minimum 3, at x = 2; absolute maximum 6, at both x = −1 and x = 5. f is continuous on [−1, 5]. f'(x) is −1 for x < 2 and 1 for x > 2, never 0, but f'(2) does not exist, so x = 2 is the only critical point. Values: f(−1) = 6, f(2) = 3, f(5) = 6.
cards.h: → the corner as a candidate, then three values
cards.n: Solving f'(x) = 0 finds nothing here; the only critical point is the corner at x = 2, where f' does not exist.

cards.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of $f(x) = x^{3} - 3x + 1$ on [−2, 2].
cards.a: Absolute maximum 3, at x = −1 and x = 2; absolute minimum −1, at x = −2 and x = 1. f is continuous on [−2, 2]. f'(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1. Values: f(−2) = −8 + 6 + 1 = −1, f(−1) = 3, f(1) = −1, f(2) = 3.
cards.h: → two critical points, two endpoints, four values
cards.n: Each extreme value is attained twice here, once at an endpoint; reporting one location, or skipping the endpoints, loses credit.

cards.q:
Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of each function on the interval.
(a) $x^{2/3}$ on [−1, 8]
(b) x² − 6x + 5 on [0, 5]
(c) √x − x on [0, 4]
(d) eˣ − 2x on [0, 2]
(e) sin x + cos x on [0, π]
(f) $\frac{x}{x^{2}+4}$ on [0, 4]
(g) $xe^{-x/2}$ on [0, 5]
cards.a:
(a) candidates −1, 0 (f' undefined), 8 → values 1, 0, 4 → max 4 at x = 8; min 0 at x = 0
(b) candidates 0, 3, 5 → values 5, −4, 0 → max 5 at x = 0; min −4 at x = 3
(c) candidates 0, 1/4, 4 → values 0, 1/4, −2 → max 1/4 at x = 1/4; min −2 at x = 4
(d) candidates 0, ln 2, 2 → values 1, 2 − 2 ln 2 ≈ 0.614, e² − 4 ≈ 3.389 → max e² − 4 at x = 2; min 2 − 2 ln 2 at x = ln 2
(e) candidates 0, π/4, π → values 1, √2, −1 → max √2 at x = π/4; min −1 at x = π
(f) candidates 0, 2, 4 → values 0, 1/4, 1/5 → max 1/4 at x = 2; min 0 at x = 0
(g) candidates 0, 2, 5 → values 0, 2/e ≈ 0.736, $5e^{-5/2}$ ≈ 0.410 → max 2/e at x = 2; min 0 at x = 0
cards.h: → candidates, their values, max and min per line
cards.n: In (a) the candidate x = 0 comes from f' being undefined; in (b) and (d) an endpoint wins, which a critical-point-only search would miss.

cards.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of f(x) = x + 2 cos x on [0, π].
cards.a: Absolute maximum π/6 + √3 ≈ 2.256, at x = π/6; absolute minimum 5π/6 − √3 ≈ 0.886, at x = 5π/6. f is continuous on [0, π]. f'(x) = 1 − 2 sin x = 0 where sin x = 1/2: x = π/6 and 5π/6. Values: f(0) = 2, f(π/6) ≈ 2.256, f(5π/6) ≈ 0.886, f(π) = π − 2 ≈ 1.142.
cards.h: → solve sin x = 1/2 in the interval, four values
cards.n: Taking only x = π/6 from sin x = 1/2 misses 5π/6, which gives the minimum; list every solution in [0, π].

cards.q: Determine the absolute maximum and minimum values of f on [0, 6], given that f is differentiable, f′(x) = 0 only at x = 1 and x = 4, and f(0) = 3, f(1) = 5, f(4) = −2, f(6) = 4.
cards.a: Absolute maximum 5, at x = 1; absolute minimum −2, at x = 4. f is differentiable, hence continuous on [0, 6], so both extremes exist and occur at critical points or endpoints. Since f' exists everywhere, the critical points are x = 1 and x = 4. Comparing f(0) = 3, f(1) = 5, f(4) = −2, f(6) = 4 gives the result.
cards.h: → candidates from the data, compare four values
cards.n: Dismissing f(6) = 4 'because it is an endpoint' is backwards; it loses only because 5 > 4, and in another problem an endpoint wins.

cards.q: Determine the absolute maximum and minimum values of f on [0, 6], given f(0) = 4, f′ continuous, f′ > 0 on (0, 2), f′ < 0 on (2, 6), and the regions between the graph of f′ and the x-axis having area 5 on [0, 2] and area 7 on [2, 6].
cards.a: Absolute maximum 9, at x = 2; absolute minimum 2, at x = 6. The only critical point is x = 2. The change in f equals the signed area under f': f(2) = f(0) + 5 = 9 and f(6) = f(2) − 7 = 2. Candidates: f(0) = 4, f(2) = 9, f(6) = 2.
cards.h: → build f-values from the areas, then compare
cards.n: Borrows Unit 6 (f(b) = f(a) + ∫f'). Adding the area 7 instead of subtracting it ignores that f' < 0 there, so f falls by 7.

cards.q: Explain why the absolute maximum of f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 3] cannot be found from its critical points alone.
cards.a: The only critical point in [0, 3] is x = 1 (f'(x) = 3x² − 3), and f(1) = −2 is the absolute minimum. The maximum is at an endpoint: f(3) = 18 > f(0) = 0. On a closed interval, absolute extrema occur at critical points or endpoints, so both endpoints must be evaluated.
cards.h: → the one critical point gives a min → the max is elsewhere → endpoints are candidates → f(3) = 18
cards.n: 'No absolute maximum, since the only critical point is a minimum' ignores the endpoints; the EVT guarantees a maximum exists.
o: f' > 0 on (1, 3], so f increases all the way to x = 3; the largest value is reached at the right endpoint.

w.a: The absolute maximum is at x = 1, the only critical point.
w.why: f(1) = −2 is the minimum; a critical point is not automatically a maximum

w.a: f has no absolute maximum because f'(x) = 0 only once.
w.why: the EVT guarantees a maximum on a closed interval

w.a: The maximum is 18 because f is increasing.
w.why: f decreases on (0, 1), and the endpoint comparison is missing

cards.q: Explain why the Candidates Test cannot be used for $f(x) = \frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}$ on [0, 3].
cards.a: The test relies on the EVT, which needs f continuous on [0, 3], and f is undefined at x = 2. Comparing f(0) = 1/4 and f(3) = 1 (f' is never 0) suggests a maximum of 1, but f(x) → ∞ as x → 2, so f has no absolute maximum on [0, 3] at all.
cards.h: → the test needs continuity on [a, b] → f undefined at 2 → f unbounded near 2 → no absolute max
cards.n: Evaluating the endpoints and declaring 'max 1' is the trap; check continuity on the closed interval before trusting the candidate list.
o: Absolute extrema are confined to critical points and endpoints only for a continuous function; a discontinuity inside the interval breaks that guarantee.

w.a: The absolute maximum is 1, at x = 3.
w.why: f takes values far larger than 1 near x = 2

w.a: x = 2 is a critical point, so the maximum is f(2).
w.why: f(2) is undefined, so 2 is not a critical point and has no value

w.a: There are no critical points, so f has no extrema.
w.why: a continuous f with no critical points still has endpoint extrema; the issue is the discontinuity

cards.q: Explain why comparing the values of f at the critical points and endpoints is enough to find the absolute extrema of a continuous f on [a, b], with no sign chart needed.
cards.a: By the EVT, f attains an absolute maximum and minimum on [a, b]. Each occurs at an endpoint or at an interior point, and an interior absolute extremum is also relative, so it lies at a critical point. The candidate list therefore contains both, and the largest and smallest values on it are the answers.
cards.h: → EVT: the extremes exist → interior extremes sit at critical points → the list is complete → compare values
cards.n: Classifying each candidate with the First Derivative Test first is not wrong, only unnecessary; the comparison of values is itself the justification.
o: A sign chart classifies relative behavior; the absolute question is settled by which candidate value is largest or smallest.

w.a: You must first show each critical point is a maximum or a minimum.
w.why: the comparison of values decides without any classification

w.a: The absolute maximum is always at a critical point where f' = 0.
w.why: it can be at an endpoint or where f' does not exist

w.a: Comparing values works on any interval.
w.why: on an open or unbounded interval the extremes need not exist

cards.q: Define concave up and concave down in terms of f' and f''.
cards.a: f is concave up on an interval where f' is increasing; when f'' exists, that is where f''(x) > 0. f is concave down where f' is decreasing, that is, where f''(x) < 0. Geometrically, concave up bends like y = x² and concave down like y = −x².
cards.h: → f′ increasing or decreasing, then the sign of f″
cards.n: Defining concave up as 'f is increasing' mixes up levels: concavity is about the slopes f' increasing, not about f itself.

cards.q: Define a point of inflection.
cards.a: A point on the graph of f where f is continuous and the concavity changes, from up to down or from down to up. If f'' exists near it, f'' changes sign there; f''(c) itself may be 0 or may not exist.
cards.h: → continuity plus a change of concavity
cards.n: Defining it as 'where f''(x) = 0' is the classic error: f''(0) = 0 for x⁴, which has no inflection point.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies a point of inflection.
cards.a: 'The graph of f has a point of inflection at x = c because f'' changes sign at x = c.' An equivalent reason: 'f' changes from increasing to decreasing at x = c' (or the reverse). The change is the reason; f''(c) = 0 is not.
cards.h: → claim + the sign change of f″ (or the turn of f′)
cards.n: 'f''(c) = 0, so there is an inflection point' earns nothing; readers need the sign change of f'' or the change in direction of f'.
