A particle with this position does travel 4π on [0, 2π]: distance traveled and arc length differ exactly when the path retraces itself.

w.a: 4π is the length, so the circumference formula must not apply here.
w.why: the circle is traced twice

w.a: The integral is wrong because the speed should be 1.
w.why: the speed really is 2

w.a: The extra 2π comes from the 2 in 2t, which should be dropped.
w.why: the 2 is real; the issue is the double tracing

cards.q: Justify that 1.440, a student's value for the length of x = t², y = t³ on 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, is reasonable, by comparing it with a length you can find without calculus.
cards.a: The curve runs from (0, 0) at t = 0 to (1, 1) at t = 1, and the segment joining them has length √2 ≈ 1.414, the shortest path between the points. The curve is not a straight line, so its length must exceed √2, and 1.440 does, slightly, since the curve bends gently.
cards.h: → endpoints (0, 0) and (1, 1) → segment √2 ≈ 1.414 is the shortest path → the curve is longer → 1.440 > 1.414
cards.n: An arc length below the endpoint distance is impossible; this check catches a dropped square or a lost factor quickly. (BC only)
o: Any inscribed polygon is shorter than the curve; the one-segment polygon from (0, 0) to (1, 1) gives √2 < 1.440.
An upper bound too: x and y never decrease on [0, 1], so the length is at most Δx + Δy = 2, and 1.440 lies between √2 and 2.

w.a: 1.440 is reasonable because it is close to 1.
w.why: no comparison that bounds the length

w.a: The length should be exactly √2, so 1.440 is wrong.
w.why: √2 is only the straight-line distance

w.a: It is reasonable because arc length is always positive.
w.why: positivity does not check the size

cards.q: Explain why $\int_{a}^{b} \left(\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{dy}{dt}\right) dt$, a student's formula for the length of a parametric curve, is wrong.
cards.a: The square root of a sum of squares is not the sum: √(p² + q²) ≠ p + q unless p or q is 0. The student's integral equals [x(b) − x(a)] + [y(b) − y(a)], a sum of net changes, which is not a length and can be zero or negative for a long curve.
cards.h: → the length element is √(x′² + y′²)dt → √(p² + q²) ≠ p + q → the integral collapses to Δx + Δy, not a length
cards.n: The student's integral is net change in x plus net change in y; a closed curve would get length 0, which exposes the error. (BC only)
o: Test on the segment x = 3t, y = 4t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1: its length is 5, but the student's integral gives 7.
Each small piece is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs x′Δt and y′Δt, and a hypotenuse is shorter than the sum of its legs.

w.a: It's fine as long as dx/dt and dy/dt are positive.
w.why: √(p² + q²) < p + q even then

w.a: The only mistake is a missing square root around the integrand.
w.why: √(x′ + y′) is still wrong

w.a: It's wrong because arc length is ∫(dy/dx) dx.
w.why: that integral is just Δy

cards.q: Explain why the arc length formula $\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + \left(f'(x)\right)^{2}}\, dx$ for y = f(x) is a special case of the parametric formula.
cards.a: The graph y = f(x) is the parametric curve x = t, y = f(t), a ≤ t ≤ b. Then dx/dt = 1 and dy/dt = f′(t), so √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) = √(1 + f′(t)²), and the parametric integral becomes the familiar one with t renamed x.
cards.h: → parametrize x = t, y = f(t) → dx/dt = 1, dy/dt = f′(t) → integrand √(1 + f′²) → the same integral
cards.n: 'Both use a square root' does not show the link; the parametrization x = t earns it (the y = f(x) formula is Unit 8's). (BC only)
o: Factor dx/dt out of the parametric integrand: √(x′² + y′²) = x′√(1 + (dy/dx)²) when x′ > 0, and x′ dt = dx.
Both integrate the length of a small hypotenuse; with x as the parameter, the horizontal leg is dx itself.

w.a: They are different formulas for different kinds of curves.
w.why: misses the parametrization x = t

w.a: Replace dt with dx and they are the same.
w.why: skips why dx/dt becomes 1

w.a: The 1 comes from dy/dt being 1.
w.why: it is dx/dt that equals 1

cards.q: Define a vector-valued function of a real variable t.
cards.a: A vector-valued function assigns to each t in its domain a vector r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩ whose components x(t) and y(t) are ordinary real-valued functions. As a position vector, its tip traces the same curve as the parametric equations x = x(t), y = y(t). Limits, derivatives and integrals are taken component by component.
cards.h: → a vector for each t; calculus component by component
cards.n: Treating r(t) as one number (adding x(t) + y(t), say) is the error; the two components stay separate throughout. (BC only)

cards.q: State the derivative of the vector-valued function r(t) = <x(t), y(t)>.
cards.a: r′(t) = ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩: differentiate each component separately, at every t where both components are differentiable. When r(t) is a position vector, r′(t) is the velocity vector.
cards.h: → componentwise derivative
cards.n: Differentiating the magnitude, or combining the components first, loses the point; product, chain and quotient rules apply inside each component on its own. (BC only)

cards.q: Define the velocity vector of a particle whose position is <x(t), y(t)>.
cards.a: v(t) = r′(t) = ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩. Its direction is the direction of motion, along the line tangent to the path, and its magnitude is the speed. It is a vector, so a velocity answer has two components.
cards.h: → vector of first derivatives
cards.n: Velocity is a vector and speed is a number; giving √(x′² + y′²) when the velocity vector is asked for earns nothing. (BC only)

cards.q: Define the acceleration vector of a particle whose position is <x(t), y(t)>.
cards.a: a(t) = v′(t) = r″(t) = ⟨x″(t), y″(t)⟩, the componentwise derivative of the velocity vector. It measures how the velocity vector changes, in direction as well as in length.
cards.h: → vector of second derivatives
cards.n: Acceleration is not the derivative of speed: a particle moving around a circle at constant speed still has nonzero acceleration. (BC only)

cards.q: State the speed of a particle moving with velocity <x'(t), y'(t)>.
cards.a: Speed = $\sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^{2} + \left(y'(t)\right)^{2}}$, the magnitude |v(t)| of the velocity vector. It is a nonnegative number, not a vector, and it is 0 only when both components of the velocity are 0.
cards.h: → magnitude of the velocity vector
cards.n: Writing x′(t) + y′(t), or |x′(t)| + |y′(t)|, for the speed is the error; speed is the length of the velocity vector. (BC only)

cards.q: A particle has x'(t) = 3t and y'(t) = 4t. Compute its speed at t = 2.
cards.a: 10. At t = 2 the velocity is ⟨3·2, 4·2⟩ = ⟨6, 8⟩, so the speed is $\sqrt{6^{2} + 8^{2}} = \sqrt{100} = 10$.
cards.h: → velocity at t = 2, then its magnitude
cards.n: Adding the components (6 + 8 = 14) is not the speed; square, add, then take the root. (BC only)

cards.q: Identify how to tell when a particle in the plane is at rest.
cards.a: The particle is at rest at time t exactly when both velocity components are 0 there: x′(t) = 0 and y′(t) = 0, so v(t) = ⟨0, 0⟩ and the speed is 0. Solve each equation and keep only the t-values common to both.
cards.h: → both components zero at the same t
cards.n: One zero component means only that the motion is momentarily vertical (x′ = 0) or horizontal (y′ = 0), not that the particle has stopped. (BC only)

cards.q: For $r(t)=<t^{3}, e^{2t}>$, find r'(t) and evaluate it at t=0.
cards.a: r′(t) = ⟨3t², 2e²ᵗ⟩, so r′(0) = ⟨0, 2⟩. Each component is differentiated separately, and the chain rule supplies the 2 in 2e²ᵗ. At t = 0 the particle moves straight up at speed 2.
cards.h: → derivative vector, then a value
cards.n: Dropping the chain-rule factor (writing e²ᵗ as its own derivative) gives ⟨0, 1⟩, wrong in the y-component. (BC only)

cards.q: A particle has velocity vector $<3t^{2}, 4t>$. Compute its acceleration vector at t=2.
cards.a: ⟨12, 4⟩. Differentiating each component of the velocity gives a(t) = ⟨6t, 4⟩, which is ⟨12, 4⟩ at t = 2.
cards.h: → one vector
cards.n: Substituting t = 2 into the velocity first (⟨12, 8⟩) and then differentiating constants gives ⟨0, 0⟩; differentiate before substituting. (BC only)

cards.q: Find r′(t) and r′(1) for r(t) = ⟨t eᵗ, ln(t² + 1)⟩.
cards.a: r′(t) = ⟨(1 + t)eᵗ, 2t/(t² + 1)⟩, so r′(1) = ⟨2e, 1⟩ ≈ ⟨5.437, 1⟩. The x-component needs the product rule, (t eᵗ)′ = eᵗ + t eᵗ; the y-component needs the chain rule, (ln(t² + 1))′ = 2t/(t² + 1).
cards.h: → product rule in one component, chain rule in the other
cards.n: Writing eᵗ as the derivative of t eᵗ drops the product rule; each component follows the ordinary rules, independently of the other. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the acceleration vector a(t) for the position r(t) = ⟨cos 2t, sin 3t⟩, and evaluate it at $t = \frac{\pi}{2}$.
cards.a: a(t) = ⟨−4cos 2t, −9sin 3t⟩, so a(π/2) = ⟨4, 9⟩. First v(t) = ⟨−2sin 2t, 3cos 3t⟩; differentiating again gives a(t). At t = π/2, cos π = −1 and sin(3π/2) = −1.
cards.h: → differentiate twice, component by component
cards.n: Losing a chain-rule factor at either step is the usual error; the factors multiply to 2·2 = 4 and 3·3 = 9. (BC only)

cards.q: Describe the direction of motion at t = 2 of a particle with velocity v(2) = ⟨−3, 1⟩, and give the slope of the line tangent to its path there.
cards.a: It moves to the left (x′(2) = −3 < 0) and up (y′(2) = 1 > 0), along a tangent line of slope 1/(−3) = −1/3, at speed √10 ≈ 3.162. The velocity vector lies along the tangent line and points in the direction of travel.
cards.h: → sign of each component, then the slope
cards.n: Reading the slope −1/3 as 'moving down' is the trap; with x′ < 0 a negative slope means rising as the particle moves left. (BC only)

cards.q:
Estimate the velocity vector and the speed at t = 2.0, with units, for a particle whose position, in meters, is recorded at times t, in seconds:
t · x(t) · y(t)
1.8 · 3.1 · 5.0
2.0 · 3.5 · 5.6
2.2 · 4.1 · 5.8
cards.h: → symmetric difference per component, then magnitude
cards.n: Leaving off units, or giving the speed as a vector, costs the point: each velocity component is in m/s, and the speed is one number in m/s. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain why the velocity vector of a particle points along the line tangent to its path.
cards.a: v(t) = ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ has slope y′(t)/x′(t), which is dy/dx, the slope of the tangent line (if x′(t) = 0 and y′(t) ≠ 0, both are vertical). So v lies along the tangent line, and the signs of its components give the direction of travel along that line.
cards.h: → slope of v = y′/x′ → that is dy/dx → same slope as the tangent line → v lies along it
cards.n: 'Because velocity shows where the particle is going' restates the claim; the slope comparison y′/x′ = dy/dx is what earns it. (BC only)
o: v(t) is the limit of [r(t + h) − r(t)]/h, a chord vector along a secant line, and the secant lines approach the tangent line as h → 0.
Over a short time Δt the displacement is about v(t)Δt, so near that point the particle moves almost exactly along v.

w.a: The velocity vector points where the particle is going, so it must be tangent.
w.why: restates the claim

w.a: The velocity vector is perpendicular to the path because it is a derivative.
w.why: confuses tangent with normal

w.a: It is tangent because its magnitude is the speed.
w.why: a magnitude says nothing about direction

cards.q: Explain why the derivative of r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩ can be found by differentiating each component separately.
cards.a: By definition r′(t) is the limit as h → 0 of [r(t + h) − r(t)]/h = ⟨[x(t + h) − x(t)]/h, [y(t + h) − y(t)]/h⟩. A vector's limit is taken component by component, so the limit is ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ whenever both component limits exist.
cards.h: → vector difference quotient → splits into two scalar quotients → limits taken componentwise → ⟨x′, y′⟩
cards.n: 'Because you can' earns nothing; the reason is that the vector difference quotient splits into two scalar difference quotients. (BC only)
o: Vector subtraction and division by h act on each component separately, so the components never interact and each limit is that component's derivative.
The same argument makes integration componentwise: a Riemann sum of vectors is the vector of the component Riemann sums.

w.a: You differentiate each part because vectors are just two numbers.
w.why: no appeal to the definition

w.a: You differentiate the magnitude √(x² + y²) because that is the vector's size.
w.why: that is the rate of change of distance from the origin

w.a: You need the product rule between x(t) and y(t).
w.why: the components are not multiplied

cards.q: Explain why a particle with position r(t) = ⟨cos t, sin t⟩ moves at constant speed although its acceleration is never the zero vector.
cards.a: v(t) = ⟨−sin t, cos t⟩, so the speed is √(sin² t + cos² t) = 1 for all t. But a(t) = ⟨−cos t, −sin t⟩ has length 1 and is never ⟨0, 0⟩: the velocity keeps turning. Acceleration measures change in the velocity vector, not only in its length.
cards.h: → speed = √(sin² + cos²) = 1 → constant → but v turns → a = ⟨−cos t, −sin t⟩ ≠ 0 → a measures change of direction too
cards.n: 'Constant speed, so zero acceleration' confuses speed with the velocity vector; |a| is not the rate of change of speed. (BC only)
o: v · a = sin t cos t − sin t cos t = 0 for every t: the acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity, turning it without changing its length.
The rate of change of speed is d/dt(1) = 0, while |a(t)| = 1; they are different quantities.

w.a: If the speed is constant, the acceleration must be zero.
w.why: velocity can change direction at constant speed

w.a: |a| = 1, so the particle speeds up by 1 unit per second each second.
w.why: |a| is not the rate of change of speed

w.a: The speed changes because sin t and cos t change.
w.why: the sum of their squares is always 1

cards.q: Explain why the speed of a particle with velocity ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ is √(x′(t)² + y′(t)²) and not x′(t) + y′(t).
cards.a: Speed is the length of the velocity vector. The components x′(t) and y′(t) are perpendicular legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the velocity vector, so by the Pythagorean theorem its length is √(x′² + y′²). The sum x′ + y′ can be 0 or negative for a moving particle.
cards.h: → speed = |v| → components are perpendicular legs → Pythagorean theorem → √(x′² + y′²)
cards.n: A sum of components is not a length: v = ⟨3, −3⟩ would give 'speed' 0 although the particle moves at √18. (BC only)
o: In a short time Δt the particle moves Δx ≈ x′Δt and Δy ≈ y′Δt, a distance √(Δx² + Δy²) ≈ √(x′² + y′²)Δt, so its distance per unit time is √(x′² + y′²).
Counterexample: v = ⟨3, 4⟩ gives speed 5, not 7.

w.a: Speed is x′ + y′ because it adds the horizontal and vertical speeds.
w.why: perpendicular rates combine by Pythagoras

w.a: Speed is |x′| + |y′|, which is never negative.
w.why: still a sum of legs, not the hypotenuse

w.a: Speed is y′/x′, the slope of the path.
w.why: a slope is a direction, not a rate of travel

cards.q: Explain why a particle with velocity v(3) = ⟨0, −2⟩ is not at rest at t = 3, and describe its motion at that instant.
cards.a: At rest requires both components to be 0, and y′(3) = −2 ≠ 0, so the speed is √(0² + (−2)²) = 2, not 0. At t = 3 the particle moves straight down at speed 2: its horizontal motion has momentarily stopped (x′(3) = 0), and the tangent line to its path is vertical.
cards.h: → at rest needs x′ = y′ = 0 → y′(3) = −2 ≠ 0 → speed 2 → moving straight down, vertical tangent
cards.n: 'x′(3) = 0, so it is at rest' is the trap; zero horizontal velocity means vertical motion, not rest. (BC only)
o: The speed |v(3)| = 2 is positive, and a particle with positive speed is moving.
x′(3) = 0 with y′(3) ≠ 0 is exactly the vertical-tangent condition, so the path is vertical there and the particle descends along it.

w.a: The particle is at rest because x′(3) = 0.
w.why: one zero component is not rest

w.a: The particle moves horizontally because the x-component is 0.
w.why: a zero x-component means no horizontal motion

w.a: The particle moves up because its speed is 2.
w.why: speed has no direction; y′ < 0 means down

cards.q: State how to recover position from velocity for a particle in the plane.
cards.a: Add the accumulated change to the known position, component by component: $x(b) = x(a) + \int_{a}^{b} x'(t)\, dt$ and $y(b) = y(a) + \int_{a}^{b} y'(t)\, dt$; as vectors, r(b) = r(a) + $\int_{a}^{b}$ v(t) dt. The integral alone is only the displacement.
cards.h: → initial value plus definite integral, each component
cards.n: Omitting the initial position is the classic slip: the integral of v from a to b is the change in position, not the position. (BC only)

cards.q: A particle has velocity <cos t, 2t> and position (3, 1) at t = 0. Find its position at t = 2.
cards.h: → ordered pair from two accumulations
cards.n: Reporting (sin 2, 4) gives only the displacement; each coordinate needs its starting value added. (BC only)

cards.q: Define the displacement vector of a particle over $a \le t \le b$.
cards.a: The displacement over a ≤ t ≤ b is the vector ⟨$\int_{a}^{b} x'(t)\, dt$, $\int_{a}^{b} y'(t)\, dt$⟩ = ⟨x(b) − x(a), y(b) − y(a)⟩: the net change in position from the starting point to the ending point, whatever the path between.
cards.h: → vector of two definite integrals
cards.n: Displacement can be the zero vector after a long trip; it is not the distance traveled, which integrates the speed. (BC only)

cards.q: Given $v(t)=<2t, 3t^{2}>$ and r(0)=<1,4>, find r(t).
cards.a: r(t) = ⟨t² + 1, t³ + 4⟩. Antidifferentiate each component, ⟨t² + C₁, t³ + C₂⟩, then use r(0) = ⟨1, 4⟩: C₁ = 1 and C₂ = 4.
cards.h: → antiderivative per component, then two constants
cards.n: One constant for both components, or none at all, fails the check r(0) = ⟨1, 4⟩. (BC only)

cards.q: Given $v(t)=<e^{t}, \cos t>$ and r(0)=<2,−1>, find r(t).
cards.a: r(t) = ⟨eᵗ + 1, sin t − 1⟩. Antiderivatives: ⟨eᵗ + C₁, sin t + C₂⟩. From r(0) = ⟨2, −1⟩: e⁰ + C₁ = 2, so C₁ = 1, and sin 0 + C₂ = −1, so C₂ = −1. Check: r′(t) = ⟨eᵗ, cos t⟩ and r(0) = ⟨2, −1⟩.
cards.h: → antiderivative per component, then two constants
cards.n: Setting C₁ = 2 forgets that e⁰ = 1; solve for each constant from the antiderivative's value at t = 0. (BC only)

cards.q: Given $v(t) = <4t^{3}, \sec^{2}t>$ and r(0) = <−1, 2>, find r(t).
cards.a: r(t) = ⟨t⁴ − 1, tan t + 2⟩. Antiderivatives: ⟨t⁴ + C₁, tan t + C₂⟩. From r(0) = ⟨−1, 2⟩: C₁ = −1, and tan 0 + C₂ = 2 gives C₂ = 2.
cards.h: → antiderivative per component, then two constants
cards.n: The antiderivative of sec² t is tan t (sec t tan t is the derivative of sec t); the constants come from r(0), not from v(0). (BC only)

cards.q: A particle has velocity $<3t^{2}, 4\cos t>$ and position (2, -3) at t = 0. Find its position at $t = \pi$.
cards.h: → ordered pair from two accumulations
cards.n: y(π) = y(0) does not mean no vertical motion: y rose while cos t > 0 and fell back while cos t < 0. (BC only)

cards.q: Evaluate $\int_{0}^{1}$ ⟨2t, eᵗ⟩ dt.
cards.a: ⟨1, e − 1⟩ ≈ ⟨1, 1.718⟩. Integrate each component over [0, 1]: $\int_{0}^{1} 2t\, dt = 1$ and $\int_{0}^{1} e^{t}\, dt = e - 1$. The result is a vector; if ⟨2t, eᵗ⟩ is a velocity, it is the displacement over [0, 1].
cards.h: → one definite integral per component
cards.n: Integrating the magnitude √(4t² + e²ᵗ) instead gives the distance traveled, a number, not this vector. (BC only)

cards.q: Find ∫ ⟨cos t, 1/(t + 1)⟩ dt for t > −1.
cards.a: ⟨sin t + C₁, ln(t + 1) + C₂⟩, which can be written ⟨sin t, ln(t + 1)⟩ + C with C = ⟨C₁, C₂⟩ a constant vector. Each component has its own antiderivative and its own constant; for t > −1, ln|t + 1| = ln(t + 1).
cards.h: → antiderivative per component, one constant vector
cards.n: A single scalar + C added to both components is too restrictive; the constant of integration is a vector with two independent entries. (BC only)

cards.q: Find v(t) and r(t) for a particle with acceleration a(t) = ⟨6t, −2⟩, initial velocity v(0) = ⟨1, 3⟩, and initial position r(0) = ⟨0, 5⟩.
cards.a: v(t) = ⟨3t² + 1, 3 − 2t⟩ and r(t) = ⟨t³ + t, 5 + 3t − t²⟩. Integrating a(t) gives ⟨3t² + C₁, −2t + C₂⟩, and v(0) = ⟨1, 3⟩ fixes C₁ = 1, C₂ = 3. Integrating v(t) gives ⟨t³ + t + D₁, 3t − t² + D₂⟩, and r(0) = ⟨0, 5⟩ fixes D₁ = 0, D₂ = 5.
cards.h: → integrate twice, fixing constants at each stage
cards.n: Using r(0) to fix the constants of the first integration mixes the stages: velocity constants come from v(0), position constants from r(0). (BC only)

cards.q: Calculate y(2), using a calculator, for a particle with $\frac{dy}{dt} = \sqrt{1 + t^{3}}$ and y(0) = −2.
cards.a: y(2) ≈ 1.241. $y(2) = y(0) + \int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{1 + t^{3}}\, dt = -2 + 3.2413\ldots \approx 1.241$. The integrand has no elementary antiderivative, so the calculator evaluates the definite integral.
cards.h: → initial value plus a calculator integral
cards.n: Reporting 3.241, the integral alone, gives the change in y, not y(2); the initial value −2 must be added. (BC only)

cards.q:
Approximate x(6) with a trapezoidal sum over the three subintervals shown, given x(0) = 4 meters and these values of a particle's horizontal velocity x′(t), in meters per second, at times t, in seconds:
t · x′(t)
0 · 1.0
2 · 2.5
5 · 4.0
6 · 3.0
cards.h: → trapezoids of unequal width, then add x(0)
cards.n: One width for all three trapezoids ignores the spacing 2, 3, 1; then add x(0) = 4 (trapezoidal sums are borrowed from Unit 6). (BC only)

cards.q: Interpret $\int_{0}^{4} x'(t)\, dt = -3$ in context, for a particle moving in the plane with x and y in meters and t in seconds.
cards.a: Over the first 4 seconds the particle's x-coordinate changes by a net −3 meters: at t = 4 it is 3 meters to the left of where it was at t = 0. The integral is a net change, so the particle may have moved more than 3 meters horizontally in total.
cards.h: → net change in x over the interval, with units
cards.n: 'The particle traveled 3 meters' earns nothing: this is a net change in one coordinate, not a distance, and the sign means left. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain why $\int_{0}^{2}$ v(t) dt alone does not give a particle's position at t = 2.
cards.a: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $\int_{0}^{2}$ v(t) dt = r(2) − r(0), the displacement. Position functions that differ by a constant vector share the same velocity, so the position r(2) = r(0) + $\int_{0}^{2}$ v(t) dt also needs the starting position r(0).
cards.h: → FTC: ∫v dt = r(2) − r(0) → only the change → add r(0) to get r(2)
cards.n: 'The integral of velocity is position' is the trap; it is the change in position, and an answer without r(0) earns nothing. (BC only)
o: Two particles with the same velocity, one starting at the origin and one at (5, 5), have the same integral but different positions at t = 2.
An antiderivative of v(t) carries a constant vector C, and only an initial condition fixes C.

w.a: The integral of velocity is position, so the integral gives r(2).
w.why: it gives r(2) − r(0)

w.a: The position at t = 2 is v(2) times 2.
w.why: rate × time assumes a constant velocity

w.a: You also need the acceleration to find the position.
w.why: velocity plus r(0) is enough

cards.q: Explain why integrating a velocity vector ⟨x′(t), y′(t)⟩ produces two independent constants of integration.
cards.a: Each component is integrated on its own: x(t) = ∫x′(t) dt + C₁ and y(t) = ∫y′(t) dt + C₂, and nothing links the two antiderivatives, so C₁ and C₂ are independent; the constant is a vector ⟨C₁, C₂⟩. Shifting the start horizontally and vertically by any amounts leaves the velocity unchanged.
cards.h: → each component integrated separately → each has its own + C → constant vector ⟨C₁, C₂⟩
cards.n: One shared + C forces equal shifts in x and y, so it cannot match an initial position such as ⟨2, −1⟩ in general. (BC only)
o: The derivative of ⟨C₁, C₂⟩ is ⟨0, 0⟩ for any C₁ and C₂, so every such constant vector gives the same velocity.
An initial position r(0) = ⟨a, b⟩ supplies two equations, one for each constant.

w.a: There is only one constant because there is only one integral sign.
w.why: the integral is taken per component

w.a: The constants must be equal because they come from the same velocity.
w.why: the components are independent

w.a: Definite integrals have no constants, so the constants don't matter.
w.why: the position still needs r(0)

cards.q: Explain why y(π) = y(0), for a particle with y′(t) = 4cos t, does not mean the particle never moved vertically on [0, π].
cards.a: y(π) − y(0) = $\int_{0}^{\pi}$ 4cos t dt = 0 is a net change. On (0, π/2), y′ > 0 and y rises by 4; on (π/2, π), y′ < 0 and y falls back by 4. The particle moved 8 units vertically in all; the rise and the fall cancel only in the net change.
cards.h: → ∫y′ dt = net change = 0 → y′ > 0 then < 0 → rises 4, falls 4 → total vertical movement 8
cards.n: 'Net change 0, so no vertical motion' confuses net change with total change; the integral of |y′(t)| measures the total, here 8. (BC only)
o: Total vertical travel is $\int_{0}^{\pi}$ |4cos t| dt = 8, not |∫ 4cos t dt| = 0.
y′(π/4) = 2√2 ≠ 0, so the particle is moving vertically at that instant.

w.a: Since y(π) = y(0), the particle moved only horizontally.
w.why: net change 0 is not zero motion

w.a: The particle was at rest vertically because the integral is 0.
w.why: the integrand, not the integral, is the instantaneous rate

w.a: The y-coordinate stays constant because cos t averages to 0.
w.why: a zero average does not make y constant

cards.q: Justify that a particle with x′(t) = 3t² + 1 is, at every t > 0, to the right of where it was at t = 0.
cards.a: x(t) = x(0) + $\int_{0}^{t}$ (3s² + 1) ds = x(0) + t³ + t. For t > 0 the integrand 3s² + 1 is positive on [0, t], so the integral t³ + t is positive and x(t) > x(0): the particle is to the right of its starting point.
cards.h: → x(t) = x(0) + ∫x′ → integrand > 0 → integral > 0 for t > 0 → x(t) > x(0)
cards.n: 'x′ is positive' is the idea, but the credit comes from linking it to x(t) − x(0) through the integral, or to x being increasing. (BC only)
o: x′(t) ≥ 1 > 0 for all t, so x is strictly increasing, and hence x(t) > x(0) for every t > 0.
The net horizontal change over [0, t] is t³ + t, which is positive for every t > 0.

w.a: The particle is to the right because x′(0) = 1 is positive.
w.why: one value of x′ does not control later positions

w.a: x(t) = t³ + t is positive, so the particle is right of the y-axis.
w.why: confuses x(t) − x(0) with x(t)

w.a: It moves right because its acceleration 6t is positive.
w.why: the sign of acceleration does not give the direction

cards.q: Explain the error in a student's claim that for v(t) = ⟨2t, 3t²⟩ the displacement over 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 is 2·v(2) = ⟨8, 24⟩, and give the correct displacement.
cards.a: Rate × time works only for a constant rate, and v(t) changes. The displacement is $\int_{0}^{2}$ v(t) dt = ⟨t², t³⟩ from 0 to 2 = ⟨4, 8⟩. Both components increase on [0, 2], so using the largest velocity, v(2), overstates each one.
cards.h: → v varies → rate × time is invalid → integrate each component → ⟨4, 8⟩
cards.n: 2·v(2) uses the velocity at one instant for the whole interval; the integral is required whenever the velocity changes. (BC only)
o: Displacement is average velocity times time, and the average velocity on [0, 2] is ⟨2, 4⟩, not v(2) = ⟨4, 12⟩.
By the FTC, displacement = r(2) − r(0) for any antiderivative r(t) = ⟨t², t³⟩ + C, which gives ⟨4, 8⟩.

w.a: Displacement is velocity times time, so ⟨8, 24⟩ is right.
w.why: the velocity is not constant

w.a: Use v(1) × 2 = ⟨4, 6⟩, since t = 1 is the midpoint.
w.why: the midpoint velocity only estimates the average

w.a: The displacement is |v(2)| × 2 ≈ 25.3.
w.why: that is not even a vector

cards.q: State the total distance traveled by a particle in the plane on $a \le t \le b$.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^{2} + \left(y'(t)\right)^{2}}\, dt$, the integral of the speed over the time interval. The square root is never negative, so no absolute value is needed, and the result is a nonnegative number.
cards.h: → integral of speed
cards.n: Integrating the velocity vector gives displacement, not distance; √(x(t)² + y(t)²) uses positions instead of rates and earns nothing. (BC only)

cards.q: Contrast displacement and total distance for a particle moving in the plane.
cards.a: Displacement is the vector ⟨x(b) − x(a), y(b) − y(a)⟩ = $\int_{a}^{b}$ v(t) dt, the net change in position, which can be the zero vector. Total distance is $\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{(x')^{2} + (y')^{2}}\, dt$, a nonnegative number, the length of the path traveled. The distance is always at least the length of the displacement.
cards.h: → vector versus scalar, net versus total
cards.n: Read the verb: 'how far from its starting point' asks for the length of the displacement; 'how far did it travel' asks for the integral of speed. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain how to decide whether a particle in the plane is speeding up at time t.
cards.a: Find the rate of change of the speed, d/dt √(x′² + y′²) = (x′x″ + y′y″)/√(x′² + y′²): the particle is speeding up where this is positive and slowing down where it is negative. Its sign is the sign of v · a = x′x″ + y′y″, so the dot product of velocity and acceleration gives the same test.
cards.h: → sign of the derivative of speed (equivalently of v · a)
cards.n: 'Positive acceleration' decides nothing in the plane. The dot-product test is equivalent, but the CED does not name it; the speed's derivative is the safe reason. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain how to find when a particle moving in the plane is farthest from the origin on a closed t-interval.
cards.a: Distance from the origin is D(t) = √(x(t)² + y(t)²). On a closed interval D is continuous, so by the Extreme Value Theorem it has a maximum; find the critical points of D, or of D², which has the same maximizer, evaluate at them and at the endpoints, and take the largest value.
cards.h: → candidates test on D(t) or D(t)²
cards.n: Skipping the endpoints misses a maximum that sits at one, as it often does (the candidates test is borrowed from Unit 5). (BC only)

cards.q: A particle has x'(t)=3, y'(t)=4 for $0\le t\le5$. Find the total distance traveled.
cards.a: 25. The speed is $\sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}} = 5$, constant, so the distance traveled is $\int_{0}^{5} 5\, dt = 25$. The path is a straight segment traced without reversing, so 25 is also the length of the displacement.
cards.h: → constant speed times time
cards.n: Rate × time works only because the speed is constant; 3·5 + 4·5 = 35 adds the legs and is never a distance. (BC only)

cards.q: A particle has $x'(t)=t^{2}-4$, y'(t)=t−2. Find the time(s) when the particle is at rest.
cards.a: t = 2. At rest requires x′(t) = t² − 4 = 0 (t = ±2) and y′(t) = t − 2 = 0 (t = 2) together; only t = 2 satisfies both. At t = −2 the velocity is ⟨0, −4⟩: the particle moves straight down there.
cards.h: → solve both, keep the common t
cards.n: Stopping at the zeros of one component (t = ±2) without checking the other is the common error; t = −2 fails y′ = 0. (BC only)

cards.q: A particle has $x(t)=t^{2}$, $y(t)=t^{3}$. Decide whether the particle is speeding up or slowing down at t=1.
cards.a: Speeding up. At t = 1, v = ⟨2t, 3t²⟩ = ⟨2, 3⟩ and a = ⟨2, 6t⟩ = ⟨2, 6⟩; v · a = 2·2 + 3·6 = 22 > 0, so the speed is increasing. Equivalently, the speed √(4t² + 9t⁴) has derivative (4t + 18t³)/√(4t² + 9t⁴) = 22/√13 > 0 at t = 1.
cards.h: → velocity and acceleration at t = 1, then the sign test
cards.n: 'The acceleration is positive' is not a reason in the plane; speeding up needs the derivative of speed (or v · a) to be positive. (BC only)

cards.q: A particle moves along $x=t^{2}$, y=2t. Find the straight-line distance between its positions at t=0 and t=2.
cards.a: 4√2 ≈ 5.657. The positions are (0, 0) at t = 0 and (4, 4) at t = 2, so the distance between them is $\sqrt{4^{2} + 4^{2}} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}$: the length of the displacement ⟨4, 4⟩, shorter than the curved path the particle actually travels.
cards.h: → two positions, then the distance formula
cards.n: Integrating the speed gives the path length (about 5.92), which answers a different question; 'distance between positions' is the straight line. (BC only)

cards.q: A particle moves with $x'(t)=3\cos t$, $y'(t)=3\sin t$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$. Compute the total distance traveled.
cards.a: 3π ≈ 9.425. The speed is $\sqrt{9\cos^{2} t + 9\sin^{2} t} = 3$, constant, so the total distance is $\int_{0}^{\pi} 3\, dt = 3\pi$.
cards.h: → speed simplifies to a constant
cards.n: Integrating the components and adding (0 + 6 = 6) gives a sum of net changes, not a distance. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain how to find the rate of change of speed at time t.
cards.a: Differentiate the speed s(t) = √(x′(t)² + y′(t)²) with respect to t: s′(t) = (x′x″ + y′y″)/s(t), or evaluate s′(t) numerically on a calculator. Its sign answers the question: s′(t) > 0 means speeding up, s′(t) < 0 slowing down.
cards.h: → derivative of the speed function
cards.n: |a(t)| is not the rate of change of speed; answer 'is the speed increasing at t = c?' with the sign of s′(c), not of the acceleration. (BC only)

cards.q: Contrast what |v(t)| and |a(t)| each tell you about a particle's motion.
cards.a: |v(t)| is the speed: how fast the particle moves along its path at time t. |a(t)| is the size of the rate at which the velocity vector changes, in direction as well as length. |a(t)| matches the size of the rate of change of speed only when a is parallel to v; around a circle at constant speed, |a| > 0 while the speed does not change.
cards.h: → speed versus change in velocity
cards.n: The rate of change of speed is d/dt |v(t)|, and that, not |a(t)|, decides speeding up or slowing down. (BC only)

cards.q: Calculate, using a calculator, the total distance traveled for 0 ≤ t ≤ 3 by a particle with velocity v(t) = ⟨ln(t + 1), 2cos t⟩, and its speed at t = 2.
cards.a: Distance ≈ 4.809; speed at t = 2 ≈ 1.378. Distance = $\int_{0}^{3} \sqrt{\left(\ln(t+1)\right)^{2} + 4\cos^{2} t}\, dt \approx 4.809$. Speed at t = 2 = $\sqrt{(\ln 3)^{2} + 4\cos^{2} 2} \approx 1.378$.
cards.h: → integral of speed shown, then calculator values
cards.n: Integrating the components and adding them is not a distance; write the speed integral out before giving the calculator result. (BC only)

cards.q: Determine the time intervals on which a particle with x′(t) = t² − 4t + 3 and y′(t) = 2t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5, is moving to the left.
cards.a: 1 < t < 3. The particle moves left exactly when x′(t) < 0, and x′(t) = (t − 1)(t − 3) is negative between its zeros t = 1 and t = 3 and positive on [0, 1) and (3, 5]. The value of y′(t) does not matter for left or right.
cards.h: → sign chart of x′(t) alone
cards.n: Using the sign of dy/dx or of y′(t) answers a different question; left or right depends only on x′(t). (BC only)

cards.q: Find the rate of change of the speed at t = 1 of a particle with velocity v(t) = ⟨2t, t² − 1⟩, and state whether it is speeding up or slowing down.
cards.a: 2; speeding up. Speed = $\sqrt{4t^{2} + (t^{2}-1)^{2}} = \sqrt{(t^{2}+1)^{2}} = t^{2} + 1$, so its rate of change is 2t, which is 2 > 0 at t = 1: the speed is increasing. Check: v(1) = ⟨2, 0⟩, a(1) = ⟨2, 2⟩, and v · a = 4 > 0.
cards.h: → simplify the speed, differentiate, read the sign
cards.n: Reporting |a(1)| = 2√2 as the rate of change of speed is the trap; the rate is the derivative of the speed, here 2. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the time at which a particle with position ⟨2t, 6 − t²⟩, 0 ≤ t ≤ 3, is farthest from the origin, and that distance.
cards.a: t = 3, at distance 3√5 ≈ 6.708. The squared distance is D² = 4t² + (6 − t²)² = t⁴ − 8t² + 36, with derivative 4t³ − 16t = 4t(t² − 4), zero at t = 0 and t = 2. Candidates: D²(0) = 36, D²(2) = 20, D²(3) = 45. The largest is at t = 3, so D = √45 = 3√5.
cards.h: → candidates test on D², then take the root
cards.n: The critical point t = 2 is the closest point (2√5), not the farthest; the endpoint t = 3 wins (the candidates test is from Unit 5). (BC only)

cards.q: Interpret $\int_{0}^{4} \sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^{2} + \left(y'(t)\right)^{2}}\, dt = 13.1$ in context, for a particle moving in the plane with x and y in meters and t in seconds.
cards.a: The particle travels a total of 13.1 meters along its path during the first 4 seconds, from t = 0 to t = 4. The integrand is the speed in meters per second, and integrating it over seconds gives meters of path, counting every stretch even if the particle doubles back.
cards.h: → total distance, interval, units
cards.n: 'The particle ends 13.1 meters from where it started' confuses distance traveled with displacement; the endpoint can be much closer. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain whether a particle with velocity ⟨−3, 1⟩ and acceleration ⟨2, 1⟩ at t = 1 is speeding up or slowing down, given that both components of its acceleration are positive.
cards.a: Slowing down. The speed changes at the rate (v · a)/|v| = [(−3)(2) + (1)(1)]/√10 = −5/√10 < 0. The large horizontal part of a opposes the leftward motion, so positive components of a do not make the speed grow.
cards.h: → speed′ = (v · a)/|v| → v · a = −6 + 1 = −5 < 0 → speed decreasing
cards.n: 'The acceleration is positive, so it speeds up' is a one-dimensional habit; in the plane the test is the sign of the rate of change of speed. (BC only)
o: v · a < 0 means the angle between v and a exceeds 90°, so a has a component opposite the motion.
Horizontally the particle moves left (x′ < 0) while x″ > 0, so its horizontal speed drops, and that outweighs the small vertical gain.

w.a: Both components of a are positive, so the particle is speeding up.
w.why: the sign of a alone does not decide it

w.a: The speed √10 is positive, so the particle is speeding up.
w.why: speed is always ≥ 0; its rate of change decides

w.a: |a| = √5 is positive, so the speed increases.
w.why: |a| is not the rate of change of speed

cards.q: Explain why a particle with v(t) = ⟨−sin t, cos t⟩ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π has the zero vector as its displacement but travels a distance of 2π.
cards.a: Displacement is $\int_{0}^{2\pi}$ v(t) dt = ⟨cos t, sin t⟩ from 0 to 2π = ⟨0, 0⟩: after one lap of a unit circle the particle ends where it started. Distance integrates the speed √(sin² t + cos² t) = 1 over time 2π, giving 2π; it counts the whole path, which net change cancels.
cards.h: → ∫v dt = net change = ⟨0, 0⟩ after one lap → ∫|v| dt = 1 × 2π → the net cancels, the total does not
cards.n: 'The particle did not move' from a zero displacement is the trap; zero net change allows any amount of travel. (BC only)
o: Distance ≥ |displacement| always, with equality only for straight-line travel without reversing; a closed loop is the extreme case.
With r(0) = ⟨1, 0⟩ the position is ⟨cos t, sin t⟩, which traces the unit circle once, and its circumference is 2π.

w.a: The displacement is 0, so the particle traveled no distance.
w.why: net change is not total travel

w.a: The distance is |∫ v dt| = 0.
w.why: distance integrates the speed

w.a: The distance is 2π because the velocity components add up to 2π.
w.why: the components integrate to 0; the speed integrates to 2π

cards.q: Justify that a particle with position ⟨2t, 6 − t²⟩ on 0 ≤ t ≤ 3 has a maximum distance from the origin, and that it occurs at t = 3.
cards.a: D(t)² = t⁴ − 8t² + 36 is continuous on the closed interval [0, 3], so by the Extreme Value Theorem it has a maximum there, at a critical point or an endpoint. Its critical points are t = 0 and t = 2, and D²(0) = 36, D²(2) = 20, D²(3) = 45, so the maximum is at t = 3, where D = √45.
cards.h: → D² continuous on [0, 3] → EVT: a maximum exists → candidates t = 0, 2, 3 → the largest value, 45, is at t = 3
cards.n: Omitting the EVT's hypothesis (continuity on a closed interval) or the endpoint t = 3 loses the justification (the EVT is borrowed from Unit 5). (BC only)
o: (D²)′ = 4t(t² − 4) is positive on (2, 3], so D² rises to D²(3) = 45, which beats D²(0) = 36, the only other rival.
The same candidates test on D itself picks the same t, because the square root is increasing.

w.a: The maximum is at t = 2 because the derivative is 0 there.
w.why: t = 2 is a minimum of D²

w.a: The distance keeps growing because t² grows.
w.why: D² decreases on (0, 2)

w.a: The maximum is at t = 3 because it is the last time.
w.why: an endpoint must be compared, not assumed

cards.q: Justify that a particle with x′(t) = 6 − 2t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5, is farthest to the right at t = 3.
cards.a: x′(t) = 6 − 2t is positive for t < 3 and negative for t > 3, so x(t) increases on [0, 3] and decreases on [3, 5]. The only critical point is where x′ changes from positive to negative, so x(3) is the greatest x-value on [0, 5]: the rightmost position.
cards.h: → x′ > 0 before t = 3, < 0 after → x increases then decreases → absolute maximum of x at t = 3
cards.n: 'x′(3) = 0' alone is not a justification; the sign change of x′, or a comparison with the endpoints, earns it (Unit 5's extreme-value reasoning). (BC only)
o: Candidates: x(3) − x(0) = ∫₀³(6 − 2t) dt = 9 > 0 and x(5) − x(3) = ∫₃⁵(6 − 2t) dt = −4 < 0, so x(3) exceeds both endpoint values.
x increases on [0, 3] and decreases on [3, 5], so no other time has a larger x-coordinate.

w.a: It is farthest right at t = 3 because x′(3) = 0.
w.why: a zero derivative can be a minimum

w.a: It is farthest right at t = 5, the latest time.
w.why: x decreases after t = 3

w.a: It is farthest right when its speed is largest.
w.why: speed does not locate the maximum of x

cards.q: Explain why the time at which a particle is farthest from the origin can be found by maximizing D(t)² = x(t)² + y(t)² instead of D(t).
cards.a: D(t) = √(D(t)²), and the square root is increasing on [0, ∞), so D(t₁) > D(t₂) exactly when D(t₁)² > D(t₂)². The two functions have their maxima at the same times, and D² avoids differentiating a square root. Take the root at the end to report the distance.
cards.h: → D = √(D²) → √ is increasing → same ordering of values → same maximizing t
cards.n: Reporting the maximum of D² (say 45) as the distance forgets the final square root; the time is shared, the value is not. (BC only)
o: (D²)′ = 2D·D′ and D > 0 away from the origin, so D′ and (D²)′ have the same sign and the same zeros.
Any increasing function of D, such as D², has the same maximizer as D.

w.a: You can square it because squaring doesn't change anything.
w.why: squaring changes values; only the order is kept

w.a: D² is the distance squared, so its maximum is the maximum distance.
w.why: the value still needs a square root

w.a: Squaring works for any function, even negative ones.
w.why: squaring can reverse the order of negative values

cards.q: State the conversions from polar coordinates to rectangular coordinates.
cards.a: x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. Applied to a curve r = f(θ), they give x = f(θ)cos θ and y = f(θ)sin θ, so every polar curve is a parametric curve with parameter θ.
cards.h: → two product formulas
cards.n: Writing x = cos θ and y = sin θ without the factor r, or swapping sine and cosine, is the slip; r multiplies both. (BC only)
x: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ

cards.q: State the conversions from rectangular coordinates to polar coordinates.
cards.a: r² = x² + y² and tan θ = y/x (for x ≠ 0), with θ chosen in the quadrant of (x, y). The inverse tangent alone returns an angle between −π/2 and π/2, so for a point with x < 0, add π.
cards.h: → two relations plus a quadrant check
cards.n: θ = arctan(y/x) without a quadrant check puts every point of the left half-plane on the wrong side of the pole. (BC only)

cards.q: State the formula for $\frac{dy}{dx}$ for a polar curve $r = f(\theta)$.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta}{f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta}$, provided dx/dθ ≠ 0. It comes from x = f(θ)cos θ and y = f(θ)sin θ, each differentiated with the product rule.
cards.h: → parametric slope with θ as the parameter
cards.n: dy/dx is never dr/dθ; dr/dθ only says how fast r changes as θ increases. (BC only)

cards.q: For $r = 1 + \cos \theta$, write $\frac{dy}{d\theta}$.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -\sin^{2}\theta + (1 + \cos\theta)\cos\theta = \cos\theta + \cos 2\theta$. Here y = (1 + cos θ)sin θ, and the product rule gives (−sin θ)(sin θ) + (1 + cos θ)(cos θ); the identity cos²θ − sin²θ = cos 2θ simplifies it.
cards.h: → build y, then the product rule
cards.n: Differentiating r alone (−sin θ) and calling it dy/dθ skips building y = r sin θ; both r and sin θ vary with θ. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain the meaning of a negative value of r in polar coordinates.
cards.a: A point (r, θ) with r < 0 is plotted a distance |r| from the pole in the direction opposite the angle θ, that is, along the ray at angle θ + π. The formulas x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ handle this automatically.
cards.h: → reflect through the pole
cards.n: Plotting |r| along θ itself puts the point in the wrong quadrant; negative r is why roses and limaçons have petals and loops in unexpected places. (BC only)

cards.q: Identify the graph of the polar equation r = a for a constant a > 0.
cards.a: A circle of radius a centered at the pole: every point is at distance a from the origin, whatever θ is. In rectangular form it is x² + y² = a², and it is traced once as θ runs over any interval of length 2π.
cards.h: → name and size
cards.n: Reading r = a as the line y = a confuses r with y; the constant is the distance from the origin. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain how to find the maximum distance from the pole on a polar curve $r = f(\theta)$.
cards.a: Maximize |r| = |f(θ)| over the given θ-interval: find where dr/dθ = f′(θ) = 0 or does not exist, then compare |f(θ)| at those θ-values and at the endpoints; the largest is the maximum distance from the pole. This is the polar question where dr/dθ, not dy/dx, is the right tool.
cards.h: → candidates test on r(θ)
cards.n: Setting dy/dx = 0 finds horizontal tangents, not the farthest point; and where r can be negative, compare |r|. (BC only)

cards.q: For $r=1+\cos\theta$, find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
cards.a: 1. With x = (1 + cos θ)cos θ and y = (1 + cos θ)sin θ: $\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = -1$ and $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = \cos\theta + \cos 2\theta = -1$ at θ = π/2, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-1}{-1} = 1$. The point is (0, 1).
cards.h: → dx/dθ and dy/dθ at π/2, then divide
cards.n: Taking dr/dθ = −sin(π/2) = −1 as the slope gives the wrong sign; build dx/dθ and dy/dθ from x and y first. (BC only)

cards.q: Convert the polar point $\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ to rectangular coordinates.
cards.a: (−2, 2√3). x = 4cos(2π/3) = 4(−1/2) = −2 and y = 4sin(2π/3) = 4(√3/2) = 2√3. The point is in the second quadrant, as the angle 2π/3 requires.
cards.h: → ordered pair
cards.n: Swapping sine and cosine gives (2√3, −2), a fourth-quadrant point; a second-quadrant angle must give x < 0 and y > 0. (BC only)

cards.q: Convert the polar point $\left(6,\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)$ to rectangular coordinates.
cards.h: → ordered pair
cards.n: Leave −3√3 exact; a rounded −5.196 is not an exact conversion, and a sign error shows up as the wrong quadrant. (BC only)

cards.q: Convert the rectangular point $\left(-1,\sqrt{3}\right)$ to polar coordinates with r > 0 and $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$.
cards.a: (2, 2π/3). r = √((−1)² + (√3)²) = 2. The point is in the second quadrant and tan θ = √3/(−1) = −√3, so θ = π − π/3 = 2π/3.
cards.h: → ordered pair
cards.n: The inverse tangent returns −π/3, a fourth-quadrant angle; (−1, √3) is in the second quadrant, so add π. (BC only)

cards.q: For $r=\theta$, find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
cards.a: −2/π. With x = θcos θ and y = θsin θ: $\frac{dx}{d\theta} = \cos\theta - \theta\sin\theta = -\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = \sin\theta + \theta\cos\theta = 1$ at θ = π/2, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{-\pi/2} = -\frac{2}{\pi}$.
cards.h: → product rule twice, then divide
cards.n: Treating r as a constant (dx/dθ = −θ sin θ only) drops a product-rule term; here r = θ varies. (BC only)

cards.q: For $r = 3 + 2\sin\theta$, find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at $\theta = 0$.
cards.a: 3/2. With r′ = 2cos θ: $\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta = 2 - 0 = 2$ and $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = 0 + 3 = 3$ at θ = 0, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3}{2}$.
cards.h: → dx/dθ and dy/dθ at 0, then divide
cards.n: dr/dθ = 2 at θ = 0 is not the slope; build x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ first, then differentiate each. (BC only)

cards.q: Write an equation of the line tangent to the polar curve r = 1 + 2cos θ at the point where $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$.
cards.a: y = 2x + 1. At θ = π/2, r = 1, so the point is (x, y) = (0, 1). With r′ = −2sin θ: dx/dθ = r′cos θ − r sin θ = 0 − 1 = −1 and dy/dθ = r′sin θ + r cos θ = −2 + 0 = −2, so the slope is (−2)/(−1) = 2.
cards.h: → rectangular point, slope from dy/dθ over dx/dθ
cards.n: Using (r, θ) = (1, π/2) as the point in point-slope form is the trap; the point must be rectangular, (0, 1). (BC only)

cards.q: Find the points (x, y) where the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ, 0 ≤ θ < 2π, has a horizontal tangent line.
cards.a: (3/4, 3√3/4) and (3/4, −3√3/4). dy/dθ = cos θ + cos 2θ = (2cos θ − 1)(cos θ + 1) = 0 gives θ = π/3, 5π/3 or π. At π/3 and 5π/3, dx/dθ = −sin θ(1 + 2cos θ) ≠ 0 and r = 3/2. At θ = π, dx/dθ = 0 as well (the cusp at the pole), so the test does not apply there.
cards.h: → factor dy/dθ, check dx/dθ, convert to (x, y)
cards.n: Setting dr/dθ = 0 (θ = 0, π) finds extreme distances from the pole, not horizontal tangents; the test is dy/dθ = 0 with dx/dθ ≠ 0. (BC only)

cards.q: Find $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$ for the polar curve r = 2.
cards.a: $-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{9}$. x = 2cos θ and y = 2sin θ, so dy/dx = (2cos θ)/(−2sin θ) = −cot θ. Its θ-derivative is csc²θ; dividing by dx/dθ = −2sin θ gives d²y/dx² = −1/(2sin³θ). At θ = π/3, sin³θ = 3√3/8, so d²y/dx² = −4/(3√3) = −4√3/9: concave down at (1, √3).
cards.h: → dy/dx in θ, its θ-derivative, divide by dx/dθ
cards.n: Differentiating dy/dx in θ and stopping (csc²θ = 4/3) skips the division by dx/dθ, exactly as in the parametric case. (BC only)

cards.q: Identify why a single point has infinitely many polar representations.
cards.a: Because the angle is periodic and r may be negative: (r, θ) and (r, θ + 2πk) name the same point for every integer k, and so does (−r, θ + π). The pole is (0, θ) for every θ. So two polar curves can meet at a point without sharing any single (r, θ) pair.
cards.h: → θ repeats every 2π → (−r, θ + π) is the same point → the pole has every θ → infinitely many names
cards.n: 'Because θ can be any angle' is too vague; name the 2π periodicity, the (−r, θ + π) form, and the pole. (BC only)
o: The point (2, π/3) is also (2, 7π/3), (2, −5π/3) and (−2, 4π/3), among infinitely many others.
A polar name is a distance and a direction; a direction is defined only up to full turns, and a reversed direction matches a negative distance.

w.a: Because r can be any number, a point has many polar forms.
w.why: a different r is a different point unless θ changes too

w.a: Only the pole has more than one polar representation.
w.why: every point has infinitely many

w.a: Each point has exactly two forms, (r, θ) and (−r, −θ).
w.why: (−r, −θ) is generally a different point

cards.q: Explain what $\frac{dr}{d\theta} > 0$ tells you about a polar curve.
cards.a: It says r is increasing as θ increases. When r > 0 the curve is moving away from the pole; when r < 0, |r| is decreasing, so the curve is moving toward the pole. It says nothing directly about the slope dy/dx of the tangent line.
cards.h: → dr/dθ is the rate of change of r → the sign of r decides away or toward → not a slope
cards.n: 'The curve is increasing' or 'the slope is positive' earns nothing; dr/dθ is the rate of change of r, not of y, and not dy/dx. (BC only)
o: Distance from the pole is |r|, so it increases exactly when r and dr/dθ have the same sign.
dy/dx combines r and dr/dθ through the product rule, so dr/dθ > 0 is compatible with any tangent slope.

w.a: dr/dθ > 0 means the curve is increasing.
w.why: confuses r with y

w.a: It means the tangent line has a positive slope.
w.why: dr/dθ is not dy/dx

w.a: The point is always moving away from the origin.
w.why: fails when r < 0

cards.q: Explain whether the point on r = 1 − 2cos θ is moving toward or away from the pole as θ increases through $\frac{\pi}{6}$, where dr/dθ = 1 > 0.
cards.a: Toward the pole. At θ = π/6, r = 1 − √3 ≈ −0.732 < 0, while dr/dθ = 2sin(π/6) = 1 > 0. The distance from the pole is |r|, and r is negative and increasing toward 0, so |r| is decreasing: the point is getting closer to the pole.
cards.h: → r < 0 and dr/dθ > 0 → r rises toward 0 → |r| falls → moving toward the pole
cards.n: 'dr/dθ > 0, so it moves away' ignores the sign of r; the distance is |r|, so check r and dr/dθ together. (BC only)
o: Moving away requires r and dr/dθ to have the same sign; here their signs are opposite.
d/dθ(r²) = 2r·dr/dθ = 2(1 − √3)(1) < 0, so the squared distance from the pole is decreasing.

w.a: dr/dθ is positive, so the point moves away from the pole.
w.why: ignores that r < 0

w.a: r is negative, so the point is behind the pole and not moving.
w.why: negative r is a real point on the opposite ray

w.a: The point moves toward the pole because r is negative.
w.why: the sign of r alone does not decide it

cards.q: Justify that the polar curve r = 2cos θ has a vertical tangent line at the point where θ = 0.
cards.a: With x = 2cos²θ and y = 2cos θ sin θ = sin 2θ: dx/dθ = −4cos θ sin θ = −2sin 2θ = 0 at θ = 0, while dy/dθ = 2cos 2θ = 2 ≠ 0. dx/dθ = 0 with dy/dθ ≠ 0 means a vertical tangent, at the point (x, y) = (2, 0).
cards.h: → x(θ), y(θ) → dx/dθ = 0 and dy/dθ = 2 ≠ 0 at θ = 0 → vertical tangent at (2, 0)
cards.n: Stating only 'dx/dθ = 0' does not justify it; the nonzero dy/dθ is what rules out 0/0. (BC only)
o: The curve is the circle (x − 1)² + y² = 1, and its rightmost point (2, 0) has a vertical tangent.
dy/dx = 2cos 2θ/(−2sin 2θ) = −cot 2θ, which is unbounded as θ approaches 0.

w.a: dr/dθ = −2sin θ = 0 at θ = 0, so the tangent is vertical.
w.why: dr/dθ is not dx/dθ

w.a: dx/dθ = 0 at θ = 0, so the tangent is vertical.
w.why: also needs dy/dθ ≠ 0

w.a: The tangent is vertical because θ = 0 is on the x-axis.
w.why: a point's location does not give the tangent's slope

cards.q: Explain why the slope formula $\frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}$ gives no value at θ = π for the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ.
cards.a: At θ = π, r = 0 (the pole), and both dy/dθ = cos θ + cos 2θ = −1 + 1 = 0 and dx/dθ = −sin θ(1 + 2cos θ) = 0. The quotient is the indeterminate 0/0, so the formula is silent; the cardioid has a cusp at the pole there, and its behavior needs a limit, not substitution.
cards.h: → r = 0 at θ = π → dy/dθ = 0 and dx/dθ = 0 → 0/0 → the formula is silent → cusp at the pole
cards.n: Calling θ = π a horizontal tangent because dy/dθ = 0 misses dx/dθ = 0; neither tangent test applies at 0/0. (BC only)
o: Wherever r = 0 and dr/dθ = 0 at the same θ, both dx/dθ = r′cos θ − r sin θ and dy/dθ = r′sin θ + r cos θ vanish.
The point reaches the pole and turns back, so ⟨dx/dθ, dy/dθ⟩ is the zero vector at that instant.

w.a: dy/dθ = 0 at θ = π, so the cardioid has a horizontal tangent there.
w.why: dx/dθ = 0 too

w.a: The slope at θ = π is 0/0 = 0.
w.why: 0/0 has no value

w.a: The formula fails because r = 0 means the point does not exist.
w.why: the pole is a point of the curve

cards.q: State the area enclosed by the polar curve $r = f(\theta)$ between the rays theta = a and theta = b.
cards.a: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{a}^{b} r^{2}\, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{a}^{b} \left(f(\theta)\right)^{2} d\theta$, for the region swept by the segment from the pole to the curve as θ runs from a to b, provided the region is traced exactly once on [a, b].
cards.h: → one-half integral of r squared
cards.n: Forgetting the 1/2 or forgetting to square r are the two most common polar-area errors; ∫r dθ is not an area. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the theta-limits for one petal of $r = \sin \left(3\theta\right)$.
cards.a: 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/3. The petal starts and ends at the pole, where r = 0: sin 3θ = 0 at θ = 0 and next at θ = π/3, with r > 0 between, so one petal is traced exactly once on [0, π/3].
cards.h: → two consecutive zeros of r
cards.n: A full 0 to 2π sweep counts all three petals, each twice; one petal runs between consecutive zeros of r. (BC only)

cards.q: Set up the area of one petal of $r = 2\cos \left(2\theta\right)$.
cards.a: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} 4\cos^{2}(2\theta)\, d\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$. r = 0 at θ = ±π/4, with r > 0 between, so that interval traces one petal. With 4cos²2θ = 2 + 2cos 4θ the integral evaluates to (1/2)(π) = π/2.
cards.h: → bounds from the zeros of r, then one integral
cards.n: (2cos 2θ)² is 4cos²2θ; squaring only the cosine (2cos²2θ) halves the area. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area enclosed by the entire circle $r=2\cos\theta$.
cards.a: π. The circle is traced once for −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 4\cos^{2}\theta\, d\theta = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (1 + \cos 2\theta)\, d\theta = \pi$, matching a circle of radius 1.
cards.h: → one tracing, then power reduction
cards.n: Integrating over 0 to 2π traces the circle twice and gives 2π; the bounds must trace the region exactly once. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area enclosed by the cardioid $r = 2 + 2\cos\theta$.
cards.a: 6π. $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi} (2 + 2\cos\theta)^{2}\, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi} (4 + 8\cos\theta + 2 + 2\cos 2\theta)\, d\theta$. Over a full period the cosine terms integrate to 0, leaving (1/2)(6)(2π) = 6π.
cards.h: → expand, power-reduce, full period
cards.n: Squaring as 4 + 4cos²θ drops the cross term 8cos θ; it integrates to 0 here, but only a correct expansion earns the setup. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area of one petal of $r = 3\sin\left(2\theta\right)$.
cards.a: 9π/8. r = 0 at θ = 0 and θ = π/2, with r > 0 between, so one petal is traced on [0, π/2]: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} 9\sin^{2}(2\theta)\, d\theta = \frac{9}{4}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} (1 - \cos 4\theta)\, d\theta = \frac{9\pi}{8}$.
cards.h: → bounds from consecutive zeros, then power reduction
cards.n: Integrating over the full 2π counts all four petals (9π/2); consecutive zeros of r bound a single petal. (BC only)

cards.q: Identify the graphs of $r = a \cos \theta$ and $r = a \sin \theta$.
cards.a: Circles of diameter |a| through the pole: r = a cos θ is centered at (a/2, 0) on the x-axis, and r = a sin θ at (0, a/2) on the y-axis. Each is traced once on any θ-interval of length π, such as [0, π]. Multiplying by r shows it: r = a cos θ becomes x² + y² = ax.
cards.h: → circle, center, tracing interval
cards.n: An area integral over [0, 2π] traces these circles twice and doubles the area; one pass takes an interval of length π. (BC only)

cards.q: Name the curve $r = a \pm a \cos \theta$ (or with sine) and describe its shape.
cards.a: A cardioid: a heart-shaped curve that reaches the pole at exactly one θ in [0, 2π), where it has a cusp, and whose greatest distance from the pole is 2a (for a > 0). It is traced once on [0, 2π] and encloses area (3/2)πa².
cards.h: → name plus two features
cards.n: A cardioid is the limaçon with the constant equal to the coefficient; r = 1 + 2cos θ is not one (it has an inner loop). (BC only)

cards.q: Contrast the three cases of the limacon $r = a + b\cos \theta$ with a, b > 0.
cards.a: For r = a + b cos θ with a, b > 0: a < b gives an inner loop (r becomes negative); a = b gives a cardioid (r just reaches 0); b < a < 2b gives a dimpled limaçon; a ≥ 2b gives a convex limaçon. The ratio a/b, compared with 1 and 2, decides the shape.
cards.h: → four inequality cases
cards.n: Missing the inner loop when a < b wrecks an area: the loop is traced where r < 0, and a 0 to 2π integral counts its area twice. (BC only)

cards.q: Recall the number of petals of the rose curves $r = a\cos \left(n\theta\right)$ and $r = a\sin \left(n\theta\right)$.
cards.a: If n is odd there are n petals, traced once on 0 ≤ θ ≤ π; if n is even there are 2n petals, traced once on 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. Each petal lies between consecutive zeros of r, an angle π/n wide.
cards.h: → two cases by the parity of n
cards.n: Odd n gives n petals and even n gives 2n; getting this wrong ruins both the bounds and the area in a petal question. (BC only)

cards.q: Name the curve $r^{2} = a^{2}\sin \left(2\theta\right)$ and describe it.
cards.a: A lemniscate: a figure-eight of two loops through the pole. The sine form r² = a² sin 2θ has its loops in quadrants I and III, along the line θ = π/4; the cosine form lies along the x-axis. Points exist only where sin 2θ ≥ 0.
cards.h: → name plus shape
cards.n: r² must be nonnegative, so angles where sin 2θ < 0 give no points; for area, r² goes straight in: (1/2)∫a² sin 2θ dθ. (BC only)

cards.q: Identify the graph of $r = a\theta$ for $\theta \ge 0$.
cards.a: An Archimedean spiral: the distance from the pole grows in proportion to the angle, so the curve winds outward from the pole with successive turns evenly spaced, 2πa apart along any ray. It never closes, so an area question must state its θ-bounds.
cards.h: → name plus growth pattern
cards.n: A spiral never encloses a region 'once around'; an area such as (1/2)∫a²θ² dθ needs stated bounds, and extra turns sweep old area again. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area enclosed by the inner loop of the limaçon r = 1 + 2cos θ.
cards.a: π − 3√3/2 ≈ 0.544. r = 0 where cos θ = −1/2, at θ = 2π/3 and 4π/3, and r < 0 between them, which traces the inner loop once. $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{2\pi/3}^{4\pi/3} (1 + 2\cos\theta)^{2}\, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left[3\theta + 4\sin\theta + \sin 2\theta\right]_{2\pi/3}^{4\pi/3} = \frac{1}{2}\left(2\pi - 3\sqrt{3}\right)$.
cards.h: → bounds where r = 0, expand, integrate
cards.n: Integrating over [0, 2π] gives the outer region plus the inner loop again; the loop alone runs between the zeros of r, where r < 0. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the total area enclosed by the lemniscate r² = 4cos 2θ.
cards.a: 4. One loop is traced for −π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/4, where cos 2θ ≥ 0; its area is $\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} 4\cos 2\theta\, d\theta = \left[\sin 2\theta\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = 2$. The other loop (3π/4 ≤ θ ≤ 5π/4) is its mirror image, so the total is 2 · 2 = 4.
cards.h: → r² goes straight in; one loop, then double
cards.n: Integrating 4cos 2θ over [0, 2π] gives 0 because it includes angles where r² < 0; integrate only where cos 2θ ≥ 0. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve r = 2 + sin θ and the rays θ = 0 and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$.
cards.a: 9π/8 + 2 ≈ 5.534. $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} (2 + \sin\theta)^{2}\, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \left(4 + 4\sin\theta + \sin^{2}\theta\right) d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left(2\pi + 4 + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{9\pi}{8} + 2$.
cards.h: → expand the square, integrate term by term
cards.n: Writing (2 + sin θ)² as 4 + sin²θ drops the cross term 4sin θ, which contributes 2 to the area. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain where the factor $\frac{1}{2}r^{2}$ in the polar area formula comes from.
cards.a: A thin wedge between angles θ and θ + Δθ is nearly a circular sector of radius r = f(θ), and a sector of angle Δθ has area (Δθ/2π)·πr² = (1/2)r²Δθ. Summing the wedges and letting Δθ → 0 turns the Riemann sum into (1/2)∫r² dθ.
cards.h: → thin wedge ≈ circular sector → sector area = (Δθ/2π)πr² = ½r²Δθ → sum → integral
cards.n: 'Because it's the formula' earns nothing; the sector area (1/2)r²Δθ is the reason, and it makes the missing 1/2 impossible to forget. (BC only)
o: A full circle is a sector of angle 2π with area πr² = (1/2)r²(2π); a sector of angle Δθ is that fraction of it.
The area element is a thin sector, not a thin rectangle, which is why r enters squared and not as a height.

w.a: The 1/2 is there because each piece is a triangle.
w.why: the pieces are sectors

w.a: r² comes from the Pythagorean theorem, x² + y² = r².
w.why: it comes from the sector's area

w.a: The area is ∫r dθ, and the 1/2 is just a correction.
w.why: ∫r dθ is not an area

cards.q: Explain the risk of integrating a polar area from 0 to $2\pi$ without checking the graph.
cards.a: (1/2)∫r² dθ adds the area swept as θ runs over the interval, so any part of the curve traced twice is counted twice. For r = 2cos θ, [0, 2π] traces the circle twice and gives 2π, double the true π. The bounds must trace the region exactly once.
cards.h: → the integral adds swept area → retraced parts are swept again → counted twice → use one tracing
cards.n: '0 to 2π is a full turn, so it is always right' is the trap; the tracing interval depends on the curve, not on the angle. (BC only)
o: r = sin 3θ traces its three petals on [0, π]; over [0, 2π] each petal is counted twice.
An inner loop (where r < 0) lies inside the outer loop, so a full sweep adds the loop's area on top of an outer region that already contains it.

w.a: Integrating from 0 to 2π always covers the whole curve exactly once.
w.why: some curves are traced in less than 2π

w.a: The only risk is a calculator error.
w.why: the integral itself overcounts

w.a: If the curve repeats, the extra parts cancel out.
w.why: r² ≥ 0, so nothing cancels

cards.q: Justify that the interval 2π/3 ≤ θ ≤ 4π/3 traces the inner loop of r = 1 + 2cos θ exactly once.
cards.a: r = 1 + 2cos θ = 0 exactly when cos θ = −1/2, at θ = 2π/3 and 4π/3, and on (2π/3, 4π/3), cos θ < −1/2, so r < 0. The curve leaves the pole at 2π/3, stays on the negative-r side (plotted opposite θ), and returns at 4π/3: one closed loop, traced once.
cards.h: → r = 0 at 2π/3 and 4π/3 → r < 0 between → pole to pole on the negative side → one inner loop
cards.n: Bounds chosen by eye from a sketch earn nothing; solve r = 0 and check the sign of r between the solutions. (BC only)
o: On the rest of [0, 2π], r > 0, which traces the outer loop; r changes sign only at these two angles.
The loop's points have r ≤ 0, so they lie on the rays opposite 2π/3 to 4π/3, around the positive x-axis near the pole.

w.a: The inner loop is traced for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π because it is the smaller part.
w.why: r > 0 on most of that interval

w.a: The loop runs from π/2 to 3π/2, where cos θ < 0.
w.why: r < 0 needs cos θ < −1/2

w.a: Negative r means those points are not on the curve, so the loop is elsewhere.
w.why: negative r is plotted opposite θ

cards.q: Explain why $\frac{1}{2}\int r^{2}\, d\theta$ gives a positive area even on an interval where r < 0.
cards.a: The integrand is r², which is positive wherever r ≠ 0, whatever the sign of r. A negative r plots the point at distance |r| on the opposite ray, and the wedge swept there has area (1/2)|r|²Δθ = (1/2)r²Δθ, so the integral still adds positive areas.
cards.h: → r² ≥ 0 → each wedge has area ½|r|²Δθ = ½r²Δθ → a sum of positive areas
cards.n: Taking |r| or flipping signs 'because r < 0' is unnecessary: squaring handles it, and a negative area signals a setup error elsewhere. (BC only)
o: The inner loop of r = 1 + 2cos θ has r < 0 for 2π/3 < θ < 4π/3, yet (1/2)∫r² dθ over that interval is π − 3√3/2 > 0.
Distance from the pole is |r|, and |r|² = r², so the sector area depends only on the distance.

w.a: When r is negative the area comes out negative, so take the absolute value.
w.why: r² is never negative

w.a: You must use (1/2)∫|r| dθ when r < 0.
w.why: that is not an area formula

w.a: Negative r gives no area because those points are behind the pole.
w.why: they are real points on the opposite ray

cards.q: Explain why one petal of the rose r = 3sin 2θ has area 9π/8, given that its total area is $\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi} 9\sin^{2}(2\theta)\, d\theta = \frac{9\pi}{2}$.
cards.a: n = 2 is even, so the rose has 2n = 4 petals, all traced once on [0, 2π]. The petals are congruent (each is the first rotated by a multiple of π/2), so they have equal areas, and one petal is (9π/2)/4 = 9π/8, matching (1/2)∫ of 9sin²2θ from 0 to π/2.
cards.h: → n = 2 is even → 4 congruent petals traced once on [0, 2π] → equal areas → divide by 4
cards.n: Dividing by 2 ('two petals since n = 2') gives 9π/4; even n doubles the petal count. (BC only)
o: Direct check: (1/2)∫₀^{π/2} 9sin²2θ dθ = (9/4)∫₀^{π/2}(1 − cos 4θ) dθ = 9π/8.
r² = 9sin²2θ has period π/2, so each petal's interval of length π/2 contributes the same integral.

w.a: n = 2, so there are 2 petals, each of area 9π/4.
w.why: even n gives 2n petals

w.a: Each petal is 9π/2 because the formula already gives one petal.
w.why: [0, 2π] sweeps all four

w.a: One petal is 9π/2 divided by 2π.
w.why: divides by the angle, not by the petal count

cards.q: State the area of the region between two polar curves with outer radius R(theta) and inner radius r(theta) on a to b.
cards.a: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{a}^{b} \left(R(\theta)^{2} - r(\theta)^{2}\right) d\theta$, where R(θ) ≥ r(θ) ≥ 0 on [a, b]: the outer curve's squared radius minus the inner curve's, integrated over the angles of the region.
cards.h: → one-half integral of a difference of squares
cards.n: Subtract the squares, never square the difference: R² − r², not (R − r)², which undercounts the area. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain how to find the theta-values where two polar curves intersect.
cards.a: Set the two expressions for r equal and solve for θ in the relevant interval. Then check the pole separately: if each curve has r = 0 for some θ, possibly different θ-values, both pass through the pole, an intersection the equation misses. A sketch also reveals points reached as (−r, θ + π) on one curve.
cards.h: → solve r₁ = r₂, then check the pole
cards.n: Solving r₁ = r₂ alone misses pole intersections and points that the two curves reach under different (r, θ) names. (BC only)

cards.q: State the general method for setting up the area of a region inside one polar curve and outside another.
cards.a: Find the intersection angles, then decide which curve is farther from the pole on each θ-interval by testing one θ in it. Integrate (1/2)(R² − r²) over each interval where the region lies inside the outer curve R and outside the inner curve r, splitting wherever the roles switch or the boundary changes.
cards.h: → intersections, outer vs inner, split where roles change
cards.n: Sketch first: which curve is outer can change at each intersection angle, and one integral over the whole range then subtracts the wrong way. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain how symmetry can shorten a polar area computation.
cards.a: If the region is symmetric about a line through the pole (often the x-axis, when r depends on cos θ), integrate over the half on one side and double the result. Confirm the symmetry from the equation first: r(−θ) = r(θ) gives symmetry about the x-axis.
cards.h: → halve the interval, double the value
cards.n: Assumed symmetry that is not there is a common source of a factor-of-two error; check r(−θ) = r(θ), or the graph, before doubling. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area inside $r=4\sin\theta$ and outside r=2.
cards.a: 4π/3 + 2√3 ≈ 7.653. The curves meet where 4sin θ = 2, at θ = π/6 and 5π/6, and 4sin θ > 2 between them. $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6} \left(16\sin^{2}\theta - 4\right) d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left[4\theta - 4\sin 2\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{8\pi}{3} + 4\sqrt{3}\right)$.
cards.h: → intersection bounds, outer squared minus inner squared
cards.n: Squaring the difference, (4sin θ − 2)², is the classic error; the integrand is (4sin θ)² − 2². (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area inside $r = 2\cos\theta$ and outside r = 1.
cards.a: π/3 + √3/2 ≈ 1.913. The curves meet where 2cos θ = 1, at θ = ±π/3, and 2cos θ > 1 between them. $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} \left(4\cos^{2}\theta - 1\right) d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left[\theta + \sin 2\theta\right]_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2\pi}{3} + \sqrt{3}\right)$.
cards.h: → intersection bounds, outer squared minus inner squared
cards.n: The region is symmetric about the x-axis, so twice the integral from 0 to π/3 also works; forgetting to double that half is the risk. (BC only)

cards.q: Contrast the setup for finding the area INSIDE BOTH $r=1+\cos\theta$ and r=1 with the setup for area inside one curve and outside the other.
cards.a: Inside both: on each θ-interval the boundary is whichever curve is nearer the pole, so add (1/2)∫r_small² dθ piece by piece, splitting at the intersection angles (θ = ±π/2 here, where 1 + cos θ = 1). Inside one and outside the other: one (1/2)∫(R² − r²) dθ over the angles where R is outside r. For these curves, inside both is 5π/4 − 2.
cards.h: → nearer curve piece by piece versus a difference of squares
cards.n: Writing R² − r² for the region inside both subtracts where it should add; the shared region is bounded by the nearer curve on each interval. (BC only)

cards.q: Find all points of intersection of the polar curves r = 1 + cos θ and r = 3cos θ.
cards.a: (3/4, 3√3/4), (3/4, −3√3/4), and the pole (0, 0). Setting 1 + cos θ = 3cos θ gives cos θ = 1/2, so θ = ±π/3 with r = 3/2, which converts to x = 3/4, y = ±3√3/4. The pole lies on both curves (r = 0 at θ = π on the first, at θ = π/2 on the second), at different θ, so the equation misses it.
cards.h: → solve r₁ = r₂, convert, then check the pole
cards.n: Stopping at θ = ±π/3 misses the pole; each curve reaches r = 0, at different angles, so the pole is a third intersection. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area of the region inside both r = 1 + cos θ and r = 1.
cards.a: 5π/4 − 2 ≈ 1.927. The curves meet at θ = ±π/2. For −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 the circle is nearer the pole, giving half the unit disk, π/2. For π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 3π/2 the cardioid is nearer: $\frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} (1 + \cos\theta)^{2}\, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - 4\right) = \frac{3\pi}{4} - 2$. Total: π/2 + 3π/4 − 2.
cards.h: → split at the intersections, nearer curve on each piece
cards.n: One integral of (1/2)((1 + cos θ)² − 1) gives the region inside the cardioid and outside the circle instead, 2 + π/4. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area of the region inside r = 1 + cos θ and outside r = 1.
cards.a: 2 + π/4 ≈ 2.785. The cardioid is outside the circle where 1 + cos θ > 1, that is, for −π/2 < θ < π/2. $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \left[(1 + \cos\theta)^{2} - 1\right] d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \left(2\cos\theta + \cos^{2}\theta\right) d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left(4 + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
cards.h: → bounds where the cardioid is outer, then R² − r²
cards.n: Bounds of 0 to 2π subtract the circle where it lies outside the cardioid; the region exists only where 1 + cos θ > 1. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area of the region inside both circles r = 2sin θ and r = 2cos θ.
cards.a: π/2 − 1 ≈ 0.571. The circles meet at θ = π/4 (the point (1, 1)) and at the pole. For 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4, r = 2sin θ is nearer the pole; for π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, r = 2cos θ is. By symmetry about θ = π/4, $A = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/4} 4\sin^{2}\theta\, d\theta = \left[2\theta - \sin 2\theta\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1$.
cards.h: → split at π/4, nearer curve on each piece
cards.n: Taking the farther circle on each piece gives the union, not the lens; inside both means the nearer curve, split at θ = π/4. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area of the region inside r = 2 + 2cos θ and outside r = 3.
cards.a: 9√3/2 − π ≈ 4.653. The curves meet where 2 + 2cos θ = 3, at θ = ±π/3, and (2 + 2cos θ)² − 9 = −3 + 8cos θ + 2cos 2θ. So $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} \left(-3 + 8\cos\theta + 2\cos 2\theta\right) d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left[-3\theta + 8\sin\theta + \sin 2\theta\right]_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} = \frac{1}{2}\left(9\sqrt{3} - 2\pi\right)$.
cards.h: → intersection bounds, expand, integrate
cards.n: Subtracting 3 instead of 3² = 9 inside the integral is the slip; both radii are squared before subtracting. (BC only)

cards.q: Find the area of the region inside both r = 3cos θ and r = 1 + cos θ.
cards.a: 5π/4 ≈ 3.927. They meet at θ = ±π/3 and at the pole. For |θ| ≤ π/3 the cardioid is nearer the pole; for π/3 ≤ |θ| ≤ π/2 the circle is. By symmetry about the x-axis, $A = \int_{0}^{\pi/3} (1 + \cos\theta)^{2}\, d\theta + \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} 9\cos^{2}\theta\, d\theta = \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{9\sqrt{3}}{8}\right) + \left(\frac{3\pi}{4} - \frac{9\sqrt{3}}{8}\right) = \frac{5\pi}{4}$.
cards.h: → split at π/3, nearer curve on each piece, double
cards.n: Running the circle's piece to θ = π instead of π/2 retraces it: r = 3cos θ is traced once on [−π/2, π/2], and r < 0 beyond π/2. (BC only)

cards.q: Explain why the area between two polar curves uses $\frac{1}{2}\int (R^{2} - r^{2})\, d\theta$ and not $\frac{1}{2}\int (R - r)^{2}\, d\theta$.
cards.a: The region is the area swept by R minus the area swept by r: (1/2)∫R² dθ − (1/2)∫r² dθ = (1/2)∫(R² − r²) dθ. A wedge of it is a slice of a ring, not a sector of radius R − r; since (R − r)² = R² − 2Rr + r², the wrong form drops 2r(R − r) ≥ 0 and undercounts.
cards.h: → region = outer sector − inner sector → ½∫R² − ½∫r² → ½∫(R² − r²); a ring slice is not a sector of radius R − r
cards.n: (R − r)² would fit only a sector of radius R − r at the pole, and the region is not one; it sits between two arcs. (BC only)
o: Check with circles R = 2 and r = 1 over [0, 2π]: the ring has area 4π − π = 3π, but (1/2)∫(2 − 1)² dθ gives only π.
A thin wedge of the region is an annular sector, whose area is (1/2)(R² − r²)Δθ.

w.a: Subtracting the radii first and then squaring is simpler and gives the same area.
w.why: (R − r)² ≠ R² − r²

w.a: You square the difference because area always squares the radius.
w.why: the two sectors are squared separately

w.a: The two forms differ only when the curves cross.
w.why: they differ whenever r > 0 and R > r

cards.q: Explain why the circles r = 2sin θ and r = 2cos θ intersect at two points, although solving 2sin θ = 2cos θ on [0, π) gives only θ = π/4.
cards.a: Both circles pass through the pole: r = 2sin θ has r = 0 at θ = 0, and r = 2cos θ has r = 0 at θ = π/2. The pole is one point with many names (0, θ), so the curves meet there at different θ-values, which setting the r's equal cannot find. The intersections are (1, 1) and the pole.
cards.h: → equal r at equal θ finds (1, 1) → each curve reaches r = 0 at a different θ → the pole is shared → two intersections
cards.n: Reporting one intersection is the trap; always check the pole separately, since r₁(θ) = r₂(θ) finds only points reached at the same θ. (BC only)
o: In rectangular form the circles are x² + y² = 2y and x² + y² = 2x; subtracting gives y = x, and then x = 0 or x = 1: the points (0, 0) and (1, 1).
The equation r₁(θ) = r₂(θ) finds points where the curves are at the same place at the same angle, a stricter condition than meeting.

w.a: They meet only once, at θ = π/4, because that is the only solution.
w.why: the pole is missed

w.a: They also meet at θ = 5π/4, the other solution of tan θ = 1.
w.why: there both give r = −√2, which is (1, 1) again

w.a: Circles always meet in two points, so there must be another.
w.why: circles can meet in 0, 1 or 2 points

cards.q: Explain why the area inside both r = 1 + cos θ and r = 1 must be split into two integrals rather than written as one.
cards.a: The region inside both is bounded, on each ray, by whichever curve is nearer the pole. For −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 that is the circle r = 1 (1 + cos θ ≥ 1); for π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 3π/2 it is the cardioid. The boundary switches curves at θ = ±π/2, so each piece gets its own (1/2)∫r² dθ.
cards.h: → inside both = nearer curve on each ray → the nearer curve switches at θ = ±π/2 → one integral per piece
cards.n: One integral with one curve, or a difference of squares, cannot follow a boundary that switches curves; split at the intersection angles. (BC only)
o: Equivalently, area inside both = area of the circle − area inside the circle but outside the cardioid, which also needs the intersection angles.
